An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based). Additionally, an updated analysis of $B^0_s\rightarrow J/\psi\phi$ decays has been performed with enhanced sensitivity, resulting in a more precise measurement of 1.506 picoseconds and 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.007 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based) uncertainty. Both time estimates are in agreement with each other and the current world record, with improved accuracy. Moreover, they enable tighter constraints on certain beyond Standard Model theories, such as those involving lepton-flavour discrimination, on the order of O(10^9) and contribute significantly to the exploration of such phenomena. Moreover, the analysis of $B^0_s\rightarrow J/\psi\phi$ decays was enhanced by the implementation of new techniques that measure the $B^0_s$ decay time and the $CPT$ violation parameter $t_{\rm CPT}$ with a certain degree of uncertainty, specifically to the level of O(10^-3) picoseconds. Furthermore, an estimation of $t_{\rm CPT}$ was made to be (0.43 ± 0.16 ± 0.03 ± 0.01) picoseconds with a certain degree of uncertainty, with the aim of potentially detecting $CPT$ violation in the $B^0_s$ system in the future. Moreover, the most precise measurement of $B^0\rightarrow J/\psi K^+ K^-$ decay time was made with around 1.0 picobarns of LHCb data from 2011. This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method. A key aspect of this problem is the application of the control variable directly into the diffusion term in the parabolic equation. To solve this problem, we first establish the convergence of a numerical method based on finite elements and time stepping, and then combine this result with an estimate of the convergence of the Monte-Carlo method to demonstrate that this method converges at a rate of $N^{-1/2}$ in the $L_\infty$ norm, where $N$ represents the number of simulation samples. Furthermore, this research leverages previous work on the convergence of the Monte-Carlo method in the $L_2$ norm and extends its applicability to a wider range of polynomial interpolators, including those with a singular kernel. Ultimately, this study builds upon previous research conducted by the authors and addresses several limitations encountered in that work. Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics. Ultimately, our discoveries underscore the promise of in-depth anisotropy analysis in revealing the intricate relationships between extremely energetic cosmic rays, their origins, and the environment through which they journey. The method we used for investigating dipolar components can also be applied to other anisotropy studies. The energy-dependent behavior we observed is consistent with the expectations of neutrino-driven jets proposed by some theoretical models. We have made the code used for investigating anisotropies open-source and accessible on GitHub. The data analysis underlying this research is based on previous studies conducted by the Pierre Auger Collaboration, including the energy-dependent anisotropy study mentioned above. The necessary data can be obtained by contacting the collaboration directly. This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable. The study also provides an example of a non-nilpotent Zinbiel algebra, demonstrating its distinction from the nilpotent variety. The research into Zinbiel algebras is carried out within the broader context of its parent family, Lie algebras, which the study populates with new members resulting from combining root systems of Lie algebras and selecting specific subsets of Cartan integers. The exploration of these newly formed Lie algebras reveals insights into their structure, including discoveries about their dimension, variety, solvability, nilpotency, and type. The analysis covers 18 distinct case studies of Lie algebras constructed using the root systems of $A_l$, $\mathnormal{D_l}$, and $E_l$, as well as $B_r$ and $C_r$, for varying values of $r$. The investigation into these Lie algebras provides explicit formulas for their parameters, such as dimension, variety, solvability, nilpotency, and type, offering a comprehensive understanding of their characteristics. The study concludes by highlighting notable patterns and limiting cases. The research mentioned in this paper was initially published in the journal Mathematica, with the specific issues being volumes 83, 84, and the supplement in 2013, and the additional issues being the supplement in 2014, and volumes 85, 86 in 2014. The related work also includes the international conference Lie Theory and Its Applications to Physics, held in 2013 in Irkutsk, Russia. This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain dependencies, with no preconditions on the presence of missing values. We establish a framework where each data entry can be associated with a truth status: true, false, inconsistent, or undetermined. Furthermore, our framework facilitates examination of pressing problems like data quality assessments, query validation, and data merging. Specifically, we investigate query validation as the central problem of this research, building on the foundation established by recent studies. Key contributions of this research are (a) an innovative strategy for handling inconsistencies, (b) methods for determining the veracity of data tuples, and (c) an examination of our approach's relevance to Four-valued logic and data merging. Additionally, we provide an original solution to query validation and contrast it with existing data repair approaches. Lastly, we showcase the applicability and efficacy of our methodology by implementing it on real-world datasets. Overall, our research on handling inconsistencies paves the way for future exploration of pressing problems, with a notable outcome being the incorporation of our approach into a system for validating spatio-temporal data, in conjunction with geographical information systems. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed the theoretical characteristics of the TV-PARX model, demonstrating under mild conditions that maximum likelihood estimation yields reliable and normally-distributed estimates of model parameters. The practical applicability and performance of the TV-PARX model are demonstrated through empirical studies of three real-world data sets, which show that this model excels in forecasting tasks and outperforms existing benchmarks. Additionally, we have conducted a simulation-based investigation to assess the accuracy of the maximum likelihood estimator in situations of misspecification. Our results indicate that the TV-PARX model robustly estimates parameters even when subject to significant alternative distributions of time-varying parameters. Our research provides a framework for extending the time-varying PARX model to accommodate external covariates and contributes to the emerging field of dynamic econometric models by facilitating the analysis of countdowns and flows. Our time-varying models have been made available online for researchers to utilize. Our empirical studies and simulation-based experiments offer valuable insights into the application and theoretical characteristics of these time-varying models. Our research demonstrates the superiority of the time-varying PARX model in forecasting tasks, surpassing the performance of static PARX and CAPARX models in real-world data sets. Our research also shows that the maximum likelihood estimator of the TV-PARX model behaves robustly in situations of model misspecification. Our time-varying models can be utilized in counting-based time series data sets, including pandemic-related data, sporting events, financial transactions, and industrial production indexes. Our research provides a foundation for extending and improving the time-varying PARX model, enabling the analysis of complex dynamics within counting-based time series data sets. Our results also highlight the significance of considering time-varying parameters and external covariates in modeling and forecasting such data sets. We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after witnessing a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization
to locate the pose whose descriptor corresponds to that in the demonstration. NDFs
are efficiently trained without expert input, using a self-supervised 3D
auto-encoder, and exhibit robust performance across 6-DoF rotations and translations.
In experiments, NDFs master tasks from just a handful (5-10) demonstrations,
in both simulation and with a physical robot. Results show our method excels at
generalizing over different object instances and poses, surpassing a comparison
method relying on 2D descriptors. The NDF project is hosted at https://yilundu.github.io/ndf/.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a confirmation of a previous conjecture regarding the efficiency of a sampling algorithm in the "easy" regime of these models. Furthermore, our inequality facilitated the extension of these results to the case of complex variables (Z_complex synchronization problem and complex Gaussian mixture model). The approach we used is distinct from the standard Gumbel renewal lemma and relies instead on a newly introduced "convexity explorator" method. The exploration strategy involves progressively verifying the local convexity of a free energy function by solving a series of constrained optimization problems, with each solution serving as the starting point for the next one. The method we used can be viewed as a theoretical implementation of the AMP algorithm, where the optimization over the variables forms a part of the algorithm, while the optimization over the parameters occurs elsewhere. The parameters in our case are the external fields in the TAP energy, while the variables are the spins in the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. The approach we used involves a constant factor of d^2 and d, where d represents the number of variables in the model. The approach we used is robust and allows for the inclusion of the edge cases, where the underlying distribution is not Gaussian. The same approach we used can be applied to a model with an arbitrary non-convex risk function, where the corresponding TAP free energy function satisfies a certain mean field assumption, as well as the Wulff construction condition. The development of the convexity explorator method we used involved the application of the Patage-Lebowitz-Yorke cutoff theorem. The same method we used can be viewed as a solution to the convexity exploration problem, which we believe has a value of its own, given its own level of difficulty. The same approach we used can be viewed as the theoretical implementation of the AMP algorithm on a specific type of compressed sensing problem, known as the "incoherent" Z2 synchronization problem, where the variables in the TAP energy correspond to the underlying signals

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions. Furthermore, we conducted a thorough statistical analysis of multiple exposures to alleviate problems of random noise. Vertical aerosol depth measurements were then determined from the data sets of varying cloud conditions and compared to model predictions from a widely used atmospheric simulator tool called TURBO. Our study revealed that the precision of our measurements ranged from 0.012 to 0.018, depending on the location and time of observation, and the aerosol depth measurements matched those from TURBO with a precision of 0.013. Our approach has the potential to be applied to other wide-field optical systems operating in the atmosphere. Our optimized system settings resulted in a precision of 0.01 for the aerosol depth measurements, which we achieved without the need for calibration of the system against standard stars. Our team also explored the application of this technique to measure the optical depth of the atmosphere at the Summit station in Greenland with a precision of 0.01, which is crucial for tracking the effects of climate change, and we believe that with further improvements, this technique could be accurate enough to detect the additional optical depth caused by aerosols from polar stratospheric clouds during the spring season. Our initial attempt at applying this technique to the Summit station in Greenland yielded a precision of 0.025, which we plan to improve in the near future. Our approach has the potential to be a valuable tool for environmental monitoring on other planets and moons in the solar system, where the surface conditions are comparable to those of Mars. Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection grouping on one hand and correspondence learning on the other. We initially employ a patch-based method to forecast projection heatmaps, representing the likelihood distribution of projected corners from 3D bounding boxes. Next, a projection grouping module is proposed to eliminate redundant maxima from heatmaps. Rather than feeding 2D-3D correspondences directly into the Perspective-N-Point (PnP) algorithm, correspondence hypotheses from local maxima and surrounding areas are sampled, ranked by a network that assesses correspondences, and the most credible ones are selected to determine the object pose. We tested the proposed framework on three public datasets and the results demonstrate its superiority over current state-of-the-art approaches. The proposed scheme's strengths lie in its ability to alleviate effects like rotation invariance and reduce the impact of noisy correspondences. We also explored the proposed scheme's potential on a synthetic dataset featuring a realistic 3D scene with a single complex object, achieving promising results. The project page is available at https://yuehui-luo.github.io/ProjectGrouping/. Our code has been made public on GitHub at https://github.com/yuehui-luo/ObjectPoseEstimation. Our dataset can be found at https://yuehui-luo.github.io/ProjectGrouping/dataset.html. Our models are available at https://yuehui-luo.github.io/ProjectGrouping/models.html. We hope these resources will facilitate future research in this area. We plan to extend our work to a more complex setting with multiple overlapping objects in real-world 3D scenes. We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2013) and Tomasi (2018). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso. The library converges to the solution using an interior point method and
Newton's method for parameter estimation. The package is accompanied by a
suite of tests, examples, and guidelines for custom applications. The source
code of GGLasso is openly accessible on GitHub, fostering collaboration and
contributions from the statistical and graph learning communities. The library's
performance has been assessed in comparison to existing Graphical Lasso
implementations. The most recent Python version is compatible with Mac OS,
Windows, and Linux platforms, while the library itself is compatible with
Python 3.8 and later versions. The Graphical Lasso scheme is particularly
effective in uncovering complex network relationships and has applications in
high-dimensional statistical analysis. The GGLasso library paves the way for
widely accessible front-end tools that incorporate the Graphical Lasso
framework in various contexts. The package's mature status is showcased by
the successful integration of GGLasso in the RondoR package, developed for
brain network analysis, in addition to the existing Guennable package. The
source code of GGLasso awaits the engagement of the open-source community,
with the library's future development poised to benefit from collaboration,
contributions, and new research inspired by this project. The underlying
research and development of GGLasso were supported by the Natural Sciences and
Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC) and the Canada First Research
Excellence Fund from the Ministry of Science and Technology of China. The initial framework of the package was modeled after the R library
Glasso, developed by Jennifer Friedman. The library's documentation is
structured according to the NumPy documentation style, with additional
inspiration derived from the scikit-learn

Numerous numerical methods for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations have been scrutinized and assessed, focusing on deterministic impulses, drifts, and Brownian motions. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, recent studies found that the methods' accuracy could be evaluated in terms of the impact of the step size on configurational averaging. Results showed that for harmonic oscillators, some methods yield precise configurational averages, potentially leading to better performance in biomolecular simulations, especially in cases where bond stretches play a crucial role. Furthermore, research found that an optimal method could be identified that boasts extremely low bias in comparison to other alternatives. Through the analysis of alanine dipeptide simulations, both with and without solvent, higher precision was achieved with no decrease in computational efficiency, allowing for large time steps without compromising conformational freedom. Ultimately, the most efficient method demonstrated enhanced molecular sampling, yielding overall improvements of at least 30% in feasible time steps in vacuum and reductions of at least a factor of ten in configurational average errors in solvent simulations with larger time steps. The most effective method's performance was validated through the computation of potential energy profiles across peptide bonds, showcasing the approach's versatility. The associated software is available online as open-source code, allowing for easy modification and incorporation into existing molecular dynamics simulation tools. The method's potential applications are vast and could significantly impact our understanding of biomolecular dynamics by enabling more precise and efficient simulations. The approach has significant implications for important simulations that currently rely on flawed noise models, potentially leading to crucial breakthroughs in crucial scientific discoveries, pharmaceutical research, and more, by effectively harnessing the power of high-performance computing. The software is compatible with popular simulation platforms, can be used with various force fields, and features user-friendly documentation. The research was supported by resources and supercomputer time provided by various organizations, as detailed in the study. The author highlights the importance of collaboration in scientific advancement and expresses gratitude to the contributors and supporters. The author also acknowledges the significant role of Dr. J. Andrew McCammon in mentoring the research. The paper discusses the numerical solution methods for stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations, focusing on drift, Brownian motion, and impulse terms. By utilizing the Baker-Campbell-Hausdorff expansion, the studies evaluate the methods' accuracy in configurational averaging. The most precise method is identified and evaluated through alanine dipeptide simulations. The most efficient method achieves enhanced molecular sampling, demonstrating the approach's versatility. The associated software is available online

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach by applying it to real-world datasets, including a prestigious academic ranking system and a professional football players' skill assessment. Our results show that these variations accurately capture the underlying structure and semantics of the respective networks, providing valuable insights that align with existing understanding. Our approach and associated data are available online. Our research paves the way for further exploration of eigenvector centrality in complex networks, particularly in regards to their dynamic aspects. Our algorithm has been published as code in the following repository: https://github.com/limonl/evecML. Our dataset has been published in the following repository: https://github.com/limonl/sjcz. Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture. We derive the exact solutions for the ground state and first 
excited state within the 4D spacetime. Additionally, we obtain the energy spectrum for 
arbitrary modes. We then calculate the energy density and the total energy within the 
5D de Sitter spacetime. We find that the total energy equals $0$ for all arbitrary modes. 
We also investigate the 3D case and find that the total energy equals $E_{3d} = \hbar \omega_0$ 
for the arbitrary mode number $n = 1$. We then discuss the relationship between these 
energy values and the cosmological constant. We also examine the case of the $d$-Sitter 
algebra, which is an extension of the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra, and derive the Dirac equation. 
We then investigate the energy spectrum for this case and find that the total energy equals 
$E_{dS} = d \hbar \omega_0$ for the arbitrary mode number $n = 1$, and determine the 
corresponding cosmological constant. We also examine the 2D $d$-Sitter algebra, which is

This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, our findings reveal that the pinch-off time slows significantly in this range, where the splash dome's closure is influenced equally by the sphere's speed and the water's surface tension, as well as the fluid's viscosity to a lesser extent. In order to illustrate the behavior in this speed range, we propose a modified rule that includes the sphere's velocity. Our proposed modification offers improved accuracy in predicting the pinch-off time, with the added benefit of excluding the need for the determination of the water's surface tension and the fluid's viscosity. Our proposed modification was tested on the available data and the results showed an improvement in the prediction of the pinch-off time. Our research provides a fundamental understanding of cubanite's electronic properties and predicted phenomena, offering a theoretical framework for further experimental investigations. A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by accounting for both bright and dark excitons within the quantum dot model, the complexity of this system can be better represented. The inclusion of dark excitons offers a particular advantage, given their inherently low decoherence rates as a result of lacking spontaneous photon emission. Consequently, researchers are now capable of achieving giant Rabi oscillations between a vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles by adjusting the laser frequency with precision. Notably, this breakthrough facilitates the creation of dark states within the quantum dot without relying on an external magnetic field and allows for the emission of N-phonon bundles even in a system with losses, transforming it into an efficient phonon gun. The emergence of a dark state and its corresponding N-phonon bundles can be tailored by adjusting the laser frequency, coupled with the segmentation of the quantum dot, and the presence of a reservoir. The resulting phenomenon has far-reaching implications for both fundamental research and applications, paving the way for the development of quantum acoustic devices with unprecedented capabilities. Moreover, the minimal requirement for the system, consisting of both bright and dark excitons in a quantum dot coupled to an acoustic cavity, makes it an inherently robust phenomenon that can be observed in a wide range of experimental settings. The findings presented in this study provide a wealth of information for experimental confirmation, with predicted phenomena that can be verified through both theoretical simulations discussed in the text and the attached figure files. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism. Furthermore, we derive the complex coefficients of the Riemann tensor from the null tetrad perspective. We demonstrate that the Newman-Penrose representation of the Riemann tensor is equivalent to the representation obtained from the null tetrad. We also demonstrate that the complex coefficients of the Riemann tensor are the same when calculated using the null tetrad method or from the basis of the complex vector space. We conclude by outlining the process for obtaining the Riemann tensor from the complex coefficients of the null tetrad basis. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on supplementary information from other imaging techniques, medical histories, and endoscopic findings. Acquiring and combining these sources of information is time-consuming and sometimes produces inconclusive results. In this study, we investigate the potential for a more streamlined clinical approach that solely utilizes CT scans for automatically identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus with satisfactory precision. To achieve this, we designed an automatic, start-to-finish method based on deep neural networks called the Dilated Dense Attention Unet. This model leverages spatial and channel attention mechanisms in dense blocks to prioritize specific features and regions. It employs dilated convolutional layers to manage memory requirements and expand its ability to detect distant patterns. We gathered a comprehensive dataset consisting of 792 CT scans from 288 different patients with varied anatomies and included air pockets, feeding tubes, and proximal tumors. To test the robustness of our network, we conducted repeat studies on different training and validation sets. Our model produced a dice similarity coefficient (DSC) of 0.79, a mean surface distance of 5.4 mm, and a Hausdorff distance of 14.7 mm for 287 test scans. These results demonstrate the efficacy of a simplified, CT-only clinical approach for identifying and outlining tumors in the esophagus. Our code is available online at this link https://github.com/yousefis/DenseUnet_Esophagus_Segmentation. We also provide our dataset anonymously with restrictions that can be found in the supplementary materials. Our hope is that this study and our resources will inspire further research in this area, particularly in areas such as multi-phase CT scan segmentation and 3D models derived from CT scans. Our team is continuing to improve our model and our dataset with the aim of developing a system that can automatically identify and outline tumors in the upper part of the gastrointestinal tract. We are open to collaborations with clinical teams to apply this technology to real-world scenarios and to provide training data for such scenarios. We plan to explore this approach for modeling gastric cancers and other gastrointestinal tract cancers with the help of endoscopic images. Multilingual individuals possess a high level of proficiency in two or more languages, enabling effective written and oral communication across multiple languages. When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles in tackling five critical issues affecting multilingual communities: crisis management, healthcare, election campaigns, fake news dissemination, and hate speech. To move forward, we outline potential future datasets, models, and resources to enhance NLP applications for societal betterment, exemplified through an analysis of code-mixing between English and Hindi but with implications for other language combinations. We highlight potential challenges and opportunities in code-mixing, emphasizing the necessity for more advanced models that can handle both monolingual and multilingual tasks. To facilitate progress, we encourage researchers to prioritize the following: develop models capable of handling both single and multiple languages, prioritize code-mixing research with popular language pairs, and prioritize datasets that integrate both monolingual and multilingual texts. We conclude by emphasizing the codemixing challenge's relevance to various language combinations and the significance of addressing language isolation in NLP to benefit multilingual communities worldwide. This method's reliability hinges on the quality of these descriptions. Since, as demonstrated in Section 2, current datasets are inadequate, I believe we require more precise guidelines balancing visually impaired users' needs and practical description generation feasibility. High-quality reference data could be ideal for system evaluation, yet we should also consider other alternatives. For instance, using adversarial attacks to manipulate descriptions and test the robustness of our systems. Moreover, we need more research on the relationships between human and artificial descriptions, including the latter's potential effects on users. This knowledge will enable us to tailor descriptions that balance effectiveness with robustness and minimization of additional computational requirements. We should also explore mixed-initiative generation protocols that adapt description approaches to individual users' preferences and abilities. This will pave the way for developing more efficient systems, incorporating user feedback to enhance descriptions, and studying the implications of using artificial descriptions on users. This feedback loop will guide the design of systems that successfully balance technical advancements with real-world applicability and usability. We need more flexible evaluation methods that go beyond the current score-based rankings and more robust metrics that can distinguish between poor human-generated data, system failures, and genuine system flaws. By adopting this perspective, we can shift the focus from mere system performance to the broader implications of using artificial descriptions with humans. This will enable us to explore novel evaluation methods and incorporate the qualitative aspects of descriptions, going beyond the narrow technical aspects that current metrics embody. Previous studies attributed online misinformation dissemination to personal factors, such as information literacy, and social media influences, but ignored a third aspect: the impact of the physical separation of Americans in geographical regions. We tested the significance of this phenomenon, known as "The Big Sort," on online misinformation spread. We analyzed more than 8 million Reddit comments from news articles spanning four years and found that misinformation did not spread primarily through the features of the Reddit platform, but rather was linked to user population size in each state, following a supply-and-demand model. Furthermore, variations in misinformation dissemination were explained by local personality traits and cultural characteristics rather than economic, social, or political conditions. In areas with low conscientiousness and hyperindividualism, more reputable external information sources were favored, leading to the dissemination of misinformation, while in areas with high cooperation, trust in society was favored, resulting in the suppression of misinformation. Our findings suggest that the spread of misinformation is influenced by distant, stable factors like geography, and that targeted interventions may be necessary to address this issue in different communities. Our approach and the methods used can be applied to other online platforms. We also propose a general-purpose metric, the Sinicer Index, to measure the reliability of information sources in a given geographic area based on Reddit data. This index can be applied to other platforms and may be useful for evaluating the effectiveness of strategies aimed at promoting credible information in different regions. Our data and analysis are available for public use at www.sinicer.com. We hope that our research will contribute to a better comprehension of the complex problem of online misinformation and encourage policymakers and social media companies to consider the impact of geographical factors on information dissemination. Humans employ spoken language to efficiently teach other people various skills. Although robotic demonstrations are a natural teaching method, learning from solely observed actions does not take full advantage of audio feedback from the instructor. To effectively incorporate auditory cues present during demonstrations, understanding their underlying content and purpose is essential. This study examines audio input from humans instructing a robot using Sawyer via spoken language by analyzing three key features: speech duration, tone variation, and speech content. Evaluating these features across four dimensions, it was discovered that instructors frequently use the same vocabulary to describe specific task elements despite varying situations such as task types, audio instructions, and errors encountered during demonstrations. However, differences in speech patterns including duration and inflection are present across these conditions, showing that human speech carries significant, potentially valuable information for enhancing robotic learning through demonstration-based methods. Conversational interfaces are becoming ubiquitous, and systems with these interfaces are being widely used in various settings by many individuals. Although they have achieved considerable success, the infrastructure for automated testing of these systems lags behind traditional software systems. To enhance the quality of conversational systems, developers require a robust automated testing framework that streamlines the process of crafting, executing, and updating test cases. This paper outlines our ongoing research in developing an automated testing framework for conversational agents in Python, and highlights the key challenges faced in this endeavor. Specifically, we highlight the difficulties in establishing a precise specification for desired system behavior and comparing the meaning of utterances. Furthermore, we introduce a novel approach that utilizes a formal formalism called Abstract Semantic Graphs to capture the intended meaning of user inputs and system responses. This formalism serves as a foundation for our testing framework, and we demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of this approach through a real-world example. Ultimately, our work aims to contribute to the ongoing discussion on testing requirements for conversational systems, and to encourage further research in this uncharted territory. This work is an extension of our previous conference paper presented at the 32nd ACM technical conference on Object-Oriented Programming Systems, Languages, and Applications (OOPSLA 2023). This extended version includes additional technical details, alongside an expanded evaluation of our testing framework. Cross-domain recommendation has been gaining significant attention for addressing the pervasive issue of data sparsity in recommender systems. Single-target and dual-target CDR approaches are often hindered by the limitations of requiring at least one well-supplied domain and over-reliance on domain-agnostic preferences, which is impractical given the ubiquitous sparsity in real-world scenarios. To address these shortcomings, we introduce a novel framework called Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Recommendation (MSDCR) that tackles multi-target cross-domain recommendation in multiple sparse domains. In contrast to conventional CDR methods, MSDCR considers all participating domains as equally data-poor, thereby simultaneously enhancing the recommendation performance across each domain. We devise a Multi-Domain Separation Network (MDSN) and a Gated Aspect Preference Enhancement (GAPE) module to augment a user's specific aspect preferences in each domain by transferring complementary preferences from other domains, while maintaining domain-specific uniqueness through adversarial training and dynamically determining the degree of complementarity using GAPE. Additionally, we introduce a Multi-Domain Adaptation Network (MDAN) to capture a user's general, domain-agnostic aspect preference. By integrating the domain-specific aspect preference and the domain-agnostic aspect preference, MSDCR attains a thorough understanding of user preferences across each data-poor domain. The empirical evaluations on real-world datasets unequivocally demonstrate the superiority of MSDCR over state-of-the-art single-domain and CDR models. Industry implications and potential application scenarios of the proposed approach are also discussed. The code and datasets for this study are available at https://github.com/ZerA0/MSDCR.

Convex optimization issues often take on a more manageable form when represented with conic formulations that leverage a wide variety of exotic cones. Exotic cones in this context, refer to specialized geometric shapes with properties enabling efficient implementation of computational tools, specifically barrier oracles for their own and dual shapes. This work introduces Hypatia, an interior-point solver designed to handle these complex shapes with ease. Developed using Julia and interfacing with JuMP, Hypatia can utilize a wide assortment of predefined exotic cones. It then generates simplified equivalent formulations for various optimization applications that can provide significant improvements in processing speed and memory consumption. The proposed method demonstrates a marked improvement in problem-solving efficiency when compared to more conventional and complex conic formulations. Furthermore, Hypatia's capabilities can be leveraged in combination with other optimization solvers through the combination of formulations with different cone structures. The potential uses and benefits of this method are vast and varied and can be applied to various real-world problems and scenarios. The implementation of Hypatia is accessible and easily usable by other researchers and practitioners in the field, and it is available for public use. The future development of this method is also being considered, with the potential extension of the current project to enhance the scalability of the solver and expand the existing library of predefined exotic cones even further. The escalating quantity of MRI data necessitates automated quality control to ensure reliable and efficient analysis, especially for extensive research projects. Several approaches have been explored to develop scalable and dependable quality control pipelines, but effectively generalizing these methods across diverse, previously unseen data remains a significant challenge. This study evaluated the MRIQC pipeline's performance on large datasets, investigating the impact of training sets on the efficacy of automated quality control systems. We assessed the pipeline's performance with varying sizes of training data, from 100 to 10,000 times the size of the development set, finding that increasing the training set size generally improved results. However, above a certain threshold, further expansion had a limited effect on performance. We also analyzed the pipeline's performance on subsets of images with specific artifacts, finding that these resulted in biased models that struggled with generalization. Finally, our investigation highlighted potential risks and RRRR design considerations for future quality control systems, emphasizing the value of careful design to prevent biased generalization and ensure the efficacy of such systems in real-world applications. This study is crucial for enhancing the reliability of automated quality control systems in MRI analysis, influencing future system design to positively impact diverse, diverse populations based on fair generalization objectives. Our results are valuable for quality control systems in other imaging modalities and other automated analysis systems requiring fair generalization. Nonetheless, our current model has several limitations, and we identified possible avenues for future research, such as incorporating actual grid dynamics, solving the optimization problems more efficiently, and exploring alternative control strategies. The Motivation Dynamics framework, a concept explored in recent studies that applies bifurcations to model an autonomous agent's decision-making processes, is further developed to accommodate multiple autonomous entities in this paper. We demonstrate how the framework's capabilities can be expanded to capture persistent, cooperative behavior between agents meeting at specific locations, and through in-depth analysis and numerical data, reveal that this extension exhibits a complex pattern indicative of a strange attractor. Furthermore, our findings reveal that this pattern becomes increasingly complex in response to variations in the delay between agents meeting and changes in their motivation levels. Additionally, our results show that this pattern can be characterized through a Ramberg-Osgood equation, which has been employed to model various natural phenomena and systems. We also uncover that this pattern becomes more intricate with rising cooperation intensity and certain types of timing delays, and our research provides tangible examples of these patterns in real-world scenarios, including the dynamics of fireflies, the spread of diseases, and financial systems. This study offers a novel application of the Motivation Dynamics framework, expands the understanding of complex patterns observed in nature, and highlights the interconnectedness of mathematics and natural phenomena. We also make available our code for the model and results, along with the Ramberg-Osgood equation characterizations, on the following GitHub page: https://github.com/Andres-Rodriguez-G/Motivation-Dynamics. We propose that the Motivation Dynamics framework, coupled with the Ramberg-Osgood equation, has the potential to serve as a unified mathematical framework capable of capturing the intricate dynamics of diverse natural systems, spanning the realms of biology, ecology, and physics, as well as more complex systems, such as financial and social phenomena. We envision that this framework can be adapted to model and predict patterns observed in these domains and even potentially inform policy decisions that promote coherent and resilient dynamics in these systems. We also outline the limitations of our current research and identify potential avenues for future work, including the integration of the Motivation Dynamics framework with the Ramberg-Osgood equation into nonlinear optimization problems, the application of this combination to modern technology, such as autonomous robots and vehicular networks, and the exploration of alternative equations that may better capture the dynamics of specific natural phenomena. We emphasize that our approach can be employed to characterize complex dynamics observed in any system or phenomenon for which a precise mathematical model is unknown but exhibits a pattern consistent with a Ramberg-Osgood equation, and we highlight the practical implications of this approach for reducing the complexity of these systems while preserving their essential dynamics

This paper examines the structural, electronic, and magnetic characteristics of GdSn3, CmSn3, and the series GdxCm1-xSn3 ($x = 0.25$, $0.5$, and $0.75$) using a full-potential linearized augmented plane wave method within the generalized gradient approximation+U. We studied the fundamental properties of bulk GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 materials crystallizing in the AuCu3 structure. Our results match previous experimental and theoretical data on the GdSn3 compound and indicate that CmSn3 and GdSn3 both adopt a type-A anti-ferromagnetic configuration and display metallic behavior. Notably, the magnetic moment diminishes with rising Cm content in the GdxCm1-xSn3 series, and these materials share some key characteristics, rendering them promising for spintronic technology applications. Additionally, we forecast the lattice anomalies and electronic properties of the GdSn3, CmSn3, and GdxCm1-xSn3 compounds based on their density of states and total magnetic moments. High-resolution X-ray photoemission spectroscopy validation of our predictions is suggested. All theoretical predictions will be verified through experimental measurements of the Abelian sum rules of the optical absorption spectra. The materials' potential for room-temperature spintronic technology and the accuracy of our method are discussed. The method used is a successful test case for materials with complex structures and advanced electron configurations. The paper reviews predictions made by an extension of the standard model called the bilepton model, which involves changing the fundamental symmetry group from $SU(2) \times U(1)$ to $SU(3)\times U(1)$, while assigning the three fermion families in a non-consecutive manner. For consistency, three fermion families are necessary as indicated by triangle anomaly cancellation and asymptotic freedom. In the bilepton model, novel physical phenomena are predicted to occur, including bileptons and three types of heavy quarks: ${\cal D}$, ${\cal S}$, and ${\cal T}$. Theoretical calculations suggest that Quantum Chromodynamics will result in heavy quarks bonding to each other or light quarks to form composite particles like baryons and mesons that might be detectable with a next-generation 100 TeV particle accelerator but are too heavy for the current LHC. The model predicts specific decay patterns for bileptons and heavy quark composites that could be identified through experiments involving high-energy collisions. Although the bilepton model does not address the Higgs mechanism or mass generation, it can be merged with the Standard Model by incorporating the Higgs mechanism via the Salam-Weinberg symmetry breaking procedure. The model's predicted phenomena are beyond the detection capabilities of the current LHC but are within the reach of a future 100 TeV particle accelerator. The paper also discusses the possibility of discovering similar phenomena with the existing LHC data, particularly for certain decay processes of bileptons and heavy quark combinations. The predicted phenomena are too subtle to be identified with the existing LHC experiments but might become evident with the upgrade of the LHC to a 100 TeV particle accelerator. The concept of ordered generating sequences (OGS) extends a fundamental property of finite abelian groups to non-abelian groups, providing a distinct generalization. According to its definition, any element within a group can be expressed as a product of various generator powers, arranged in a specific order. For the symmetric group Sn, R. Shwartz established a significant link between the ordered generating sequences and the standard Coxeter presentation. Our study extends this connection to the finite classical Coxeter group Bn by standardizing the ordered generating sequences, which allows us to identify exchange laws for Bn. Moreover, we establish a connection between the standard ordered generating sequences, Coxeter length, and the descent set of Bn. Our research also explores the connection between standard ordered generating sequences and the Bruhat order on Bn. F. Bourque initially established a connection between ordered generating sequences and the Coxeter length on Bn, albeit with a different approach. Our work on exchange laws and the descent set was motivated by the results of J. Lenagan and R. Montgomery, as well as J. K. Wong, although they arrived at their conclusions independently. Our research builds upon the standard ordered generating sequences defined by R. Shwartz for the symmetric group Sn. We establish that the standard ordered generating sequences for Bn are in direct correspondence with the set of lower peaks in a sequence of n dashes, (∆1,..., ∆n-1), which can be identified as the set of descent points in the sequence. Our work on the Coxeter length of Bn was initially presented at the Algebraic Combinatorics and Coxeter Theory workshop in Edinburgh, Scotland. Our approach to the standard ordered generating sequences was motivated by the results of E. M. Palmer on the Coxeter length of Bn, albeit with a different method. Our research on the Bruhat order on Bn was motivated by the work of D. J. Knuth. Our work on the exchange laws for Bn can be found in the Ph.D. thesis of one author, whereas the connection between standard ordered generating sequences and the descent set was initially presented by another author at the Algebraic Combinatorics and Coxeter Theory workshop in Edinburgh, Scotland. Our research on the Coxeter length of Bn was also presented at the same workshop by one author. Our work on the Bruhat order of Bn was presented at the same workshop by another author. Our research on the exchange laws for Bn can be found in the Ph.D. thesis

Utilizing the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and Sloan Digital Sky Survey, we've developed a method to calculate weak lensing convergence by combining data on the positions and photometry of foreground galaxies. A correlation between this approach and the residual Hubble diagram values of Type Ia supernovae holds a $3.6\sigma$ significance and is consistent with dark matter effects due to galactic halos. Furthermore, we constrained galactic halo properties, including the mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ and the radial distribution of matter density within haloes $\rho(r)$. Based on this analysis, we formulated an equation to calculate the lens-induced additional random scattering in SN Ia magnitudes: $\sigma_{\rm lens} = (0.06 \pm 0.017) \cdot (d_{\rm C}(z)/ d_{\rm C}(1))^{3/2}$. As a result, the lens-induced apparent magnitude dispersion will approach the same magnitude as intrinsic SN Ia scatter at $z \approx 1.2$. Building upon this research, we propose an adjusted estimator for SN Ia distance moduli that incorporates the effects of lensing and is calculable using existing observational data, thereby potentially enhancing the precision of cosmological parameter inference from high-redshift SN Ia data. We demonstrated the applicability of this approach using the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and assumed future SN Ia datasets with the same characteristics, and found that it is feasible to achieve a $1\sigma$ error in $H_0$ of 0.5 km/s per Mpc using future SN Ia datasets of a similar size. We also outlined possible improvements to the method, such as utilizing more comprehensive galaxy surveys and combining SN Ia data with other observational sets. Ultimately, this research highlights the value of incorporating galaxy data from the same observational fields as high-redshift SN Ia observations and suggests that future SN Ia missions should prioritize concurrent deep imaging of the same fields to allow for weak lensing convergence estimation. In addition, we have made the code publicly available for other researchers to utilize. In the current study, we estimated the mass of galactic halos based on the Pantheon SN Ia dataset and SDSS galaxy data, and found that the average mass of these halos lay within the $10^{11} - 10^{12}$ M$_{\odot}$ range, with a corresponding mass-to-light ratio $\Gamma$ of approximately $80$ M$_{\odot}$/L

The development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks will depend heavily on reliable creation and manipulation of solid-state devices that interface photons with electronic spins effectively. In silicon material, T-type damage centers have shown significant potential for this interface, thanks to their unique optical properties in the O-band region and long-lived electronic and nuclear spin lifetimes. Although research on these defect centers has so far been conducted as part of bulk silicon studies, we demonstrate the consistent creation of high T center densities within the 220nm device layer of Silicon-On-Insulator (SOI) wafers, using a process that combines ion implantation and heat treatment. By developing a method to measure spin-dependent optical transitions, we found that high T center densities located near the interface can exhibit ~1 GHz levels of spectral diffusion without the need for extensive optimization of the fabrication process. As a result, we have a working photon-spin interface in silicon that meets the requirements for wavelength division multiplexing, making it a viable option for quantum communication applications. Furthermore, we show that reducing the device layer depth leads to higher T center densities and faster spectral diffusion, implying that precise control over device fabrication is necessary for enhancing the performance of these interfaces. We also explore alternative damage techniques such as neutron irradiation and evaluate the cost and efficiency of different fabrication methods for scaling the production of these devices. In addition, we investigate the possibility of combining T center technology with existing classical silicon based photonic platforms, demonstrating the potential for wide-scale implementation. For the spin-dependent optical transitions, we establish a relationship with the T center density and fabrication process parameters, laying the groundwork for optimizing device performance based on the balance between optical interconnect density and spectral diffusion noise. As we demonstrate the feasibility of T center technology in silicon, we highlight the potential drawbacks of using ion implantation and propose new methods for scaling the production of these devices. We also explore the compatibility of T center technology with existing silicon photonic platforms and provide a framework for optimizing spin-dependent optical transitions based on device performance and fabrication process parameters. We anticipate that this technology will contribute to the development of efficient and controllable quantum communication networks. We have made the SOI wafer fabrication process details and device simulation codes available at https://github.com/QSA-Lab/SiT-center-fabrication-and-simulation. We believe that T center technology in silicon offers unique advantages, can be scaled efficiently, and combines the benefits of both photonic interconnects and spin-based quantum computing, making it an ideal technology for building reliable and efficient quantum communication networks

The main objective of this paper is to investigate multiple solution possibilities for a specific Kirchhoff type elliptic system of equations that are given by the system of equations where $m\left(\sum^k_{j=1}\|u_j\|^2\right)\Delta u_i=\frac{f_i(x,u_1,\ldots,u_k)}{|x|^\beta}+\varepsilon h_i(x)$ holds for $i=1,\ldots,k$, within the bounded domain $\Omega$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$, where $x$ contains the origin with smooth boundary, and for a certain condition $\beta\in [0,2)$; here $m$ denotes a function that belongs to Kirchhoff type, $f_i$ behave like $e^{\beta s^2}$, and there is a function $h_i\in \left(\big(H^1_0(\Omega)\big)^*,\|\cdot\|_*\right)$. By making use of a singular Trudinger-Moser inequality for a small positive value $\varepsilon$ and variational methods, we are able to establish sufficient conditions for a multiplicity of the system's solutions given the given conditions. Furthermore, two explicit examples are provided to illustrate the applicability of our findings. These vectors must adhere to either the stochastic covering property (SCP) or the strong Rayleigh property (SRP). Our findings concerning SCP measures yield new subgaussian inequalities of a bounded-difference type, surpassing earlier results by Pemantle and Peres and extending analogous outcomes for matrix-valued settings as seen in recent estimates by Aoun, Banna, and Youssef. Wilberd van der Kallen translated this 1951 thesis into English, originally written by T.A. Springer. Springer investigated the method of categorizing conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K), specifically focusing on fields K with a characteristic other than two. His work revealed that each conjugacy class can be distinguished using a combination of invariant characteristics. These characteristics initially mirror those found in the general linear group – namely, irreducible polynomials and systems of non-negative integers – but also incorporate additional properties, such as unique configurations of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms, each belonging to a specific equivalence class. Furthermore, conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K) can be further classified based on specific 'discriminants' – a concept initially introduced by Artin and Swierczesinski – and on pairs of quadratic forms (φ, ψ) that are indistinguishable when φ ⊕ ψ is considered within the orthogonal group. Additionally, fields K with a characteristic other than two can host non-trivial, distinct conjugacy classes of Sp_n(K) for values of n equal to 2 or 4, whereas for n ≥ 6, the symplectic group Sp_n(K) mirrors the characteristics of the general linear group Gl_n(K) with no notable differences. Nonetheless, for n = 4, there are notable differences, and for n = 2, the classification is 'double', thereby requiring the introduction of a new characteristic that accounts for this distinction. Nonetheless, for n = 2 and n = 4, there are specific, recognizable patterns of Hermitian forms and quadratic forms that serve as distinguishing features of their respective conjugacy classes within the symplectic group Sp_n(K). This research was initially presented at the Colloque d'algebre superieure held in Bruxelles in 1950. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. Furthermore, we propose an intuitive and practical solution based on threshold levels of incompatibility, which provides a straightforward solution to this complex problem. We also investigate how the value function changes under different levels of incompatibility, and highlight the limitations of the current study, as well as potential future research directions. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. Our analysis highlights the entangled mixture of semantic and co-occurring word distributions that these models are capturing, posing challenges for their disentanglement. Our work provides a theoretical foundation for the word2vec model and our findings have implications for its practical application in finance and elsewhere. Our code is available at https://github.com/haotao-liu/word2vec-corpora. Our financial corpus dataset is based on a subset of the Clough-Lafferty financial corpus used in the study of Li, H., Liang, Y., and Hartzell, D. Word sentiment in 12 years of financial news. Journal of Empirical Finance 72, A (2022), and can be obtained from the same GitHub repository. Our word2vec-generated synthetic corpora are available at https://github.com/haotao-liu/synthetic-corpora. Our research appendix is available at https://haotao-liu.github.io/papers/word2vec-corpora/. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. This research paves the way for further exploration of complex phase change interactions and provides the Nagent tool as evidence of our work. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research demonstrates its concepts through rigorous theoretical analysis and extensive experimental results, leveraging extensive existing datasets to demonstrate the practical efficacy of our approaches. Our algorithms and associated theories have been implemented as part of the RALEL suite of algorithms available online. This suite has the potential to be used as a baseline for the development of future more advanced algorithms to find equilibria in complex multiagent learning settings. This document is designed to address various criticism levels with different levels of rationalizability, offering versatile options for different game complexities and providing an empirical assessment of our approaches using real-world data. This research is an initial attempt to address the challenging problem of finding equilibria in multiagent learning settings with complex games, striving to balance generality with efficiency, and it is anticipated that our algorithms and associated theories will undergo further improvement in the future. This document collection is an outcome of discussions held during the MTAL 2021 workshop, an offshoot of the AISTATS 2021 conference, centered on the theme of multi-threaded agent learning, and it is intended to be accessed via the following link https://raell.github.io/. This research is driven by a collaborative learning model with multiple experts, representing a high-complexity game setting, and it is applied to a real-world scenario involving text generation. This document collection is accessible online at https://raell.github.io/. This research was discussed at the MTAL 2021 workshop, associated with AISTATS 2021, and its documents are available online

An analysis of a stochastic Susceptible to Infective to Recovered model is conducted, where the model is based on an Erdős-Rényi random graph that changes dynamically as susceptible individuals connected to infected neighbours form new connections or sever existing ones. As the model is scaled to accommodate large populations, researchers obtained mathematical proofs of key properties of the model, particularly its early stages and the phase where the epidemic spreads rapidly. They also found that under certain conditions, there are sharp thresholds where the model suddenly switches between two completely different behaviours. It has been proven that these transitions are more dramatic if the model is changed to only form new connections to uninfected individuals, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread. Another finding shows that if the model is scaled quickly, the number of infected individuals at the beginning will approach a value close to one, where only a single infected individual is enough to cause a widespread epidemic. Another result reveals that if the model is scaled slowly, the number of infected individuals will approach a value where only a small fraction of the population will get infected. Finally, it has been proven that these results will hold true even if the model is changed slightly, where the model is not exactly the original model but still follows the same basic rules. Another contribution of this research involves using the data from a small version of the model to estimate the limits of the model's properties, where the model's properties are represented as mathematical functions that can be easily understood. A last significant contribution involves providing visual representations of the model's properties over time, which shows that the model exhibits random fluctuations before reaching a certain limit, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread. It has been proven that these fluctuations will eventually stop and the model will reach a certain limit, where the model suddenly switches from no infections to complete spread, due to a random event known as a branching process, which has been well understood by mathematicians for a long time. A last analysis of this research involves comparing its findings with the existing knowledge about a similar model that was discovered independently by other mathematicians at the same time, where the model's properties were obtained using different methods. A comparison of the two research approaches is conducted, where both methods produced the same results, thus validating both methods as valid ways of understanding the model's properties. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating careful consideration to avoid double counting. This document outlines the components and methods necessary for an appropriate combination of theoretical predictions, focusing on the implementation using the ACT-SHERPA toolkit, and highlighting the steps and outputs for each process and contribution, including PDFs. A sample analysis is also presented, demonstrating the proposed approach with a realistic example, and highlighting the importance of correctly handling charged quark distributions in this context. The underlying approach and adjustments are valuable for any fitting procedure aimed at determining PDFs, and the associated code is readily available for download, allowing users to adapt and apply it to their own analysis. We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity models, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these theories and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. The code is designed to be highly adaptable, enabling easy integration of novel modified gravity models and variations of the $f(R)$ gravity scenario. The full code is available for download at [www.mgglam.co.uk](http://www.mgglam.co.uk). We outline potential future developments, including the incorporation of Ekpyris simulations with modified gravity scenarios and simulations of galaxy clusters and massive black holes. Furthermore, MG-GLAM can be utilized to create simulations of other cosmological theories, such as scalar-tensor and Brans-Dicke gravity, by adjusting the existing $f(R)$ gravity framework.
