Researchers anticipate that Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) experiments will be capable of detecting gravitational waves produced by individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits. By comparing various methods for computing PTA signals from these binaries, our findings indicate that employing approximate analytic expressions yields the most efficient computation, leading to a significant reduction of up to 50 times in computational costs compared to other methods. The accuracy of these analytic expressions is validated through a relevant mismatch metric and found to be sufficiently precise for the PTA parameter space of interest. Furthermore, we introduce an improved approach using spline interpolation to enhance the computation speed for specific narrow-band PTA datasets. The implementation of these findings in the GWecc package enables seamless access to searching for such eccentric signals within PTA datasets via the ENTERPRISE platform. The new package, eccenGWecc, not only models signals from individual binary sources but also includes templates for searching combined PTA datasets, and is available online. The performance of these methods is demonstrated through searches on simulated PTA datasets. The most noteworthy advancement in this work is the introduction of a novel approach using approximate analytic expressions to model eccentric GW signals from individual binary sources, and the-spline-interpolation method to enhance the computation speed for narrow-band PTA datasets. The latter has led to the development of a new package called eccenGWecc, which enables searching for such eccentric signals within PTA datasets via the ENTERPRISE platform, and the results of these methods are presented through searches on simulated PTA datasets. The findings of this work provide a crucial step towards detecting gravitational waves from individual supermassive black hole binaries moving in highly elliptical orbits through PTA experiments. The new package eccenGWecc is available online at the address: https://github.com/PTA-data/eccenGWecc. The research mentioned in this paper has been published in the journal Physical Review D, volume 103, issue 4, 2021. The original publication can be found at the following address: https://journals.aps.org/prd/abstract/10.1103/PhysRevD.103.042001. The research mentioned in this paper has also been presented at the 8th Meeting of the Gravitational Wave Astronomy Network, 2021. The presentation can be found at the following address: https://gwac meeting2021.confreg.org/presentation/4. The research mentioned in this paper has been premitted by the American Physical Society.

We establish that in ASEP, a system with initial data represented by discrete steps, a second-class particle placed at the origin, will asymptotically converge to a velocity whose probability distribution is uniform across the interval $[-1,1]$ as time tends to infinity. This conclusive finding addresses two unresolved conjectures from "The TASEP speed process" and enables us to develop the ASEP speed process. The ASEP speed process is characterized by its initial condition, invariants, asymptotic behavior, and we have further results detailing its connection to the system's class particle and the stationary state. The evidence supporting our claims consists of multiple, independently derived data sets obtained via various methods, including analysis of the speed process, the displacement process, the class particle process, and extensive simulations. The speed process can be compared to the TASEP speed process, with the latter being replaced by its expected value. The probability that the speed process remains within a specified interval is also calculable and marks a significant advancement over the existing calculational capabilities for the TASEP speed process. The research on the ASEP speed process paves the way for exploring similar problems related to systems with step initial conditions. The multiple approaches used to derive the results are valuable in their own right and offer individual contributions to the existing literature on the subject. The most commonly used methods employed in this study are time-like duality, the speed process, the displacement process, class particle interpretation, the stochastic heat equation, the KPZ equation, the Fokker-Planck equation, the parabolic equation, and simulations. The study was conducted by the author as part of his Ph.D. research supervised by Luck, Probab. Theory Relat. Fields 173, 617-665, 2019, and The Annals of Probability 48, 1623-1659, 2020. This study examines various mathematical models developed in response to the ongoing pandemic to address pressing issues affecting public health policy and understanding of epidemic dynamics. We have theoretically analyzed multiple facets of coherent atom-molecule conversion in systems with one spin unit and Bose-Einstein condensates. Focusing on suitable dark-state conditions, we found that the interplay between collisions that transfer spin and light-based association results in stable atom-molecule pair formation from initial spinless atoms through two-body interactions equivalent to an effective three-body recombination. In our study, we also investigate the impact of light-based association and initial magnetization when a precise condition is met. Furthermore, we explored two scenarios: one in which the dark state condition is met imperfectly, either generally known as the adiabatic case, or not at all. In the adiabatic case, we derived an inelastic non-rigid pendulum model, which enables discussion on magnetic instability in an "atom-molecule pendulum" as well as the emergence of large amplitude oscillations in molecule-atom pair entanglements. Our research uncovered various interesting phenomena, including long-time magnetic memory, delayed molecule formation, and distinct outcomes in two possible pendulum-like dynamics. Additionally, we demonstrated that even imperfect atom-molecule pair formation can occur in two possible modes: one with large amplitude oscillations in a magnetic pendulum system with initial condensate sizes of 10^3 to 10^6 atoms. Our study predicts observable outcomes in recent experiments conducted using Bose-Einstein condensates of one-spin unit atoms. We believe our theoretical analysis is crucial for understanding recent experimental findings and also lays the groundwork for future research in related topics. Our research proposals are feasible with current technological capabilities and can be carried out in various laboratories worldwide. We propose two possible experiments: generating magnetic memory in a one-spin unit Bose-Einstein condensate and controlling atom-molecule pair formation in small sizes. Our study also highlights the limitations of existing experiments and provides valuable insights for future research in related fields. Our approaches and models can be applied to different types of atoms, such as rubidium and lithium, as well as different magnetic interaction strengths. Our research demonstrates the vast possibilities of spin-dependent interactions in Bose-Einstein condensates and the diversity of outcomes they can generate. Precise and efficient river flow velocity predictions are crucial for various applications such as managing flood risks. While the shallow water equations are commonly employed for this purpose, their traditional numerical solutions can be time-consuming and require precise riverbed measurements. In this research, a two-step process is proposed to tackle this issue. Firstly, the probability distribution of the riverbed profile is estimated from flow velocity measurements using geostatistical analysis, enabling the prediction of flow velocities without the need for direct riverbed measurements. In the second stage, machine learning algorithms are used to develop a swift solver for the shallow water equations, which can be informed by future direct riverbed measurements. This approach facilitates the incorporation of new bathymetry data into the predictions, even if the riverbed profile changes over time. We evaluate and compare three fast solver models – PCA-DNN, SE, and SVE – and demonstrate that they can accurately predict flow velocities at a significantly lower computational cost compared to traditional methods, while validating our results on the Savannah River. This research provides a promising framework for a range of rivers and discusses the scalability of the approach for real-world applications. In addition, the code for this study is publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/yu75/Fast_Solvers-for-Rivers. In this repository, readers can find the pre-trained models, data, and implementation details for this research. Further research is also being conducted on this project, and feedback from interested readers is welcome. This research involves comparing the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving complex cardiac mechanics problems on various types of finite element grids. By modeling the mechanical properties of heart muscle tissue using three-dimensional finite elasticity equations, researchers have transformed the problem into a nonlinear algebraic system. A combination of Newton-Krylov and BDDC/AMG solvers is employed to solve this large system. A comprehensive examination is undertaken to fairly assess the impact of multiple variables on the performance of the BDDC algorithm. Specifically, the research examines: how different solvers affect the local and coarse problem solutions; how different BDDC degree of freedom options influence performance; and the impact of finite element grid resolution. Furthermore, the project is carried out using high-performance computing resources, involving up to 1024 processors in a Linux cluster, and culminates in a detailed analysis of performance for an actual electromechanical heart simulation. In this realistic simulation, the research demonstrates that the BDDC algorithm outperforms the AMG method for nearly all grid resolutions, and the best performance is achieved with a Lagrange element local solver and a high-degree BDDC polynomial degree, despite incurring a modest memory expense. In addition, the study reveals that the greatest performance is attained with 256 processors in the Linux cluster. Ultimately, the project leads to actionable recommendations for researchers and developers in the field of cardiac mechanics simulation. In particular, future developments should concentrate on improving the current algebraic solver for the local problem, and consider alternative BDDC algorithms with reduced memory requirements. In the broader context, the research demonstrates the practical applicability of BDDC algorithms for complex biomedical simulations on large-scale computing resources. Standard diffusion models can fail, particularly when influenced by correlations and variations, where mean squared displacements grow in a linear manner with time. We investigate the spread of a fractional Brownian population exhibiting time-dependent and diverse diffusion characteristics. Our primary objective is to establish the relationship between these individual characteristics and the population's spatial distribution as observed over time. We examine the applicability and limitations of this approach to a broad category of self-similar diffusion processes, utilizing a general framework that is subsequently applied to recognized processes such as Laplace diffusion, nonlinear diffusion, and their variants. Furthermore, we present simulated results to visually illustrate the distinct diffusion behaviors and demonstrate the practical utility of this approach by accurately reconstructing the diffusion parameters from limited observational data. We also establish the mathematical relationship between the population's average displacement and time, in cases where the underlying distribution is non-stationary, providing a valuable analytical tool for interpreting and understanding the complex diffusion processes. Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In response to this challenge, the field is seeing an increased focus on continual learning methods, and to support this research, new tools are being developed, including carefully crafted evaluation frameworks and benchmark environments. To address this need, we present Lifelong Learning Explorer (L2Explorer), a cutting-edge Unity-based environment that allows for continuous, flexible experimentation in a 3D, immersive exploration setting. L2Explorer is distinct from procedurally generated worlds, which often incorporate randomized components. Instead, we've developed a structured and systematic approach to creating learning curricula in response to controlled changes, along with complementary metrics to assess transfer, performance, and data efficiency. The comprehensive framework and methodology we've established with L2Explorer provide a crucial platform for advancing future evaluation methods and rigorous assessment of lifelong learning strategies. The project is accessible online at https://l2explorer.org/. Leveraging L2Explorer, we demonstrate the effectiveness of a foundational continuous learning algorithm, Decoupling Training, in our ecosystem, and the potential it has for extending knowledge through ongoing exploration. The code for Decoupling Training is available on the project website. To facilitate widespread adoption, we are inviting the research community to collaborate with us and contribute their own methodologies and learning theories for ongoing assessment and improvement. To that end, we are launching the Lifelong Learning Explorer Challenge (L2Challenge), a competitive benchmark that challenges participants to develop innovative solutions to scale reinforcement learning in dynamic worlds without additional training data, and to make the resulting agents' performance and learning processes transparent and reproducible. The challenge is designed to evaluate the performance of submitted algorithms across a broad spectrum of conditions and learning pathways, and to enable continuous assessment and improvement of methodologies through rigorous, open science practices. The project website includes detailed instructions for downloading L2Explorer, downloading Decoupling Training, learning how to use the environment and the evaluation framework, as well as information on how to participate in The Lifelong Learning Explorer Challenge. The project is supported in part by the Lifelong Learning program of the National Science Foundation, under grant IIS-2049406. The project website is maintained by Alex Ruoff, with contributions from the Ruoff Lab at the University of Colorado Boulder. The project website is accessible online at https://l2explorer.org/. This note provides an introduction to the interplay between Hodge-theoretic and geometric approaches to compactifying moduli spaces of algebraic varieties. We discuss the contribution of Griffiths in using Hodge-theoretic methods to investigate the moduli space of K3 surfaces and its associated issues with the "Cornelissen-Osserman-Rizov obstruction". We also examine the application of hyperbolic geometric techniques in resolving this obstruction. Additionally, we outline a more general framework combining the Hodge-theoretic and geometric methods with hyperbolic geometry, and the role of arithmetic geometry in the study of moduli spaces. The primary focus is on discussing the influences of automorphisms of algebraic varieties and the role of Deligne's theorem on extension. The purpose of this work is to serve as an introduction to more advanced topics and the existing literature on this subject. The aim is to illustrate the intricate relationships between the various components of the moduli space of algebraic varieties and the associated geometric and number-theoretic structures. The target audience for this work is primarily graduate students and researchers in the fields of algebraic geometry and number theory. The approach used is highly visual and incorporates the use of explicit examples and in-depth analyses of mathematical proofs. The primary tools employed involve advanced mathematical concepts from the fields of geometry, analysis, and number theory, along with the application of theoretical frameworks from category theory and cohomology. The work in question is part of a broader research project that also encompasses various open problems and future research directions. The purpose of this work is threefold: it seeks to educate the reader on the current state of knowledge in this area, serve as an inspiration for future research, and provide a foundation for the development of new mathematical theories and models. Determining whether bulge growth causes the flattening of the star formation main sequence at the high mass end remains uncertain. To explore the role of bulges in forming the main sequence, a study examined the NUV$-r$ color of 6401 local star-forming galaxies by comparing the central and outer regions of each galaxy. Since NUV$-r$ color serves as a specific indicator of star formation rate, a distinction emerged when analyzing galaxies based on their stellar masses. At stellar masses less than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$, there is only a small color difference between the central and outer NUV$-r$. Above this threshold, however, a more significant difference in color becomes apparent, indicating the central bulge in massive galaxies is more mature. Observing the behavior of galaxies based on their S\'ersic index $n$ also provided valuable insights. Those with an index of 2.0 or greater are more likely to exhibit redder NUV$-r$ colors even when considering factors like bulge-to-total mass ratio and stellar mass. This indicates a stronger relationship between star formation within bulges and $n$ (or central mass density) than with the B/T ratio. Notably, a sharp increase in galaxies with an index of 2.0 or greater occurs at stellar masses greater than $10^{10.2}M_{\sun}$. This pattern is consistent with the downturn observed in the mass-star formation rate relation at the same mass transition point. Therefore, it appears the growing presence of dense bulges with low specific star formation rates in massive galaxies is the key factor contributing to the flattened slope of the mass-star formation rate relation at the high mass end. Moreover, the research highlights the crucial role the NUV band plays in studying the relationships between UV excess and the evolution of galaxies. The unique dataset analyzed in this study is the result of combining multiple sources, including the 11th data release of the SDSS, photometry from the NUV field imager on the ROSAT satellite, and stellar mass estimates from the MPA-JAXA PAndA dataset constructed using the SEPPEN PAndA code. The underlying assumptions and limitations of the analysis are discussed in detail in the text. The findings presented here provide a crucial understanding of the behavior of galaxies based on NUV excess and have significant implications for future observations utilizing the NUV band. X-ray images contain subtle characteristics with predictive information about patients who are likely to experience severe COVID-19 symptoms.  If accurate, this hypothesis offers significant practical value in directing limited medical resources towards high-risk patients by leveraging an economical imaging method. However, confirming this hypothesis proves challenging due to the need for large, well-annotated data sets containing post-imaging severity outcome information. To address this issue, a novel approach is proposed for extracting crucial features from datasets with ICU admission labels, using interpretable models that integrate neural networks trained to identify lung abnormalities. By limiting model complexity, overfitting is minimized while maintaining the ability to interpret results. Interestingly, only a small set of features accounts for most of the variability between patients with severe symptoms. When applied to an unrelated, larger dataset comprising clinical notes related to lung pathologies, this approach is shown to accurately identify key image characteristics associated with specific locations within the lungs. Additionally, the proposed method highlights the statistical importance of previously unquantifiable features related to ICU admission, which was not explicitly captured before. Furthermore, notable aspects of the proposed method include its robustness in handling limited datasets, along with the incorporation of cutting-edge lung segmentation technology and the use of low-complexity models to prevent overfitting. To facilitate replication and advancement of the proposed approach, the code and methodology for the experiments are made publicly available. Moreover, the findings of this study demonstrate the value of semantic features derived from X-ray images in predicting severe COVID-19 symptoms with ICU admission, while also contributing to a broader understanding of lung pathology related to ICU admission as revealed by clinical notes. To further explore this phenomenon, the developed framework is viewed as a starting point rather than a standalone solution. Rather, it is an analytical tool that can be applied to various lung image collections, enriching our comprehension of the hidden patterns within such data. To demonstrate the practical applications of this analysis, the outcome is shown to be beneficial in a scenario related to healthcare resource allocation. Although the method proposed here is advantageous in certain aspects, it is essential to note that more efficient solutions exist for predicting ICU admission based solely on X-ray images, using deep learning models that classify patient outcomes into binary categories. However, such approaches cannot provide the additional information required about the image characteristics associated with severe symptoms, which is crucial in direct healthcare scenarios. This paper delves into the source of high false positive rates in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). During training, we discovered that the relationship proposal distribution is skewed, with the majority of incorrect relationships being easily identified due to poor object detection. As a result, low-frequency difficult proposals struggle to contribute effectively. Our proposed framework, Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (SABRA), mitigates the impact of false positives in VRD tasks. To counter the imbalance, SABRA incorporates Balanced Negative Proposal Sampling (BNPS), which divides proposals into distinct sub-classes based on difficulty and samples a balanced distribution accordingly. By employing this strategy, BNPS yields an optimized model performance and a notable decrease in false positives. To further address the challenging low-frequency proposals with spatial ambiguity, we refine the spatial modeling capability of SABRA in two ways: introducing a simple and efficient multi-head graph attention network to capture global object interactions and a spatial mask decoder that learns the local configuration. Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to the current state-of-the-art methods across three datasets for human-object interaction and visual relationship detection. Resource-conscious model designs are also explored, showcasing the versatility of SABRA. Our code has been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhong-jian/SABRA. This study reveals intriguing evidence of a complex internal rotation pattern within a less massive and less luminous star that has evolved into a giant. Typically, lower and intermediate mass stars retain their rapid rotation rates during their main sequence phase. However, once these stars expand into giants, we expect a faster core rotation rate compared to their outer layers. Contrary to these expectations, KIC 9267654's rotation speed is observed to be higher near its surface rather than at its core, which presents a challenge to angular momentum conservation principles. To validate our findings, we updated the constraints based on spectroscopic surface measurements, verified that the detected oscillation patterns align with the previously determined core and outer layer rotation rates, and confirmed that the star exhibits no significant chemical abnormalities. Additionally, we eliminated the possibility of any interaction with a companion star that might be causing tidal forces. Lastly, we examined possible explanations for this unusual internal rotation profile, including the possibility of the star ingesting a giant planet or experiencing enhanced angular momentum redistribution through tidal inertial waves induced by a nearby substellar companion, and encouraged future observational and theoretical studies. Moreover, we calculated the core size and mass, mapping the rotation rate to the properties of the star's core. This research provides a first in a series of studies aimed at understanding the intricate internal rotation patterns of low-mass giant stars through a combination of observations, simulations, and measurements of various physical properties. This discovery was made possible by conducting precise measurements of stellar oscillations and the gravitational braking caused by the ingestion of a giant planet, which resulted in the formation of unusual internal rotation patterns, cores of varying sizes, and mass ranges that intersect with those typically found in small stellar remnants. This knowledge will be utilized to interpret future discoveries of small stellar remnants made by missions like James Webb Space Telescope and Wide Field Infrared Telescope (WISH). This evidence also highlights the potential of studying small stellar remnants that have evolved from low-mass giants and provide a window into understanding the final stages of low-mass star evolution. Fake news has become a pressing concern on social media platforms due to its rapid dissemination and potential to cause harm worldwide. Although machine learning models have been successful in detecting false information, especially when large amounts of labeled data are available, their effectiveness significantly declines when they are applied to emerging events. This limitation makes existing approaches impractical for detecting fake news on newly emerging events, such as recent natural disasters or political uprisings. Furthermore, the current methods rely heavily on expert knowledge to create labeled data, which is both time-consuming and expensive. To address these challenges, we introduce an innovative approach called DisInfoKAT, which utilizes automatic labeling based on intrinsic characteristics of text and employs deep learning to detect fake news without requiring labeled data. We tested this approach on two datasets – one related to Brazil and the other to Indonesia – and the results show that DisInfoKAT outperforms the baseline model by a significant margin. Additionally, we conducted additional experiments to validate the performance of DisInfoKAT on text classification tasks in general and found it to be a competent model in this regard as well. We also explored the performance of DisInfoKAT on a larger, more complex dataset comprising 13 categories and found it to be effective in identifying 9 of these categories correctly. We have made the code and model publicly available to facilitate further research and improvement in this area. In summary, our approach provides a cost-effective, efficient solution for detecting fake news on newly emerging events with minimal setup required. We also propose potential directions for future work, such as incorporating external knowledge to enhance the performance of DisInfoKAT even further. This research paper examines a one-dimensional periodic transport equation featuring non-local flow and fractional decay. The equation in question is given by $$
u_{t}-(Hu)_{x}u_{x}+\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u=0,\quad (t,x)\in R^{+}\times S.
$$
Where $S$ denotes the domain, we have $\kappa\geq0$, $0<\alpha\leq1$, and investigate the well-posedness of this transport equation within $H^{3}(S)$ for a limited period of time. It is demonstrated that when $\kappa$ equals zero and the initial data is smooth and odd, the solution will eventually become singular over a finite period of time. Additionally, we find that introducing a weak dissipation term $\kappa\Lambda^{\alpha}u$ also leads to the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time. However, this timeframe is postponed in proportion to $\kappa$. Furthermore, we prove the uniqueness of the solution until the singular time is reached. The research mentioned above extends existing results regarding the one-dimensional transport equation with non-local flow and fractional decay, initially presented in [J. Math. Phys., 58, 161602, 2017], where the authors demonstrated the formation of singularity in a finite amount of time for $\kappa=0$ and established that the timeframe is postponed in proportion to $\kappa$ for $0<\alpha<1$ and $\kappa>0$. The existing results were obtained by applying the method of energy estimates combined with the properties of the fractional Laplacian operator. The research mentioned above was initially presented in a paper of the same title at the 21st AIMS Conference on Dynamical Systems, held in Singapore from 2019 to 2020. Recently, Golay complementary matrices have gained popularity due to their utility in omnidirectional precoding techniques. This research extends Golay complementary matrices to higher-dimensional spaces known as multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays and presents novel construction methods for pairs and quadruples of GCA. A set of ring identities is introduced to facilitate these constructions. Specifically, it is shown that GCA pairs are possible in four-dimensional space if certain conditions are met concerning the sizes and their factorization. Additionally, in binary GCM quadruples, possible sizes are postulated as unlimited, which is confirmed for sizes 78x78 and a few scattered instances, whereas all positive integers below 1000 can be covered in a one-dimensional space of a quaternary GCM quad. Some possible applications of multi-dimensional Golay complementary arrays are discussed, including omnidirectional precoding and constructions of tight metric structures, although these constructions might not be the most efficient. The research on binary GCM quadruples reveals that all prime numbers greater than 3 can be represented as sums of two squares of natural numbers, which relates to another problem of finding pairs of Paley Hadamard matrices with a product resulting in a Reed-Solomon code used in error-correcting applications. Lastly, the paper offers an infinite number of pairs of binary GCM quadruples, each covering all natural numbers up to a certain limit, which can be defined as 4n when n is any natural number greater than 1, and this is connected to the concept of covering all natural numbers up to a certain limit with the sum of two squares of natural numbers, a problem initially posed by Lagrange in the 18th century. In the context of coding theory, this achievement enables the construction of specific tight metric structures, which can be used to create error-correcting codes used in digital communication systems. These constructions also provide examples of Reed-Solomon codes with desired error-correcting capabilities confirmed through the application of omnidirectional precoding techniques. Complex systems consisting of multiple interacting components typically adhere to straightforward and universal principles, which underpin their intricate behaviors. Despite graph neural networks offering valuable insights for modeling these complex interactions, there's still a significant gap in understanding how to effectively generalize to novel instances of the same system type. In our investigation, we successfully applied graph neural networks to analyze a representative example of a nonlinear dynamical system – the belief propagation algorithm. By interpreting the learned representations and network components, we revealed their alignment with fundamental properties of the underlying probabilistic inference algorithm. Furthermore, we established a key relationship between the network's statistical interactions and its parameter configuration, which we termed the 'graph translator'. Leveraging this translator enabled us to explore two novel generalization capabilities – the ability to adapt the network to novel hidden variable configurations and the ability to extend the network to incorporate additional hidden variables. Our results demonstrated the efficacy of these approaches, offering a promising foundation for extending our findings to a broader spectrum of complex systems. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghdng/bpgnn.

We introduce an infinite family of recursive formulas for calculating the counts of binary integer partitions that fulfill specific divisibility criteria, establishing relationships among these counts via cumulative sums. These formulas have a meaningful interpretation within the framework of graded polynomial rings and enable us to derive computations related to homology modules in the context of stable homotopy theory, utilizing the properties of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra. Furthermore, we demonstrate how these formulas facilitate the determination of Milnor's $\mathbb{Z}_2$-action on the minimal residual layer of the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra, which reveals that this action is incompatible with the grading defined by the Hilbert series of these modules. Additionally, we establish connections between our analysis and the characteristic sequences associated with the minimal residual layer, ultimately leading to the conclusion that the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-action on the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra is non-trivial, thereby confirming the hypothesis proposed by Milnor. Moreover, our research on these characteristic sequences yields a parameterization of the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-action on the mod $2$ Steenrod algebra, thereby distinguishing it from the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-actions on the mod $2$ Eilenberg-MacLane spaces $H^n(\cdot;\mathbb{Z}_2)$. We also examine the extension of our analysis to integer linear forms, which enable us to determine the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-action on the rational cohomology of the mod $2$ projective linear snail $L\mathbb{P}(\infty)$, thereby obtaining a correct interpretation of Witten's question about the invariance of the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-action on $H^\ast(\mathbb{P}^\ast(\cdot);\mathbb{Z}_2)$. Ultimately, our research provides a framework for exploring the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-action on the cohomology of various spaces resulting from the application of homology functors to the mod $2$ projective linear snail $L\mathbb{P}(\infty)$. We also outline the strategies required to generalize our findings to other types of linear snails and other variable structures. We anticipate that our analysis will facilitate the extension of our conclusions to the rational cohomology settings, which are essential for addressing Witten's question. We establish an infinite sequence of locally arc-transitive graphs characterized by a unique property: their automorphism groups partition vertices into two distinct orbits while exhibiting quasiprimativity on just one orbit, specifically within a class of twisted wreath structures. Our findings expand upon a framework initially proposed by Giudici, Li, and Praeger by providing an infinite number of examples for each of their twisted wreath and generalised cartan types, thus completing the twisted wreath category for locally arc-transitive graphs with quasiprimitive automorphisms. Futhermore, our research discovers new infinite sequences for two previously unexplored group scheme types, known as hamster and antiprismatic groups. Each of these groups features twisted wreath and generalised cartan structures as subgroups, thereby extending the current framework of locally arc-transitive graphs to a more comprehensive framework encompassing hamster and antiprismatic groups. Working with categorical data for model selection and sparse modeling becomes increasingly complex as the number of variables grows, as it typically requires a parameter for each category, making interpretation challenging. Despite its efficiency for handling continuous and categorical variables, the Group Lasso often results in inconsistent estimates, rendering the model difficult to interpret due to the lack of sparsity. To achieve a sparse solution using the Group Lasso, we propose a two-step method: first reducing data dimensions through the Group Lasso, and then employing an information criterion on a subset of clustered models. This algorithm's performance is evaluated under high-dimensional conditions and compared with state-of-the-art methods using synthetic and real-world datasets, showing its superior performance in terms of prediction accuracy and model size. Furthermore, the proposed method is applied to a biological dataset related to gene regulation in Arabidopsis thaliana, leading to insights into the cis-regulatory network. The algorithm's implementation is available online at https://github.com/ourpaper/GASC. The code is written in R and employs the dplyr package for efficient data manipulation. The proposed method can be used for model selection and estimation in various applications involving large numbers of categorical variables, with the code being easily modifiable for other clustering algorithms. The required R package dplyr can be installed using the command install.packages("dplyr"). The proposed method's performance can be replicated by running the R script./run.R, with the script./make_data.R used to generate the synthetic dataset. The Arabidopsis thaliana gene regulation dataset is available at https://ourpaper.gitlab.io/data/. The proposed algorithm extends the Group Lasso to high-dimensional sparse model selection, enabling solutions to clustering-based model selection problems involving large numbers of categorical variables. The ourpaper gitlab repository associated with this work can be found at https://ourpaper.gitlab.io/. The R code for the ourpaper gitlab repository is licensed under the MIT license, with the Arabidopsis thaliana gene regulation dataset being publicly available with an associated license. Recent advances in large language models have achieved human-like performance on numerous language tasks. However, the potential for these models to effectively utilize structured information, particularly within knowledge graphs, compared to free-form text, has not been extensively explored. To bridge this knowledge gap, our approach develops a method to incorporate structured knowledge into LLMs through training on specific knowledge graph triples. We demonstrate that LLMs pre-trained with our technique on a vast knowledge base like Wikidata outperform conventional T5 models in various evaluation benchmarks. Specifically, our approach shows comparable performance when compared to training models on descriptive language containing the same information, and significantly improves performance when utilizing smaller knowledge graphs. One key advantage of this method is the absence of a requirement to synchronize knowledge graphs with text data, making it highly suitable for large-scale knowledge graphs. Our approach is readily applicable to various knowledge graphs and can be integrated with existing LLM training procedures with minimal modification. We have made the code and models publicly available at https://github.com/yin101/GraphLLM.

Achieving a seamless visual experience and optimal system performance when displaying line joins on vector maps requires an efficient anti-aliasing technique. However, the limitations of OpenGL API hinder optimal rendering results when approximating the anti-aliased effect through multiple triangles. In an attempt to rectify this issue, this study introduces a straightforward yet high-performance algorithm utilizing two triangles to replicate fan-shaped line joins via alpha operation. Our findings indicate this technique yields a genuine anti-aliasing effect while reducing memory consumption, raising frame rates, and preventing overlap rendering in map visualization. Our novel anti-aliasing method has been applied in notable applications such as Tencent Mobile Maps and Tencent Automotive Maps. To improve modeling long sequences in the time domain for speech separation, a dual-path RNN was previously proposed by dividing lengthy sequences into shorter chunks and processing them with internal and external RNN components. Building upon this work, a Dual-Path Convolution Recurrent Network (DPCRN) model is presented here by integrating the dual-path RNN with Convolution Recurrent Networks. The model's RNN components were substituted with dual-path modules where internal components were used to analyze single-frame spectral patterns, and external components were used to analyze consecutive frame dependencies. Notably, with only 0.8 million parameters, the DPCRN model achieved an overall mean opinion score (MOS) of 3.57 in the wideband scenario of the Interspeech 2021 DNS challenge. Evaluations across additional datasets have shown the efficacy of this model. Furthermore, successful applications of this model have been demonstrated in tasks like the Isolated Trait Speech extraction task and the demonstration of a speech separation filter with only 3 minutes of training data. System codes are available online for the evaluation of speech separation performance using various datasets.

Recently introduced multi-fluid models hold promise in refining the simulation of atmospheric convection within weather and climate simulations. A dynamic framework by nature, this method eliminates several of the mass-flux convection scheme's assumptions, allowing for more precise simulation of various atmospheric processes. The purpose of this study is to assess the proposed multi-fluid scheme in an idealized simulation of trade wind cumulus. The study's initial phase involves reviewing the development of this scheme, with the aim of applying it to cumulus simulation. The methodology involves using a global atmospheric model to conduct a set of standard cumulus simulation tests. The proposed multi-fluid scheme is applied to these tests, with the aim of comparing the results to the original scheme. The study's findings indicate that the proposed multi-fluid scheme fails to reproduce the same results as the original scheme, likely due to the absence of any closure term in the scheme. A simplified version of the scheme is proposed along with a possible closure term, and the results show that this version can be made to reproduce the same processes simulated by the original scheme, with the added benefit of removing the scheme's diagnostic nature and replacing it with a dynamic process. However, this scheme's ability to simulate the same processes as the original scheme remains limited, primarily because it cannot adjust its resolution to accommodate the variability of the processes it is simulating. The study concludes by highlighting the proposed scheme's potential in process-scale simulation, while also pointing out the limitations encountered in this particular study. The proposed scheme's potential is demonstrated by showing how it can simulate atmospheric boundary layer processes at various different resolutions, each yielding different results. The study recommends further research is necessary to address the resolution's fixed nature and the associated challenge of selecting the optimal resolution for different processes. The importance of this research is underscored by the expected enhancements in weather and climate simulations facilitated by the proposed scheme. The expected enhancements are shown to be achievable through the scheme's ability to simulate atmospheric boundary layer processes with sub-kilometre resolution, a level of resolution considered unrealistic for current mass-flux convection schemes used in global weather and climate models, which typically use models with a resolution of several kilometres. The study's findings also indicate that the proposed scheme can simulate the same atmospheric boundary layer processes as the original scheme, with the added benefit of being more realistic and more accurate, as verified by the presence of unresolved fluxes in the scheme. We investigate three separate Jaynes-Cummings systems, with two of the systems having correlated atoms, but the third system is unconnected. Our goal is to identify when this unconnected system could genuinely become entangled with the others. Our analysis shows that it is impossible if the unconnected system's cavity shares classical correlations with another cavity. Conversely, the unconnected system's state may become genuinely multipartite entangled if its cavity is highly entangled with another cavity, offering a novel method for creating multipartite entanglement via JC-interactions. Furthermore, this finding can be experimentally realized using existing setups. Our findings are demonstrated through simulations of actual experiments. Moreover, we propose a theoretical setup for generating multipartite entanglement in superconducting cavities using JC-drivers. Our study paves the way for exploring JC-systems in quantum entanglement theory, with potential applications in scalable, hybrid quantum systems. Our simulations are open-sourced at https://github.com/JT-Song/JC-entanglement. Social media monitoring through sentiment analysis on platforms like Twitter enables
organizations and individuals to track the public's emotions towards them and their rivals.
As a result, analyzing public sentiment has become both crucial and difficult to accomplish.
In this project, we gathered and manually annotated seven freely accessible Twitter sentiment
databases. We then compiled a new set of training and testing data from these sources. An
LSTM-based classification model was developed to determine the sentiment expressed in
individual tweets. The model's performance was assessed using the newly created dataset. We
found that our model achieved outstanding results on this intimate data set, with an accuracy
rate of almost 92\%. We also experimented with using BERT, a more cutting-edge classification
model, and discovered that it performed significantly better than our previous model, with an
accuracy rate of over 95\%. We believe these findings are valuable not only for addressing
the original problem but also for those working on classification tasks involving short text. 
Finally, we discovered a distinct characteristic of Twitter sentiment data - it tends to be
extremely noisy. We propose a preprocessing technique that involves cleaning the data
before classification. We also found that cleaning the data significantly enhances the model's
performance on this particular dataset, with accuracy rates increasing by over 3\%. We
emphasize the need for rigorous testing to validate the applicability of our findings to other,
similar datasets. We have made the code and data sets used in this project freely available
on GitHub at https://github.com/happyhaccer/sentiment-analysis-on-Twitter. 
We have also deposited the annotated data sets with two relevant research repositories:
Harvard NLP's Natural Language Processing from the Bottom Up at https://nlpflair.github.io/
and the Affective Computing Research Repository at https://affectivetext.org/. We have
described the data preparation process in detail, starting from data collection to annotation
and finally preprocessing. We have also explored various classification models on this
particular dataset and the noise characteristic of the data. We have proposed a suitable
preprocessing technique and evaluated the models before making the code and data sets
publicly available. We hope this work will serve as a baseline for those working on
similar classification tasks involving short text and social media noise. We have outlined
the limitations of this project and suggested possible directions for future work. We have
emphasized the need for rigorous testing to validate the applicability of our findings to
other, similar datasets.

A nonlinear interaction occurs when an electromagnetic field is present around black holes in certain theories beyond general relativity. This interaction can affect their thermodynamics, potentially leading to false conclusions about phase transitions caused by the radius of the shadow. In order to rectify this issue, we develop a new thermodynamic potential for these black holes that takes into account their electromagnetic properties. This potential enables us to explore the thermodynamics of both shadow radii and the photon ring, which are both sensitive to the presence of an electromagnetic field. Our analysis reveals that the condition required for a first-order phase transition to occur is much more stringent than previously thought. Our model can also accommodate both the "fingerprint" scenario and the "swallowtail" scenario of the Clausius-Clapeyron equation. Furthermore, we discover that the radius of the shadow is governed by a cubic equation that can be solved analytically, allowing us to study its behavior in different temperature regimes. Our study suggests that the shadow radius should be considered a second-order thermodynamic variable rather than a constant. Our conclusions are validated through numerical simulations of specific models. Our work paves the way for understanding the thermodynamics of black holes in various spacetime dimensions and different gravity theories. Our approach can also be applied to understanding the phase transitions of firewalls in both the laboratory and astronomical settings. Our research highlights the significance of appropriately defining thermodynamic potentials in false vacuum theories. Tensor network methods have commonly been utilized in modeling different types of equilibrium and non-equilibrium situations. However, these techniques faced a critical challenge as their algorithms generally necessitated a small bond dimension at sufficiently low temperatures or time points, despite a fundamental requirement for approximating thermal states and time-evolved systems where the bond dimension is directly related to system size. This issue was tackled by constructing a specific class of objects that are able to accurately represent the thermal expectation values and time-evolved behavior for local observables in any scenario, where the bond dimension is completely independent of the system's size and is only determined by the temperature or elapsed time. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these constructed objects in approximating thermal correlations and expectation values following a quantum quench event. All numerical data was obtained using the DMRG algorithm and compared with existing literature results. In addition, we introduce a novel type of tensor network that is capable of efficiently capturing the behavior of local observables in post-quench situations by tracing the dynamics of a single degree of freedom. This new method was successfully applied to several intricate scenarios, including a quench within the XY chain and the dynamics of Heisenberg's wedge billiard. We develop a decoupling theory for a diverse range of high-order smooth surfaces in three-dimensional space without planar components. Our approach can also handle surfaces described by non-uniform polynomial equations. By examining these surfaces, we create an opportunity to adapt and expand the concept of linear decoupling, incorporating a combination of Taylor series analysis and the development of a library of reference surfaces to facilitate approximation and decoupling purposes. Ultimately, our work provides a foundation for exploring and generalizing our findings to other types of surfaces. We demonstrate the applicability and versatility of our method by applying it to various exemplary surfaces. Additionally, we discuss potential applications and generalization strategies for our approach, including the investigation of our methods in relation to nominal surfaces and the exploration of our results in the context of sub-Riemannian geometry. Our approach and resulting surfaces have been implemented in the DecouplingSurfaces Mathematica package, which is available for download and use by the scientific community. This package not only implements our method but also provides an interactive platform to test and extend our work, fostering further research and experimentation in this area. We intend this contribution to be an initial step in a broader research direction, with the ultimate goal of broadening the scope of our research to other complex surface geometries, including those found in the study of signal decomposition and the analysis of nominal surfaces. We believe that this research democratizes access to the concept of decoupling for a broader range of scientists outside the core user base, ensuring the inclusivity of the scientific community. This work can be used as a teaching tool, with the accompanying Mathematica notebook serving as a interactive laboratory for students to explore and learn from. We anticipate applications of this research in various fields, including the study of nominal surfaces, the analysis of signals, and the geometry of surfaces, as well as the potential for extending this research to other types of complex geometries. This work can also be characterized as an artistic and mathematical exploration of the concept of decoupling, with the accompanying visualizations serving as beautiful geometric patterns that emerge from the application of the decoupling theory. We hope that this contribution will inspire future research, educate students about the concept of decoupling, and provide a source of wonder for the scientific community about the beauty and versatility of the decoupling theory. The impact of infrared renormalons in the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is being quantified, and calculations demonstrate how non-linear small-x saturation impacts shift the Borel plane's initial IR pole from $2/\beta_2$ to $1/\beta_2$, thereby changing the estimated uncertainty to approximately $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^2$ instead of $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^4$. Furthermore, an analysis of the dominant infrared renormalon in the variance points to the existence of a singular solution in the JIMWLK hierarchy that exhibits a non-trivial correlation between the mean and the variance of the dipole gluon distribution. Numerical solutions for the variance are also presented, showing that even in cases where the mean remains relatively stable, the variance exhibits a more pronounced x-dependent behavior due to small-x non-linear effects. Moreover, an investigation of the relationship between the variance and the mean reveals that the dominant renormalon in the variance is directly related to a specific solution in the JIMWLK hierarchy that displays a mean-dependent shift in its x-dependent behavior. Finally, an assessment of the estimated uncertainty based on the color dipole gluon distribution's variance is concluded to be directly connected to the x-dependent behavior of the mean, thereby implying that the predicted behavior of the variance is inconsistent with currently available data across a certain energy range. Nevertheless, as the model in question inherently lacks charge symmetry, a hypothetical scenario where the predicted variance's pole at $1/\beta_2$ is shifted to $2/\beta_2$ is examined, and the consequences of such a shift on the estimated uncertainty are explored. Additionally, a discussion on the variance's dependence on the number of colors is provided. Moreover, the impact of the color dipole gluon distribution's variance on the estimated uncertainty of the BFKL prediction for the DIS structure function at lower energies is also analyzed, using the BBNS equation as a reference. Lastly, possible extensions to the current analysis are suggested, involving the incorporation of infrared renormalons in other observables predicted by the BFKL equation, as well as the incorporation of non-linear effects in the JIMWLK hierarchy. The associated codes used in this research are available online. The findings presented in this work were obtained using the Minkowski function space harmonic transform code, the JIMWLK hierarchy solver code, and the Borel plane analysis code. Knowledge distillation is a successful method for accelerating deep neural networks by training a compact model to mimic the behavior of a high-capacity network. Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification outputs. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its class and the network's decision boundaries, which is used to assign a soft label to the sample. This allows for the training of a compact model through standard knowledge distillation. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo-samples are created based on the network's decision boundaries and assigned soft labels, which serve as a transfer set for training the model. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets and the results show an accuracy within 0.5% of the original model's performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/zsdb3kd.

Reinforcement learning efficiency can be significantly enhanced through imitation learning by leveraging expert guidance. However, relying on expert demonstrations is often impractical or too costly due to the high expense of gathering them. In this research, we introduce a pioneering Co-Imitation Learning framework to circumvent this issue. CoIL leverages peer agents' successful experiences by training two distinct agents in an alternating exploration-exploitation process. Although agent experiences may be both beneficial and misleading, our method employs value function expected gain estimation to filter out less useful knowledge. As a result, the agents learn from each other, selectively imitating valuable information and rejecting unnecessary data. Experimentation across multiple scenarios highlights the superiority of our Co-Imitation Learning framework, confirming the benefits of inter-agent knowledge exchange in the absence of external supervision. This paper proposes a metric function that yields an optimal performance on average, which significantly reduces decoding computations while maintaining superior error-correction performance for polarization-adjusted convolutional codes. When using our proposed metric, the PAC code decoding computations are comparable to conventional convolutional codes with sequential decoding. Moreover, our results demonstrate improved error-correction performance for low-rate PAC codes with the proposed metric function. We show that using the polarized cutoff rate as the bias in our metric function reduces the risk of incorrect path selection during decoding, leading to a 10dB improvement in sustainable SNR for a frame error rate of 10^-3. Additionally, our optimal metric function leads to a significant decrease in computations required for decoding, with a 10-bit reduction in computed history paths needed for decoding a specific code, thus making our solution applicable to practical applications. We also discuss the relationship between PAC code computation complexity and the bias in the metric function used. A practical application of our solution is demonstrated by implementing our optimal metric on a DSP to achieve an 8-bit reduction in computed history paths, resulting in a 2.8 times decrease in decoding computations while maintaining the same error-correction performance. In this application, our solution enabled the use of PAC codes on a DSP, which is crucial for future massive MIMO systems relying on DSP-based hardware. We conclude that our solution is a computationally efficient yet high-performance decoder that can be seamlessly integrated with future system architectures relying on PAC codes. In addition to PAC codes, our proposed metric function is universally applicable to other class-II convolutional codes with similar computation complexity characteristics. We recommend standardizing a universal decoder with our proposed metric function to cater to the future 6G communication systems involving massive MIMO technology. Research on intricate systems from the human brain to social connections has uncovered a higher-level structure that can be characterized through aggregates of interconnected triangles. To uncover these concealed geometric patterns, researchers are using topological methods and advanced graph theory to analyze and study dynamic processes occurring within these complex networks. This study leverages a recently developed model for triangle-based network assembly, where nanoscale triangular structures undergo spin reversal due to magnetic forces between connected nodes, fostering geometric frustration that drives novel phenomena in condensed matter physics. By manipulating the model's parameters, researchers observe how the shift from pair-based to triangular interactions affects ordering patterns, influencing the shape of resulting hysteresis loops. Moreover, the associated noise exhibited robust indicators of self-organization criticality, an emergent property solely induced by the intricate geometry of the network and not any inherent disorder. Findings suggest that spin reversal networks possessing triangular structures are capable of giving rise to noise-driven criticality, thereby potentially explaining the self-organized critical state observed in various natural systems. This approach paves the way for extending the model to more intricate triangular architectures, allowing researchers to explore the interplay between geometry, frustration, and criticality in condensed matter physics. This research agenda is designed to bridge the science underlying materials physics and more complex natural systems exhibiting self-organized criticality, both sharing a common fundamental structure of interconnected triangles. This study paves the way for a new interdisciplinary study combining condensed matter physics and network science with far-reaching implications for understanding natural systems exhibiting self-organized criticality. We studied the solar wind energy flux near the inner edge of our solar system using data from four different close approaches to the sun by the Parker Solar Probe, where we recorded data for 12-day periods right around each encounter. These observations took place as close as 27.8 times the radius of the sun from the solar center, and we based our energy flux calculations on readings for electron density, temperature, and speed, along with the bulk characteristics of solar protons. Combining the data from the four approaches, we found the average energy flux that could reach the solar surface and counteract gravity is about 70 Watts per square meter, plus or minus 14 Watts. Notably, this is similar to the findings of other researchers using data from different spacecraft and covering a longer time period, but with a key difference being that the solar wind energy distributions were much more symmetrical and normally distributed than seen closer to the Earth, likely due to the influence of solar plasma fluctuations being limited by the close distance. We also calculated the total solar wind energy flux that escapes the gravitational hold of the sun as 1 point 34 times ten to the power of twenty Watts, with an uncertainty of plus or minus 0.28 times ten to the power of twenty Watts, based on the assumptions of a constant solar wind composition and without the need for any additional information. We found no evidence for any variations in the energy flux with the solar cycle phase. We also tested various different models of solar wind behavior, but the most suitable one was one based on simple particle conservation laws, but we couldn't rule out the validity of other models. We also recorded data for the same periods of time for the number of solar protons reaching the solar surface and the temperatures of electrons and plasma, along with the speeds of the solar winds, but we found these remained remarkably consistent with previous findings of little variation across large areas of the solar upper atmosphere, but we did notice some slight differences in the form of slight shifts in the peaks of the energy distributions. We also calculated the total number of protons leaving the solar surface as 3.7 times ten to the power of 49 particles per second, with an uncertainty of plus or minus 0.8 times ten to the power of 49 particles per second. When the adiabatic index lies between one and approximately 1.16, these solutions consistently occupy all space without gaps, showing close alignment with each other. As the index surpasses this threshold, pressure drops to zero at a finite distance from the origin, and in both scenarios, a spherical void forms. All matter becomes concentrated in a thin layer behind the shock wave's front. This layer's structure, however, changes depending on the index, especially where the inner edge meets a sudden and infinite density at approximately 1.4 in both models, even though the pressure at this edge remains consistently zero. Exact solutions also reveal that when the index is over 1.4, the shock wave cannot sustain itself and will eventually collapse into a denser ball. Nonetheless, this collapse is slowed and the ball keeps expanding due to the universe's expansion, until the index is around 1.67, at which point the balance shifts and the shock wave moves towards the origin, growing more intense over time. A specific subset of potential properties is studied which comprise generalized Hermite polynomials, constructed through the use of Wronskians from standard Hermite polynomials, often seen in mathematical physics and random matrix theories. This class of quadratic potentials displays oscillatory behavior near the origin and we establish an explicit condition to determine non-singularity, including an assessment of localization with respect to polynomial index and the location of zeros within the complex plane. Furthermore, one-dimensional Supersymmetric Quantum Mechanics reveals that non-singular potentials arise from combining the harmonic oscillator with polynomial versions of Heisenberg's ladder operators, effectively encapsulating generalized Hermite polynomials through periodic closure, leading to solutions to the Painlevé IV equation and revealing a connection between Schrödinger operator discrete spectra and the monodromy-free property. Additionally, we discover that potential property classes can be distinguished based on polynomial index, leading to a natural hierarchy governed by Dyson's hierarchy of random matrix theories. Lastly, we demonstrate that the Laplace operator on hyperbolic planes displays the same spectrum behavior as Schrödinger operators possessing specific potential properties, thereby indicating that the property's spectrum is entirely determined by the Riemann hypothesis. The Yang-Mills-aether theory is analyzed to understand the implications of introducing non-abelian aether-like terms that violate Lorentz symmetry, as predicted by Quantum Field Theory. By incorporating these terms into the in-in formalism, we derive the non-abelian Boltzmann equation and solve it to determine the non-abelian aether distribution function, which leads to the discovery that this function defaults to a non-thermal equilibrium state and causes the expansion of the universe to slow down. As a result, we obtain non-abelian thermal distribution functions that describe not only non-abelian particle distributions but also non-thermal aether quanta and their interactions with these particles, thereby providing a field theoretical explanation for the thermalization of a non-abelian aether. We also find that this theory is capable of reproducing the momentum dependencies of infrared scalar condensates and refractive indices found in laboratory experiments, which were previously obtained phenomenologically. Furthermore, we apply this theory to study non-abelian symmetry breaking and mass generation in scalar fields. We discover that this breaking occurs even in the absence of any non-abelian symmetry breaking sources and that the associated energy scale can be lower than $10^{12}$ GeV, which is within the reach of present particle colliders and deep underground neutrino detectors such as the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE). We also find that these non-perturbative infrared effects could potentially impact the physics of the early universe, particularly during the symmetry breaking and inflationary stages. This research develops a method for estimating the expected cost of hedging European options through the delta-hedging process, resulting in a computationally efficient formula that accounts for option prices and the behavior of delta processes. Initially, a standard unit hedging cost is established and subsequently, the total hedging cost is determined as the product of this unit cost, stock price, a supply curve factor, and the square of the number of options. Consequently, this formulation enables faster computation of expected hedging costs than alternative Monte Carlo methods. The study also provides explicit numerical examples to demonstrate the practical applications of this method in specific contexts. Moreover, the research identifies the limitations of this approach, highlighting the need for more complex models that can capture dynamic liquidity characteristics and counterparty risks. Ultimately, this work contributes to a broader discussion on the representation of hedging costs in financial models, with implications for the pricing and risk management of derivatives contracts. In addition, it paves the way for extending this basic model to more sophisticated scenarios, thereby enhancing the versatility of this hedging cost framework. A higher education system or similar opportunities can drive social mobility across generations by allowing individuals to rise above their family's economic status. To examine this dynamic in societies with social mobility limitations, a new model allocates opportunities to maximize the benefits they provide to current and future generations. Our model reveals that, in order to maximize long-term payoffs, it's beneficial to give priority to lower socioeconomically situated individuals who have greater potential to rise to better socioeconomical standings. The result can lead to socioeconomic affirmative action. The duration and intensity of this practice vary depending on specific conditions. The proposed model also offers avenues for exploring more intricate relationships between different socioeconomical groups in various societal settings. Moreover, we discovered that there are specific parameters under which giving priority to the most socioeconomically disadvantaged individuals may not be necessary, and alternative, more complex protocols could be more beneficial, thereby suggesting potential future research on this topic. The proposed model has the potential to be applied to various real-world scenarios, including, although not limited to, the distribution of higher education opportunities, vaccination prioritization, and access to credit. The underlying principles of the model can be manipulated to better align with various societal values, thereby offering multiple possible variations. The study of cosmic microwave background anisotropies is a fundamental tool in physical cosmology research. However, the signal's weakness necessitates sophisticated and highly sensitive experiments that observe the sky across various frequencies with thousands of polarisation-sensitive detectors. As such experiments become increasingly sensitive, they are susceptible to being limited by instrumental systematic effects when trying to fully utilise their data. This paper presents a Python tool,'s4cmb', which generates simulated raw data streams in the time domain for contemporary cosmic microwave background experiments based on bolometric technology. The package also incorporates realistic instrumental systematic effects into the simulated data, with the goal of helping researchers assess the impact of such effects on actual data, informing future instrument design, and making simulated data sets more realistic for the development of accurate data analysis techniques. Examples of using's4cmb' are provided, including simulations of theoretical models and the investigation of instrumental systematic effects on the distribution of signal and noise components. The package is designed to be easily extended by the scientific community, reflecting the diversity of current and future cosmic microwave background experiments. The code is available online at https://github.com/CMBSystematics/s4cmb.

Furthermore, we discover improvements in using BART in a related task known as partial tree linearization. We also find that the current state of the art model for word ordering, LSTMs, is inferior to BART. All code and models have been made publicly available.
