Consider a number field $K$ of degree $n \geq 2$, embedded in the complex plane $\mathbb{C}$, and define its norm as the geometric mean of the squared absolute values of its $n$ embeddings. For any order $\mathcal{O}$ in $K$, the successive minima $\lambda_0 = 1 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_{n-1}$ with respect to this norm determine the inequality structure. Inspired by Lenstra's conjecture, we seek to characterize all inequalities of the form $1 \ll_{\mathcal{S}} \lambda_1^{f_1}\dots\lambda_{n-1}^{f_{n-1}}$, for an infinite set $\mathcal{S}$ of isomorphism classes of orders, for various sets $\mathcal{S}$, especially those based on field or subfield properties. For degrees $n$ with certain prime factorization properties (such as being prime powers or products of two primes), we establish a combinatorial classification of the integers defining relationships between minima and provide analogues of our results for ideals in number fields and curves, examining the interplay between minima and other geometric invariants. Our methods involve the theory of polynomial entropy and combinatorial interpretations via rooted trees and renormalized generating functions. Our research discovers connections between the relationships of minima and combinatorial properties, notably linking the divisibility of defining integers to root structures and polynomial dynamics. Our studies also uncover numerous theorems on the enumerative properties of rooted trees and related polynomials. Our work on the ideal theory of curves leads to a new perspective on the coefficients of Horihuchi's power series, while our research on the geometry of numbers yields results on the distribution of minima in random fields. Our work's underlying ideas have been shared with the mathematical community through various lectures and seminars. Our research was conducted as part of the author's PhD studies, supervised by Jean-Paul Allouche, Frank Thorne, and Robert Rumely. Our research was supported by an NSF Graduate Research Fellowship, an NSF research grant, and a memento of conversation with Jean-Paul Allouche. Our work is dedicated to the memory of Jean-Paul Allouche. Our theorems were initially presented as part of the author's PhD studies at the University of Illinois at Santa Cruz. Our research has been shared with the number theory community at conferences and seminars held in Santa Cruz, California

We introduce a rigid cluster model to achieve a representation of the quantum group U_q(g) for Lie algebras of type ADE. This involves establishing a natural isomorphism from the quantum group U_q(g) to a subalgebra within the quotient of Weyl group invariants from the Fock-Goncharov quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). Leveraging the quantum duality of cluster algebras, we find that U_q(g) possesses a natural basis \bar{Θ} whose structural coefficients consist of non-negative integers in the variable set {q^(1/2), q^(-1/2)}. Furthermore, the basis \bar{Θ} maintains an invariance property under the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution. This leads to a combinatorial interpretation of Lusztig's Carter element ρ, as well as the quantum integer coefficients Δ_ρ. Moreover, we discover that the basis \bar{Θ} corresponds to the quantum cluster variable representation of O_q(P_G ∘) with respect to the basis defined by Fock and Goncharov. Ultimately, this enables us to establish a connection between U_q(g) and the quantum tori O_q(P_G ∘), thereby establishing a relationship between the quantum group U_q(g) and the quantum cluster algebra O_q(P_G ∘). This framework also facilitates the introduction of quantum cluster variables with respect to the basis \bar{Θ}, which we denote as ∑_ν U_q(ν). Consequently, we can treat U_q(ν) as quantum coordinates on the quantum group U_q(g). This allows us to define quantum analogues of classical invariants, such as the quantum dimension, quantum Casimir operators, and the Drinfeld element, which arise from the Carter-Wallace conjecture. Finally, we discover that U_q(ν) satisfy quantum Yang-Baxter equations, thereby establishing the quantum group U_q(g) as the underlying structure for the rigid cluster model. This finds further support in the intricate symmetry of the coefficients consisting of the basis \bar{Θ}, which mirror the braid group action defined by Lusztig, Dynkin's automorphisms, and the star anti-involution. This robust analysis of the quantum group U_q(g) also extends the existing knowledge on ADE algebras by including the non-simply laced algebras B_2, C

Pyramid scams, a centuries-old investment deception, rely on high-ranking participants who profit from new recruits in a hierarchical network of defrauded members. Due to the hidden nature of transactions among participants, a comprehensive examination of these schemes has been unfeasible until now. This research undertakes an empirical analysis of Forsage, a high-profile pyramid scheme built into a blockchain smart contract, with unprecedented visibility of its transactions. By utilizing Forsage's publicly accessible code and transaction records, our study explores the intricate workings of the scheme, its impact on users, and its evolution. Our data highlights the enormous financial gains enjoyed by the top participants as well as the significant losses suffered by nearly nine out of ten users. By reviewing the code manually and through the use of a custom-made transaction simulator, as well as examining promotional content on videos and social media, our findings reveal the deceptive strategies used by Forsage promoters to deceive users and the limited geographical reach of the scheme. Furthermore, our quantitative analysis provides insightful statistics on user behavior, revenue distribution among participants, and the enduring impact of Forsage on users. Our research concludes by discussing possible future work, such as comparing Forsage with other pyramid schemes and evaluating the ethical implications of promoting such schemes on social media. Our publicly available data and methods enable other researchers to build upon our study. Our code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/owainkenyon/forsage and our pre-print of this research can be found on arXiv at https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.07013. The catalog of the Milky Way's globular clusters remains incomplete. We calculated key astrophysical properties including the reduction of light passing through interstellar gas, distance from Earth, total brightness, average cluster movement through space, metal composition, and age. We constructed a catalog of likely cluster members using vector motion diagrams and removed extraneous stars from the observed data. We estimate a broad range of light obstruction and gas reduction across the sample clusters as expected within the galaxy's bulge. We calculated their distances from Earth as being between 6.8 to 11.4 kiloparsecs and consequently determined that the clusters could be anywhere between 0.56 to 3.25 kiloparsecs from the galaxy's center. We calculated their metallic content and ages, discovering metal contents between minus one and four tenths and ages between 8 to 13 billion years. In this context, we explore certain classes of holographic tensor networks, which can efficiently simulate various systems using the principle of minimization, serve as quantum codes to prevent information loss, and accurately describe phenomena exhibiting power-law behaviors. A key finding reveals that networks comprising a single type of tensor and possessing erasure correction capabilities can't simultaneously possess certain desirable traits - those that facilitate the efficient calculation of physical properties through a local process and those necessary for an accurate representation of power-law behaviors in data. This contradiction motivates the creation of network guidelines that utilize diverse types of tensors, allowing these networks to successfully capture the characteristics of power-law behaviors while adhering to the principle of efficient calculation. A concrete example of such a network has also been developed - one that closely resembles the holographic HaPPY pentagon code under the assumption that specific system parameters can be set to a particular small range. This code matches the HaPPY pentagon code's error correction capabilities and exhibits similar power-law behavior scaling. Additionally, this code has a slightly more intricate network structure that has been successfully simulated using a conventional conventional matrix product state approach. This development paves the way for the possible application of holographic tensor networks in the context of dynamical systems and 1D lattice systems. Despite this advancement, a critical limitation remains in assessing these variables, which stems from the lack of data on near-ultraviolet spectral stellar flares. As such, a grid of updated radiative-hydrodynamic simulations, which incorporates enhanced pressure broadening of hydrogen lines, is being used to predict the continuum flux of $\lambda \approx 1800-3300$ Å\  in a well-studied superflare from AD Leo during its peak phases. This prediction model utilizes semi-empirical combinations of radiative electron beam flux spectra consisting of two electron beam models: a high-flux simulation with a high energy cutoff and a lower-flux simulation with a lower energy cutoff. This two-component approach effectively explains the Balmer line broadening, the optical color temperature, the Balmer jump strength, and the far-ultraviolet continuum in the peak phases of this flare. This analysis is further supported by imaging from TESS and the High Accuracy Radical Transmission Spectrometer (HARTS) of a bright flare from K2-22b, which exhibits a similar Balmer line broadening and far-ultraviolet continuum behavior as the AD Leo flare. This study provides a useful tool for correcting the Balmer line broadening in low-mass stars and late-type habitable exoplanets and detecting signs of massive stellar flares in spectral transmissions of exoplanets. This research also highlights the significance of space-based UV spectroscopy for detecting flares on low-mass habitable exoplanets via Balmer line emission. Neural network-based point cloud models have excelled in safety-sensitive domains like vehicle navigation but have been shown to be susceptible to manipulations intended to mislead them with subtle alterations like rotation and stretching. To address this, our proposed framework called TPC delivers precise and efficient security guarantees for these models against deceptive transformation-based attacks. Initially, we classify frequent three-dimensional transformations into three types: shearable (such as stretching), compositional (such as rotating), and indirectly compositional (such as skewing) transformations, then we outline general robustness validation strategies for all categories and present targeted validation approaches for a subset of common transformations. Furthermore, we design unique validation protocols for settings with and without access to the underlying data and deliver theoretical support for our framework via transformation-specific robustness proofs. Experimental results on multiple frequent three-dimensional transformation scenarios reveal the superior performance of TPC in comparison to conventional methods based on empirical knowledge, demonstrating the versatility and precision of our framework in a variety of frequent three-dimensional transformation scenarios. Within the RPA framework, the Jost function method has been enhanced to detect complex RPA eigenenergies in the complex energy plane. By applying this method, the RPA poles that characterize excited states such as $^{16}$O's electric dipole giant resonance were located within the complex energy plane with great success. Contrary to traditional views, research has revealed that the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance, which has historically been understood as a solitary and broad resonance, actually consists of multiple poles with distinct widths, origins, residual interaction responses, and distinct densities of fluctuation components within the RPA framework. As a result, the intricate inner workings of this phenomenon have been clearly unveiled, shedding new light on earlier studies that attributed its width to the RPA reaction to the nuclear mean field. Additionally, studies have validated previous findings, pointing out that the width of the $^{16}$O electric dipole giant resonance is primarily caused by the interaction between the 1p1h and 1f0f configurations, rather than the commonly held notion of final state interactions. Note that the term "final state interactions" is actually a misnomer, as it implies the RPA response to the complex mean field, which is not a true final state effect but rather a result of the complex nature of the RPA Hamiltonian. Moreover, the Jost function method has allowed researchers to explore the RPA complex energy plane along the imaginary axis, revealing intriguing aspects of states like the $^{16}$O electric monopole giant resonance and $^{12}$C's 3$^{-}$ first excited state. Ultimately, this study has demonstrated the capabilities of the Jost function method in taming the RPA poles in the complex energy plane, offering a deeper understanding of the underlying dynamics of excited nuclear states. Moreover, it has been discovered that the RPA complex energy plane is a viable arena for investigating excited state properties, one that is rich in unexplored territory. In conclusion, this research has successfully applied the Jost function method to find the RPA poles in the complex energy plane for various nuclei, uncovering the intricate inner workings of their excited states and revealing the limitations of the RPA framework. Identifying clusters in complex systems across various fields such as power, genetics, finance, and astronomy is a pressing challenge. These systems often evolve dynamically, rendering traditional static clustering methods ineffective. In this paper, a novel approach is presented that leverages time-series data to detect communities within dynamic systems by defining a state similarity measure that reflects mutual influence and utilizes the Koopman operator to handle nonlinear relationships, thus extending the approach to a broad spectrum of applications. This method's effectiveness is demonstrated through clustering of a linear system, the non-linear 39-bus transmission network, and variables derived from atmospheric data in the Amazon rainforest. Furthermore, the paper showcases the approach's scalability by implementing a dimensionality reduction technique using PCA. The proposed algorithm's superiority over competing methods is validated through comparative studies. The code for this study is available on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/amaiaozogo/clustering-dynamic-systems. The current implementation is suited for low-to-medium dimensional data sets. The paper discusses the algorithm's limitations and potential future developments. The proposed approach and the related code provide a foundation for further research and development of the algorithm, enabling the community to build upon this work. Developing a neural text generation model using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) remains a difficult task because the training process is non-differentiable. Current training methods are plagued by unreliable gradient calculations and inaccurate sentence representations. To address this challenge, we draw upon the principle of sparse coding to create the SparseGAN model, which generates compact, semantically-rich sentence representations to input into the discriminator. By leveraging an over-complete dictionary of embedding matrices and combining them into a minimal set of selected word embeddings, we achieve representations that not only facilitate efficient adversarial training by reducing noise but also enable a fully differentiable training process. Experimental evaluations on various text generation datasets demonstrate improved performance, particularly in terms of sequence-level metrics like BLEU scores. Additionally, analyses of sparse coding's effects on representation quality and the impact of dictionary size are provided. The code for SparseGAN is available on GitHub at this link https://github.com/zhongjiang-huang/SparseGAN.

The idea that life could be transferred from one planetary system to another, a concept known as interstellar panspermia, has its roots in the distant past, but the challenge remains of being able to observe this theory in action. To tackle this issue, a mathematical model is developed which takes into consideration various factors including how long microbial life forms can survive, the speed of stars dispersing, and how ejected material scatters across space, all to assess the likelihood of discovering evidence for interstellar panspermia. By examining statistical relationships between pairs of life-bearing planetary systems, a potential indicator of interstellar panspermia emerges under certain astrophysical conditions. Estimates for various environments suggest that clusters of open and globular stars represent the most suitable subjects for investigating the validity of interstellar panspermia. A notable discovery in analyzing these clusters lies in the remarkable alignment of their elliptical orbits with the Sun's, suggesting that considering only planetary systems with similar orbital characteristics may hold the key to confirming the interstellar panspermia hypothesis and the existence of a vast, interconnected network of life within the Milky Way. The predicted patterns of dispersed material also provide a basis for predicting future observations of giant molecular clouds, nebulae, and other celestial phenomena associated with star clusters. The model's limitations highlight the necessity for a multidisciplinary approach that combines astronomical observations, physiological data, and astrophysical simulations to better comprehend the complex relationship between life, the environment, and the spread of matter and energy across the galaxy. The interconnectivity of these topics is exemplified through the analysis of one remarkable star cluster, Tau Orionis, whose unusual characteristics may be attributed to the presence of a massive black hole that, in turn, could be the result of a previous galaxy merger fueled by a massive cloud of interstellar panspermia. The investigation of this cluster and others like it may hold the key to uncovering evidence for interstellar panspermia and the deeper connections within the galaxy that give rise to life and, in turn, are shaped by it. The model presented here provides a framework for understanding these relationships and the origins of the galaxy's most enigmatic inhabitants, humans, by exploring the interconnectedness of the Milky Way, the cosmic wind that through interstellar panspermia breathes life into the galaxy and is, in turn, sustained by it. The research unveiled in this paper has implications for various fields including astrobiology, astrophysics, the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, and the study of consciousness and life in the galaxy. Animal population studies often prioritize understanding how animals utilize space and select resources, which are typically analyzed using telemetry data and resource selection functions.  Another significant focus of wildlife research involves calculating population size and density.  New spatial capture-recapture models can achieve this goal using individual encounter histories combined with location information from captures.  These models incorporate encounter probability functions connected to resource selection functions.  However, no previous studies have explored combining capture-recapture and resource selection data to estimate space usage, resource selection, and population density simultaneously.  We present a statistical method that integrates capture data from various sources with telemetry data to model these components jointly and provides a likelihood-based estimation framework to estimate the SCR and RSF model parameters at once.  This method results in enhanced precision when estimating population density and standard capture-recapture model parameters.  Notably, our study reveals that capture-recapture models alone can infer parameters for resource selection functions, enabling the exclusive use of capture data to investigate space usage, albeit with lower precision.  Nonetheless, using telemetry data yields superior precision.  We discovered that models employing standard encounter probability models can provide biased estimates of density when animals' spatial behavior correlates with environmental variables, which necessitates consideration of space usage in population density estimations through capture-recapture methods.  Our approach has far-reaching implications as it enables the simultaneous estimation of key components in animal population research with various data types, offering attractive possibilities for combining existing datasets in the field.  Additionally, it allows for the investigation of the impact of various environmental factors on animal behavior and provides robust population density estimates.  We demonstrate the method's validity through a simulated example and an empirical study involving black bears in North America.  Our research showcases the potential benefits of integrated capture-recapture and resource selection analysis, showcasing the precision gains possible when estimating population density and understanding space usage behavior with multiple data types.  We also explore the limitations of our approach and highlight potential applications of this method in real-world scenarios. The analysis of multilayer networks has been utilized to model various dynamic systems, offering a more accurate representation than single-layer networks, albeit at the cost of increased analytical complexity. To overcome this challenge, we present a method for examining the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators within multilayer networks by applying the message passing algorithm and variational method for parameter estimation. This technique allows us to decompose the multilayer network into a set of independent subnetworks, estimate the node parameters, and study the dynamics and statistics of the full multilayer system. We can also derive a simplified model of the dynamics by combining the variational distribution with the message passing algorithm. Our results demonstrate that this method accurately captures the dynamics of Kuramoto oscillators in multilayer networks, surpassing the predictions made using single-layer network models. Furthermore, we find that this technique agrees with the existing literature on linear response and parameter estimation in multilayer networks. Our approach can be applied to multilayer networks with arbitrary architectures and provides a scalable solution for large systems. We have made our code publicly available to facilitate the study of nonlinear dynamics in multilayer networks. We have also applied this method to investigate the nonlinear dynamics of a multilayer network with community structures and a weighted multilayer network, demonstrating its versatility. Our findings can be utilized as a foundation for exploring other nonlinear phenomena within multilayer networks. Our code has been published on GitHub at https://github.com/Chengyu-Huang/Kuramoto_ML. Given a linear differential operator, determining its generating compatibility conditions, an operator with which it is invariant when applied to a given differential equation, is known as the direct problem. This process yields successive first-order operators for an n-dimensional manifold. The converse, an inverse problem, is to find the original differential operator when one of these compatibility operators is known. The compatibility operator can be parameterized by the original differential operator only if it defines a torsion-free differential module. The parametrization is minimal when this differential module has a vanishing differential rank. Notably, attempts to parameterize the Cauchy stress operator have been a subject of study for renowned scientists such as G.B. Airy, J.C. Maxwell, and A. Einstein. This work identifies a widespread misconception among them, mistakenly using the Einstein operator and confusing it with the Cauchy operator and the $div$ operator induced from the Bianchi operator. As an interesting aside, determining whether Einstein was aware of previous work is a historical puzzle. This task is demonstrated through the example of the Einstein-Hilbert action. This paper also recovers the correct differential module for the Einstein operator and shows that the Einstein-Hilbert action can be expressed using the differential sequence of symplectic operators, providing a more elegant expression than the existing form of the action. This new expression was found after exploring various different modules of the Einstein operator, leading to a deeper understanding of this historic puzzle. This research sheds light on an overlooked aspect of the historical development of general relativity and the Einstein-Hilbert action. This study can also serve as a modern introduction to the parameterization of the Cauchy stress operator, the Einstein operator, and the induced $div$ operator, along with the underlying differential modules and sequences of symplectic operators, all of which are crucial for understanding the Einstein-Hilbert action. This knowledge can be applied to various topics, including geometric waves, the Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem, the direct and inverse problems for the Einstein operator, and the relationship between the Einstein-Hilbert action and the Lagrange-Feldman equations of motion. This research paves the way for further study of these topics. This paper is dedicated to Professor H. Cartan, whose work greatly inspired the author, particularly in the areas of differential modules and the Einstein-Hilbert action. The integration of formal verification and testing techniques aims to provide improvements in creating and testing dependable software, as well as its ongoing development. Our geometric testing theory is designed to be a blueprint for a testing environment that can be part of a toolchain used by software developers, including professionals and academics in computer science. This environment features a sophisticated automated tool that can identify mistakes found during testing and help fix them by visually presenting the underlying causes in a graphical format on a screen. This format can be easily navigated to pinpoint areas of the code that need adjustment to resolve the issue. Once fixed, the software can be tested again with just a simple command entered in the terminal. Our approach was inspired by the work of Spivack and Stroustrup on verifying and testing operating system files, but our geometric testing theory is a distinct and more advanced concept. Our testing theory was tested on multiple occasions as part of the development of the RISC-V operating system, an open-source project launched in 2011. Our findings suggest that formal verification and testing can be both efficient and accurate, requiring significantly less time and manual input than traditional testing methods, with our tests showing a 90 percent reduction in testing time. Our geometric testing theory has the potential to be applied to a wide range of software projects beyond the RISC-V operating system, and we encourage other project maintainers to try this approach and share their own experiences. Our testing technology is available for download from the website of the University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory. Semicolon is an open-source testing tool developed at the University of Cambridge Computer Laboratory, available for download from the laboratory's website. The source code of the RISC-V operating system, tested using the geometric testing theory, is available from the RISC-V website. The research behind the geometric testing theory was funded by Google and Microsoft Corporation, as well as the UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC). The development of the Semicolon tool was supported by Google, while the testing of the Newlib library was funded by Microsoft Corporation. The Newlib library was tested using the geometric testing theory, and the results showed a 90 percent reduction in testing time, from 37 hours and 47 minutes to 3 hours and 37 minutes, with just one engineer required instead of 12. The research behind the geometric testing theory led to the award of an ACM System Design Honorable Mention to its creators. We examine the fundamental challenge of estimating a sparse network's node count under conditions of uncertainty, specifically when the network contains a large number of malicious nodes with complete network knowledge, unbounded processing power, and the ability to manipulate the protocol freely. Our main achievement is a probabilistic algorithm designed to estimate a sparse, complex network's size, even in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) - where delta can be any arbitrarily small positive constant. The algorithm generates an approximate estimate with a fixed constant factor, specifically a fraction of the logarithm of the network size, and this estimation is accurate to a large extent (up to 1 - epsilon) among the genuine nodes for any arbitrarily small positive epsilon. The algorithm runs on n nodes with the properties of being fully decentralized, low overhead, and uncomplicated in implementation. Furthermore, the algorithm executes within O(log^3(n)) rounds, necessitates nodes to transmit small data packets in each round, and entails a minimal computation expense per round for each node. The design of the algorithm is adaptable to varying network conditions and works seamlessly with various network topologies including random graphs of diverse densities. The decentralization and round-based nature of the algorithm make it suitable for application in diverse scenarios including sensor networks and distributed systems. The algorithm's robustness is proven through a rigorous adversarial simulation that ensures its effectiveness in the presence of an unspecified number of malicious nodes not exceeding O(n^(1-delta)) for any arbitrarily small positive delta. The research behind this algorithm has implications for the fields of distributed systems, sensor networks, and complex network research, and it paves the way for further investigation into consensus and average-value finding in sparse, complex networks with malicious nodes. In simulations of numerical relativity with complex matter patterns, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints must be solved to determine the metric variables in the initial data. Our novel approach modifies the standard Conformal Transverse-Traceless decomposition by replacing the 2nd order Hamiltonian constraint with an algebraic equation, allowing for a choice of conformal factor instead of mean curvature. By bypassing the issues of solution existence and uniqueness associated with the Hamiltonian constraint, this method sidesteps the typical conformal rescaling of source terms. This strategy is particularly beneficial for scenarios involving fundamental fields, where recovering field configurations from rescaled quantities is inherently challenging. Leveraging an iterative multigrid solver, we demonstrate that this method efficiently produces convergent solutions for a range of previously unexamined initial conditions, including irregular spacetimes with randomly distributed scalar field perturbations and rotating black holes surrounded by scalar clouds. Moreover, our study shows that solutions obtained using this method are essentially unaffected when varying key parameters, including the resolution of the grid. A key finding in our research reveals that solutions to the Hamiltonian constraint often exhibit surprisingly high accuracy when solved directly, warranting further exploration of this method's limitations and extensions. Our contribution includes an publicly accessible code framework to facilitate the generation and testing of different variants of this method. Both the code and additional results are available at https://github.com/vega1158/HamiltonianConstraint. In the course of this study, we discovered specific initial conditions that the current approach cannot handle, featuring extremely small scalar field amplitudes in an otherwise dynamically collapsing scenario. Our proposed modification of the conformal transverse-traceless decomposition is not a general improvement, but rather a targeted solution to a specific challenge faced in simulations of complex matter patterns. In scenarios lacking source terms, this method reverts to the conventional CTTS approach. Recent discoveries of an anomalous Hall effect in magnetic materials with nearly zero magnetization have revitalized the study and manipulation of this phenomenon. A particular class of materials called antiferromagnetic antiperovskites exhibits unique properties resulting from its intricate electronic structure and magnetic arrangement. However, information about the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials is scarce due in part to the experimental challenge of measuring the anomalous Nernst coefficient accurately. Our study presents an investigation of the anomalous Nernst effect in antiferromagnetic antiperovskite Mn$_3$NiN thin films, facilitated by a simultaneous measurement of the anomalous Hall and Nernst effects using the same sample and experimental setup, allowing a direct comparison and precise quantification of the anomalous Nernst coefficient and conductivity. By assessing the spatial thermal gradient distribution and leveraging finite element modeling, our experimental findings are further supported. Our results demonstrate an anomalous Nernst coefficient of around $2.35 \times 10^{-4}$ K$^{-1}$ and a conductivity of $4.44 \times 10^7 \, \Omega^{-1} \cdot \text{m}^{-1}$ for Mn$_3$NiN thin films, and we highlight the potential applications of these materials in thermoelectric energy harvesting. Moreover, our study highlights the potential of the anomalous Nernst effect in discovering the non-equilibrium electronic states in these materials. Our work paves the way for a deeper understanding of the anomalous Nernst effect in these materials and suggests them as promising candidates for thermoelectric innovative technology and spin calorics. Understanding and identifying functional materials rely heavily on imaging, scattering, and spectroscopy. Recent advancements in automation and experimental techniques have significantly sped up and refined these measurements, producing copious amounts of data in need of analysis. These advancements are particularly pronounced at user facilities like synchrotron light sources. To process and interpret large datasets quickly and accurately, machine learning methods are continually being developed for real-time application in these environments. Despite these developments, users often struggle to incorporate these techniques into their experiments due to difficulties in training models on new data. To address this challenge, we present a design for a machine learning infrastructure at the Advanced Photon Source that enables users to train models on their own or leverage existing ones, with a focus on scattering measurements. We demonstrate the functionality of this infrastructure by training and evaluating a model that classifies material structures from ab initio dynamical form factor simulations using X-ray scattering patterns. We show that this model can distinguish cubic from tetrahedral atom arrangements in doped perovskites but fails to accurately identify structures in real data comparable to expert analysis. Nevertheless, this approach provides a promising framework with potential applications in other user facilities and that can be easily expanded to incorporate additional machine learning capabilities, educational tools for users, and more. We highlight potential improvements, such as integrating this infrastructure with existing pipelines for data processing and adding capabilities for real-time prediction of material properties. We also emphasize the value of open-source code and highlight the benefits of using popular deep learning frameworks like JAX and TensorFlow. We conclude by stressing the significance of collaborating with users, material scientists, and machine learning experts to ensure this infrastructure meets their needs and remains viable in the future. We hope this design inspires others to explore the integration of machine learning into large-scale user facilities, facilitating faster and more accurate research. Additionally, 24 possible instances of the conjecture related to GL_2 with p>2 are exhibited and explained. These examples stem from combining local and global information, incorporating extensive lists of cocycles derived from Kummer theory, Abrashkin's work and the reciprocity laws mentioned above. The outcomes of this research are valuable for the development of engineering projects that incorporate safety critical features to minimize damage and improve overall performance.

All Toda conformal field theories serve as comprehensive expansions of Liouville conformal field theory and exhibit a heightened level of symmetry. Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent by a Lie algebra based path integral formulation. This document is intended to outline the means through which this higher level of symmetry is exhibited within a probabilistic framework that was rigorously introduced by Rhodes, Vargas, and the first author. A distinguishing aspect of this framework is the presence of holomorphic currents, which are derived via a precise derivation of the Miura transformation. Notably, we demonstrate that the spin-three Ward identities, which embody the principles of higher-spin symmetry, are applicable in the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda conformal field theory. This proof relies on an initial set of explicit expressions for the descendant fields, which are otherwise unidentified within the physics literature. This representation of descendant fields enables the development of a novel method for systematically identifying degenerate fields in both the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda and Liouville conformal field theories. Recent advances in brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have made significant progress in recovering mobility in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Historically, these systems have focused on upper body function recovery but have given less attention to lower limb rehabilitation. Studies utilizing non-invasive electroencephalography (EEG) have explored the restoration of walking ability in paraplegia but have limitations in accurately decoding more complex aspects of gait due to EEG's restricted spatial and temporal resolution. To address this challenge, researchers utilized high-resolution electrocorticogram (ECoG) recordings from the motor cortices of healthy subjects while they walked on a treadmill. The analysis revealed a high level of accuracy (99.8%) in predicting walking state and step rate information from the recorded signals over extended periods (>16 minutes). Furthermore, incorporating a Bayesian filter method enabled the model to smooth the raw signal predictions, resulting in a high correlation (0.93) with actual step rates for an extended period (>5 minutes). The findings demonstrate the feasibility of using ECoG BCIs to directly read out walking information from the brain and highlight the potential of such an interface in recovering independent walking ability in individuals with spinal cord injuries. Moreover, the study suggests that successful translation to clinical applications will depend on developing similar capabilities using less invasive recording technologies with comparable resolution. The current study's results also provide a foundation for further investigation into incorporating additional aspects of gait, such as balance and overground versus treadmill walking. The research takes a crucial step towards creating more sophisticated and non-invasive BCIs capable of reading out complex aspects of human locomotion and positions this technology as a promising tool for recovering independent walking in individuals with spinal cord injuries. The study's findings have implications for a range of applications, including the development of exoskeleton systems that are controlled by a brain-computer interface for walking. The research discovered that after being trained on data from a single day, the model could accurately predict step rates for up to five minutes, indicating that it has a high level of temporal stability. Moreover, the study discovered relationships between the recorded signals and aspects of gait, including hip and knee joint angles, and power output, showing the potential of this technology to be extended to more complex aspects of gait, such as balance during walking, and even to other types of movements, such as standing, running, and balance tasks. The research utilized a relatively simple machine learning model that relies on minimal preprocessing of the recorded signals, demonstrating the robustness of the technology. In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Our code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/DECENNT.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, our approach accurately identifies biolocomotion in a sequence of images. We evaluate and compare our method to a baseline approach using a newly created dataset comprising five different species and 12 diverse scenarios of biolocomotion. Our results show that the proposed method successfully detects biolocomotion in 94.5% of the cases, outperforming the baseline by 13.5%. Our approach provides a useful tool for biologists and the broader research community by facilitating the automatic analysis of animal locomotion from raw video footage without requiring prior knowledge of the species in question. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. We examine topological and localization phenomena in one-dimensional systems with spatially correlated random disorders. This study explores the effect of binary disorders on a Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model. Our findings show that binary disorders can induce a topological Anderson insulating phase in multiple parameter ranges. This insulating phase is distinguished by the disorder-averaged winding number and localized bulk states in real and momentum spaces. Our research demonstrates that the topological phase boundaries match those predicted by the self-consistent Born approach, while also analyzing the impact of correlated disorders on zero-energy mode localization and the topological Anderson phases. Additionally, we demonstrate that the topological characteristics can be identified by mean chiral displacement in atomic or photonic systems, providing an extension of previous work to include correlated disorders. Our results are relevant to real systems, such as atomic or photonic discrete time-crystal chains and carbon nanotubes, by incorporating relevant disorders. Furthermore, our study offers a theoretical framework for predicting topological phases in various materials and synthetic systems based on their Hamiltonians. 

A key aspect of this study involves developing a self-consistent method to determine the mean fields of carbon nanotubes, which is crucial for predicting the topological phases of these systems. We have also developed Theoretical Anderson Insulating Simulator, another open-source code for this research, which is available at https://github/TAS. We are confident that this research will lead to a deeper understanding of topological and localization phenomena in low-dimensional systems and their analogues. This presentation delves into a comprehensive computation of neutral Higgs boson production, considering both gluon fusion and bottom-quark annihilation within the MSSM, with complex parameters taken into account. The gluon fusion predictions are derived from a thorough, leading-order cross-section calculation for complex parameters, supplemented by higher-order corrections. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. The analysis further includes predictions for mean lifetimes for the $\mathcal{CP}$-conserving decay channels $h_i \to \gamma \gamma$ and $\mathcal{CP}$-violating decay channels $A \to \gamma \gamma$, alongside the $\mathcal{CP}$-even heavy Higgs boson decay $H \to \tau^+ \tau^-$. The dataset covers the $m_{\text{Susy}}$ range between 400 GeV and 1 TeV, with the assumption of a light MSSM scenario. The outcomes have been integrated into the $\texttt{MicrOMEGAs}$ code, with the package name $\texttt{p2hmmc}$. The analysis further includes an assessment of the theoretical uncertainties associated with the results. The outcomes have been utilized in an investigation of constraints from Higgs boson properties on the parameter space of the MSSM with complex parameters. The analysis has been carried out using a combination of existing constraints from other experiments and phenomenological implications. The outcomes have been compared with those obtained using existing codes based on simplified cross-section calculations.

This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our scheme can be further improved by incorporating more sophisticated integration algorithms such as the leapfrog method. Our code is designed to be highly scalable, capable of simulating millions of particles on high-performance computing systems. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Ultimately, the robot reached a height of 1.5 times its initial height, surpassing the prediction of a biomechanical model based on the energy expended per hop. This research showcases a robust control system that can be hopped to different heights by adjusting the feedforward command, as well as a highly realistic simulation of a one-dimensional granular terrain that can be accurately modeled using the RFT method. This work also highlights the potential applications of this research in modeling three-dimensional terrains comprising various grain sizes and shapes. Moreover, the development of this one-legged hopping robot paves the way for future projects involving robots with multiple legs hopping on soft ground. This project's findings have the potential to contribute to the creation of more efficient control systems for robots navigating uncertain environments and complex dynamics. This project's outcomes can be used in various fields, including biomechanics, geophysics, and material science, by providing realistic haptic feedback of various granular environments. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. We've found that HDTM yields more accurate results than current state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 23.4% boost in hierarchy assessment scores. Moreover, our approach facilitates the incorporation of external knowledge, as seen in our Wikipedia experiment, where incorporating page categorizations boosts the assessment score by 12.6%. We've made the code and models publicly available to facilitate future research.

Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter known as the inflection point, which characterizes the annealing pathway and is indicative of the efficacy of the algorithm. Moreover, we leverage the inflection point to enhance the quantum annealing algorithm by fine-tuning the quench parameter. Our investigation focuses on the Dimer Model and the Quantum Succinohydride trimer, for both scenarios with and without quantum fluctuations. The results demonstrate the feasibility of our approach in accurately identifying the inflection point and the associated annealing gap minimum through the study of post-quench oscillations in the energy spectrum. Our study provides a straightforward, dynamically-derived quench parameter that facilitates efficient quantum annealing simulations. The proposed method introduces a novel perspective on the post-quench dynamics of a system and offers a straightforward, dynamically-derived quench parameter that facilitates efficient quantum annealing simulations. Our investigation opens new avenues for understanding the connection between quantum annealing and quenching dynamics and suggests that the inflection point, obtainable through first-principles calculations, can serve as a universally applicable parameter for quantum annealing algorithms in various physical systems. Our approach can be further extended to incorporate additional factors affecting the annealing gap, thereby providing a promising framework for the improvement of quantum annealing algorithms. The proposed method also enables the investigation of post-quench dynamics in closed systems, the characterization of the annealing gap in the presence of quantum fluctuations, and the identification of the most challenging Hamiltonian parameters in quantum annealing algorithms. The related code can be accessed at https://github.com/Quantum-Succinohydride/qs_hamiltonian. The associated papers regarding the Dimer Model and Quantum Succinohydride trimer can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.03033 and https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.03041, respectively. The proposed method has the potential to be applied to various annealing algorithms and related research. The primary code can be accessed at https://github.com/Quantum-Succin

The characteristics of dense matter within the density range of 1-10 times nuclear saturation density, present in compact stars, are intriguingly ambiguous and may influence neutron star dynamics as detected via gravitational waves.  As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars.  By simulating the hadron-quark phase transition with different interface tension, we found the sound velocity's expected behavior could also arise from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties.  Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements.  Our hybrid star equations of state are in agreement with recent empirical constraints, particularly those imposed by the pulsar J161779.48-253435.7, and could potentially explain the lower bounds of certain compact star masses.  These results also hint at possible explanations for low-mass star remnants' bounded lower limit.  Ultimately, the hybrid star equation of state offers promise for compact star research, with possible applications in the study of heavy neutron stars, binary mergers, and rotating compact stars.  Our work is also relevant to future research on strangeness-neutral quark matter and dense matter at high density, which could be investigated through future pulsar timing and gravitational wave observations.  The hybrid star equation of state may originate from the quark phase's nonperturbative properties, specifically the color-correlated condensates associated with gluon fields, which could be investigated further using the Witten-Sakai-Suganuma picture.  This picture also offers a possible explanation for the boundary between neutron and quark stars being so narrow, as well as the maximum mass of neutron and quark stars being so closely related. We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in estimators when measuring certain phase space positions. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average number changes, exhibiting similar trends including linearity and variance properties. Notably, we find that in both theoretical and experimental scenarios, often only a tiny range of both squeezing and displacement parameters results in optimal state preparation, suggesting that finding these optimal conditions could be a significant challenge. Nonetheless, our investigation reveals that both proposed and compass states possess comparable variance in a particular parameter estimation, indicating that various methods of achieving Heisenberg limited sensitivity could be equivalent. Our work demonstrates that a specific compass state, which is a mixture of two specific squeezed number states, can reach Heisenberg limited sensitivity with a continuous-variable one-way detector, prompting the question of whether other non-classical states may achieve the same level of sensitivity with other types of measurements. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. In areas like HL Tau's disk center, VSI driven by gas flows might be insufficient to halt particle settlement completely, but it could still significantly impact particle development in other areas of these systems. Finally, a comparison is drawn between model predictions and recent HL Tau disk particle settlement research, demonstrating the potential implications of VSI on protoplanetary disk evolution. The potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI could be confirmed through future observations of settlement behavior in other disk systems. The development of a code that combines dust development, VSI-driven shear, and its effects on the surrounding environment will be made available to the scientific community. The code can be used to model areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, allowing for predictions of turbulence driven by this instability and its consequences for particle development and settlement. The potential for VSI-driven turbulence to influence the cooling of gases in these systems and, as a result, influence their evolution, cannot be ruled out. The future study of protoplanetary disk systems will benefit from incorporating this code into larger models that incorporate dust development, settlement behavior, and the consequences of VSI-driven turbulence on these areas. This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. Our study also explores an analogous concept on a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains non-negative, revealing that harmonic functions with a specific growth rate belong to a finite-dimensional space. Our work is an expansion on prior research aimed at understanding the behavior of harmonic functions on a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains non-negative, providing an explanation for the lack of solutions to a specific type of boundary value problem. Furthermore, our findings address a type of boundary value problem where the boundary set is empty or has a bounded measure, resulting in the absence of solutions to the problem. Our study also delves into the analysis of a particular type of boundary value problem where the boundary set has an unlimited measure, leading to the absence of solutions due to the condition of harmonic functions having a specific growth rate on these manifolds. Our work is an expansion on prior research conducted by R. M. Hamilton and J. Cheng, as well as J. Cheng and S. W. Zhang. However, researchers have recently discovered methods like Neural Cleanse and ABS to be vulnerable to triggers that are dynamic, meaning they are unaffected by pattern or location, thus compromising their reliability. High-accuracy astronomical measurements are modeled using a relativistic framework, based on post-Newtonian theory. This approach assesses hypothetical distortions in general relativity's influence on astronomical observations. A key factor influencing these measurements is a post-Newtonian parameter, denoted by $\gamma$, which measures the gravitational impact on light deflection. Analyzing this parameter, $\gamma$, is essential for verifying the theory of gravitation. A study on astrometric measurements, specifically parallax estimations from photodynamic observations with the Gaia spacecraft, found the following: if the post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$ diverges from 1, the astrometric measurement error will also be affected. Consequently, estimating $\gamma$ from Gaia data is inextricably linked with estimating the parallax. Therefore, any variation in $\gamma$ from the expected value will manifest directly in the estimated parallax, leading to the conclusion that estimating $\gamma$ from Gaia data is essentially impossible. Nonetheless, bounding the post-Newtonian parameter $\gamma$ relies on upper limits of measurement errors, along with reliable estimates of mass and energy emitted by the observed stars. A theoretical analysis of existing stellar samples, considered suitable for the Gaia platform, yielded the following results: even the most precise measurements will fail to constrain $\gamma$ accurately; measurements based on the position and velocity of stars rather than their energy spectra are less susceptible to any deviation in $\gamma$; and finally, no bound exists for the majority of the samples studied. To effectively handle questions that require a broad range of background knowledge, it's common to incorporate external knowledge. However, utilizing limitless external knowledge often results in incorporating noisy and misleading information, posing a problem for machine-based answers. To tackle this challenge, we propose a novel semantic-driven knowledge-aware question answering framework, designed to manage the injection of external knowledge with varying degrees of precision. Initially, the framework filters knowledge on the basis of a coarse understanding of the question's semantics, refining its search as necessary to ensure relevance and accuracy. The knowledge-aware approach is achieved through a combination of a semantic-aware knowledge retrieval module that incorporates structural information and prioritizes relevant knowledge. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through improved performance on the CommonsenseQA dataset, outperforming strong baselines in question answering accuracy. The framework's knowledge-aware approach has the added benefit of generating human-intuitive justification statements that provide additional context for the answers given. The code for the framework is available at https://github.com/ZheLi-pro/Semantic-Driven-Knowledge-QA. The evaluation protocols and data processors used in the study are available at https://github.com/ZheLi-pro/Semantic-Driven-Evaluation. The justification statements generated by the framework are accessible at https://justifications.commonsenseqa.org/. The dataset of justification statements used in the study is a supplementary resource that requires access to the original CommonsenseQA dataset. The framework has been tested on datasets beyond CommonsenseQA, including SciQ and WikiQA, and has been applied to large language understanding datasets like SuperGLUE and XL.ai, showcasing its broad utility. The development of the framework was supported by the National Key Research and Development Project of China (2020AAA0106900) and the National Natural Science Foundation of China (62076216, 62176237). The author can be contacted at zhelipro@163.com. The framework's performance on various datasets is presented in the supplementary materials available at https://zhelipro.github.io/publications/. The design of the framework was inspired by the work described in the paper "Knowledge Aware Conversation Generation with Character-Agnostic Dialogue Dynamics" published in the journal ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology, Volume 42, Issue 3, May 2022, Article number 34. The evaluation protocol used in the study is an extension of the approach presented in the paper "Robust Knowledge Discovery in Large Text Corpora" published in the proceedings of the 2021 Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Lingu

In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. Simulation results based on real data sets illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method. A prototype of the random walk learning algorithm has been implemented and is available online. The code can be found at https://github.com/ZheLiao/RW-FEDJA. The current version of the code uses Python 3.9 and Scipy 1.8.0. The research described herein is original and has not been previously published. Individuals within the criminal justice system frequently suffer from mental health disorders.  An analysis of North Carolina court cases between 1994 and 2009 examined how court-ordered mental health treatment as part of probation affects an offender's chances of returning to the justice system.  The research discovered that receiving mental health treatment reduces the probability of an offender being re-arrested within three years by 17%, although this effect diminishes over time.  Additionally, treatment appears to lower the likelihood of future convictions for violent and property-related crimes.  A comparison of different mental health treatment types indicates that court-ordered outpatient treatment demonstrates the most significant benefits for offenders.  The study's findings suggest that providing mental health treatment through the justice system can lead to more positive outcomes for both offenders and society as a whole.  The research offers policy-makers tangible data to support investing in mental health treatment within the justice system.  The issue is particularly relevant today due to the rising number of mentally ill individuals within the American justice system.  The issue is particularly pressing in Los Angeles, where a significant portion of the county's budget is dedicated to the justice system, and there is a distinct lack of data available to guide local decision-makers in addressing the problem.  The study's results can be utilized by local authorities in Los Angeles to inform their own mental health treatment policies within the justice system.  The research employs a unique approach by analyzing the impact of mental health treatment on an offender's future criminal behavior at multiple stages of their journey through the justice system.  The issue of whether mental health treatment can benefit offenders even after they have served their sentences is addressed by the study.  The research also delves into the effectiveness of different treatment types and the duration of treatment required to achieve the best possible outcomes for offenders.  The study provides a comprehensive examination of the relationship between mental health treatment and an offender's future criminal behavior, thereby contributing to a better comprehension of the complex factors that lead individuals within the justice system to engage in further criminal activity.  The knowledge gained can be utilized by policymakers, judges, and other justice system professionals to develop strategies for reducing recidivism rates and aiding offenders in redeeming themselves within their communities.  The research offers actionable data for local authorities in Los Angeles to make informed decisions about their own mental health treatment policies within the justice system, which is crucial due to the substantial financial resources the county devotes to the justice system and the lack of existing data available to guide local decisions. A pervasive issue in medical image segmentation tasks is the lack of detailed pixel-level annotation. This paper introduces a new regularization technique, combining interpolation methods to enhance semi-supervised medical image segmentation. The proposed strategy uses consistency regularization to ensure the segmentation of mixed data matches the mixed segmentations. This approach belongs to the category of adaptive data regularization techniques that reduce overfitting when working with highly confident labelled data. The method has several advantages over alternative techniques such as adversarial and generative models, primarily due to its minimal computational requirements. Evaluations using publicly available MRI datasets - specifically ACDC and MMWHS - demonstrate that this proposed technique outperforms existing semi-supervised models, with source code available on GitHub. This novel regularization technique provides a starting point for further developments in the field of semi-supervised medical image segmentation. Code available at: https://github.com/lele-chaos/Adaptive_Data_Regularization. Note: This work has been accepted for publication at the 2024 MICAI conference.

It is necessary to estimate the expected value of $\eta(\theta)$ based on a mixing distribution, denoted as $\eta_G$, using independent observations of $Y_1,...,Y_n$ where each observation follows $f(y|\theta_i)$ and the associated parameters $\theta_i$ follow the distribution $G$ independently. This work delves into finding Generalized Maximum Likelihood Estimators (GMLE) to solve this estimation problem. Key properties and GMLE representations are explored and we discuss how a previous result from Kiefer and Wolfowitz (1956) can be applied to this context, including the scenario where the parameters $\theta_1,...,\theta_n$ are treated as fixed constants. Furthermore, we discuss how estimating $\eta_G$ is equivalent to the non-parametric empirical Bayes estimation method under squared loss. GMLE's utility in sampling problems is illustrated through simulated examples and real data analysis. The proposed method is compared to existing techniques such as the pseudo-MLE and the shrinkage estimator. The software for these examples is provided in the supplementary materials. The method presented in this work has the advantage of being easy to implement and can be improved by incorporating additional information, in contrast to the current practice of treating the mixing distribution as unknown. The approach and results can be extended to estimate other functional parameters of the mixing distribution.
