Knowledge tracing has seen significant advancements through deep learning-based models, however the underlying factors behind their success remain poorly understood. A primary challenge lies in comparing these approaches, due to the lack of standardization in data preprocessing procedures and evaluation protocols. These inconsistencies hinder real-world applicability in educational settings. To address these limitations, we present PyKT, a Python-based platform for valid and standardized evaluations across various deep learning knowledge tracing methods. This benchmark platform incorporates PyTorch integration to ensure seamless implementation of existing deep learning knowledge tracing models and provides a standardized preprocessing protocol to ensure data consistency across models. Empirical studies conducted on PyKT highlight critical findings, including the risk of overfitting in deep learning knowledge tracing models and the unequal performance of these models when evaluated on test data. These discoveries emphasize the significance of rigorous experiments, adequate sampling, and thorough consideration of data preprocessing in knowledge tracing research. We anticipate PyKT to be a valuable resource for the community, propelling the field forward through transparent and standardized research practices. The PyKT benchmark is accessible on GitHub at the address mentioned below.

Given any manifold $M$, we demonstrate that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses closed range in $C^\infty(M)$. Additionally, if the manifold $M$ does not consist of any compact components, it follows that $P$ is surjective within $C^\infty(M)$. This is accompanied by an exploration of its applications to Helmholtz decomposition. Furthermore, it is proven that if a Lie group $G$ has no compact components in its manifold form, then the operator $X \mapsto \delta X$ is surjective across $C^\infty(G)$. This leads to a successful verification of an essential criterion for notching out an interesting subset of invariant differential operators under the conjugacy action of the Lie group $C^\infty(G)$, comprised of smooth maps from $G$ to itself. This achievement paves the way for an in-depth analysis of their intrinsic properties. In the process, some previously unknown information about the operator $\delta$ is uncovered, including the fact that it factors $\Delta$ in the context of Lie groups like $SO(n+2)$ and $SO(o+2)$. Moreover, a pertinent example is provided to demonstrate that there are Lie groups for which this relationship does not hold. This lies in contrast to the findings for the Lie algebra setting. Recently, end-to-end neural automatic speech recognition systems have achieved high accuracy, however, these systems demand considerable amounts of data and advanced computational power. Transfer learning has been proposed to overcome such challenges even across linguistic barriers, for example using a trained English model for German ASR. We explored this approach with much less related languages, specifically adapting an English model for Czech ASR, and discovered a simpler transfer method that significantly boosted the effectiveness. We used a modified alphabet without accents to make the transfer easier and observed this strategy to be extremely successful. Furthermore, our technique demonstrated potential when applied to Czech data alone, employing a coarse-to-fine training style. We were able to accomplish notable reductions in training time as well as the word error rate (WER). Our most successful outcome revealed a 19.6% decrease in WER over the random initial model when employing a small amount of annotated Czech data. Notably, our finest outcome used just 0.6 hours of annotated Czech speech. We also assessed the impact of our technique on various data sets and speech rates, discovering that our method is highly effective across various scenarios. Our proposed technique has the potential to be integrated into present-day ASR pipelines with minimal additional costs. Code available at https://github.com/czech.AI/fsttools/tree/master/tools/mert. Our novel TD learning approach overcomes several challenges robots encounter when navigating underwater.  By leveraging Gaussian Process regression, our method significantly boosts data efficiency by limiting TD updates.  To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods.  By deriving the posterior of the value function and utilizing its moments, we developed SPGP-SARSA: a new algorithm for offline policy evaluation.  Our results show that SPGP-SARSA outperforms the existing state-of-the-art in sparse methods and matches the accuracy of its precise equivalent while successfully being applied to underwater navigation.  Our approach also has a model-based variant known as SPGP-TD, and our experiments demonstrate that both methods excel in various underwater scenarios.  Our work paves the way for a wide range of applications involving sparse Gaussian Process models and delayed rewards.  Our code is available at https://github.com/HaithamAl-Awadhi/SPGP-SARSA.  Our project also involves a simulator for underwater robots navigating around virtual seaweed, accessible at https://haitham-al-awadhi.github.io/UnderwaterRobots/.  Our most compelling finding shows that our approach can successfully navigate this challenging environment, illustrating the versatility of our method.  Our work was supported by the EPSRC Centre for Doctoral Training in Autonomous Intelligent Systems and Robotics, a Wellcome Trust Institutional Strategic Support award, and an Amazon Web Services Educate Research Grant.  Our project was presented at the 2023 Conference on Robot Learning.  Our research was conducted under the supervision of Thomas Kalagay, Michael A. Osborne, and Stephen A. Marsland. We employ a 1+1+2 covariant semi-tetrad method to describe a static and spherically symmetric relativistic star comprising two fluids with anisotropic pressures, leading to the derivation of anisotropic Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations in covariant form. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts. Furthermore, using the 1.8 solar mass maximum mass limit, three known single-fluid solutions are examined. Lastly, three unknown parameters in the novel solutions are determined numerically using a nonlinear fitting method. These solutions satisfy both anisotropic and causal conditions, and correspond to solitons with regular horizons, albeit with small inner holes. These solutions also match the mass and radius of the known solution exactly, with improvements in the size of the solitons due to anisotropic pressures. The novel solutions' horizons' radii are found to be 16.853km, whereas the radius of the known solution is set to 16km. The novel solutions' masses and radii are found to be 1.799 solar masses and 10.821km respectively. We also investigate the impact of the anisotropic pressures on the novel solutions' masses and radii. The novel solutions are found to possess masses and radii of 1.841, 10.475km solar masses and radii in the case of $\alpha=0.01$, and 1.799, 10.821km solar masses and radii in the case of $\alpha=0.05$, where $\alpha$ denotes the anisotropic pressure parameter. Consequently, the novel solutions obtained here can serve as models for extreme mass ratio inspirals. The novel solutions are also applicable to the biospheres that may potentially exist within the surfaces of relativistic stars. The research method employed here can be extended to dynamic and rotating multi-fluid star cases. The issue of the novel solutions' inner holes could be resolved by the Casadiei-Diana-Starobinski mechanism, and even avoided altogether by the inclusion of quantum anisotropic pressures. The novel solutions' horizon's small inner hole could also be explained by the Tolman's surface tension argument. The research on the novel solutions also raises the question of whether there are multi-fluid star solutions that can survive the test of general relativity. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC across different language pairs and native speaker status. Our results indicate substantial gains across four datasets, with NIST-style exact match accuracy improving by 2.5 to 5.2% in many cases. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhongjiehua/LM_GEC_DDA. Moreover, our approach demonstrates potential applicability to other text modification tasks. With its cost-effective nature, this method offers an attractive solution for tasks with limited target domain data. The associated costs and performance trade-offs are thoroughly examined in our experiments. The proposed model is straightforward and employs standard deep learning components, enabling broad utilization across various settings and application scenarios. The related work section is accompanied by an empirical analysis of various factors, including the impact of source domain size, model pretraining, and the effectiveness of optimizers on target domain performance. Furthermore, our approach is compared to a state-of-the-art multi-domain GEC model, showing performance on par with or surpassing the current benchmark without the need for pseudo data. The associated code for our method is available on GitHub at https://github.com/zhongjiehua/LM_GEC_DDA. The issue of adapting sequence-to-sequence based GEC models to new domains with limited resources is addressed, fueled by empirical observations on existing datasets, including the presence of language pairs and native speaker status as separate domains. The proposed method leverages the strength of source domains to facilitate target domain adaptation, enabling the development of more general GEC models. The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, we discussed the limitations of our findings in the context of allocating goods to any number of agents. In the process, we obtained a generalization of a result established by Caragiulo, Paoulac, and Tsai, as well as another one of Plaut and Roughgarden. In the former case, our contribution involved showing that Round-Robin's fairness properties persist when considering any number of agents, whereas in the latter instance, we obtained the weakened fairness condition mentioned above. We also explored the relationship between our findings and those of Plaut and Roughgarden in the context of their method, which extends our investigation to two agents with heterogeneous valuations. In addition, we provided a new characterization of mechanisms with pure Nash equilibria inducing allocations that are fair up to any good in the case of two agents with heterogeneous valuations. Moreover, we discussed the potential implications of our investigation for the integration of strategic behavior into fair allocation frameworks. We also explored the relationship between our findings and those of Plaut and Roughgarden in the context of their method,

UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. The discovery of a similarly isolated HII region in the galaxy ESO 540-17 also hints at the galaxy's unusual dynamics being more widespread in this region of space. The research on UGC 8839 and ESO 540-17 highlights the significance of investigating the galactic halos through the study of extreme star formation. The unique dynamics of these galaxies may have implications for our understanding of galaxy interactions and the distribution of mass within galaxies. The extensive radio data from the VLA also enabled the discovery of three previously unidentified low-luminosity active galactic nuclei. The detailed radio, optical, and Hubble Space Telescope imagery used in the study allow for a comprehensive analysis of these galaxies. The research employs computational simulations to explain the observed star formation and present possible scenarios for the galaxy's evolution. The study on UGC 8839 and ESO 540-17 are valuable contributions to our knowledge of rare galaxy interactions and the formation of galaxy halos. The discovery of the low-luminosity active galactic nuclei in these galaxies adds to the existing database of such objects. The various observational tools employed in the study highlight the significance of multi-wavelength observations in the analysis of galaxies. The simulation data generated during the study are available for use by the scientific community. The research on the HII regions in these galaxies may help explain the distribution of mass within galaxies and has implications for the understanding of galaxy interactions and halos. The study also emphasizes the potential of extreme star formation to reveal the hidden masses and interactions in galaxies. The various datasets employed and generated during the research provide valuable resources

The results are further examined to determine correlation functions of two quark fields within a pion, expressed in terms of the Dirac matrices $\gamma_5$, $\gamma_\mu$, and $1$. Our approach establishes a direct connection between these matrix correlations and the quark currents in the pion, providing insight into the underlying physics. Our findings confirm that correlation functions associated with odd-parity quark fields are significantly smaller than those with even parity, reflecting the predominant contribution of even-parity quarks to the pion's charge and axial charges. Our lattice study also compares these charges to their continuum limits, leveraging continuum limit continuum extrapolations employed in previous research. A notable agreement between these results and those obtained utilizing the perturbative approach in QCD is observed. This agreement is particularly evident when utilizing the improved Kogut-Susskind quark action on coarse lattices. A further investigation into the matrix correlations of two quark fields within a pion reveals their temporal and spatial dependencies, shedding light on the quark distribution within the pion. Our study also delves into the correlation between the quark fields at the ends of a pion, discovering that the magnitude of these correlations diminishes in direct proportion to the distance between the quarks. Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is closely tied to understanding how
mass accretion rates are influenced by a star and its disk properties.
However, accurately using observed relations in this context is hampered by
not properly accounting for variations in mass accretion rates, a problem
especially prevalent in earlier stages of star formation. Conversely, we found
large-scale variations in mass accretion rates of one specific object, XY
Monet, and these fluctuations could be explained by an oversized
single-threaded accretion column in its disk. Based on this discovery, we
reexamined previously accepted relations that incorporate the $R_{\mathrm{acc}}$
parameter, which we now believe are incorrect. Instead, we propose a new
approach where mass accretion rates are calculated through $R_{\mathrm{acc}}$,
the radius of the accretion column, and the properties of the disk and star. 
We reanalyzed XY Monet's data and found its mass accretion rate to be 2.6 
times greater than previously thought, and we think this is a more accurate 
value due to the column's variability. If we use the previous method based 
on the $R_{\mathrm{acc}}$ parameter, we would overestimate the mass accretion 
rate by a factor of three. Thus, our new analysis yields a more stable and 
less prone to error value for XY Monet's mass accretion rate. 
We also looked into other objects with high mass accretion rates, like XY 
Monet, and found that their mass accretion rates are not always constant and 
can vary by as much as tenfold in a matter of days, with periods of lower 
activity in between. We think these variations could be linked to an 
unstable disk, specifically one with an oversized accretion column, and it 
could hold the key to understanding why some stars stop accreting and why 
their disks stop evolving as expected. 
We also explored the mass accretion rates of some other objects with similar 
characteristics to XY Monet, like HHH79 and MWC 297, and found their mass 
accretion rates are also not always constant and can vary by as much as 
fiftyfold in a matter of weeks, with periods of lower activity in between. 
We think these variations could be linked to an unstable disk, specifically 
one with an oversized accretion column,

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based value function to assess the importance of each trajectory and prioritize the most beneficial ones. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior performance in complex scenarios and settings, including both single-agent and multi-agent scenarios, and demonstrates the advantages of attention mechanism over traditional approaches. Our work and methodology are thoroughly evaluated and compared with six baseline methods, leading to a deeper understanding of the limitations and strengths of different solutions. The SIT framework's code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/keg-ai/SIT. The underlying evaluation data have been deposited on a Zenodo platform at https://doi.org/10.52853/D156588. The design and implementation of the SIT framework have been patented (CN501141181S, CN501141182S, CN501141183S). We developed a novel approach for registering MV images, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network, in both 2D and 3D. Traditional image registration techniques are largely intensity-based and leverage optimization algorithms to align images, yet they fall short for low-quality megavoltage images and have limited capture ranges. To overcome these challenges, we employed a Convolutional Neural Network, resulting in a dataset-based comparison using 50 brain images, which demonstrated improved results relative to conventional methods. The effectiveness of our technique was further validated on a larger dataset of 100 abdominal images and megavoltage images, showing it outperformed conventional methods registration capture ranges by 4-5x and 2-3x, respectively. Additionally, our model successfully applied to 3D images, demonstrating potential for extension to higher dimensions. The code for this research has been made publicly available on GitHub, along with the benchmark dataset. Nonetheless, further evaluation is necessary to fully assess the robustness of our approach to varying clinical datasets and protocols. The potential of this Convolutional Neural Network-based method to enhance megavoltage image registration has been demonstrated; however, future work must concentrate on integrating this technique with existing treatment planning systems and exploring methods to decrease the manual effort required to prepare training datasets. The underlying challenge of acquiring sufficiently diverse training datasets remains a critical obstacle to widespread clinical adoption. The current version of the code and dataset can be found at https://github.com/QinbinHe/MV-IR-NET. In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Additionally, our study highlights the distinction between single-particle entanglement and the entanglement of two particles, highlighting the mistaken perception that single-particle entanglement is inherently two-party in nature. Ultimately, our findings provide a practical illustration of how single-particle non-locality can give rise to two-party entanglement, thereby demonstrating that two-party entanglement arises from an over-simplification of single-particle entanglement rather than being a fundamental phenomenon. We also propose that single-particle non-locality could serve as the basis for a new class of quantum applications, taking advantage of its unique capacity to become 'tuned in' to the characteristics of a specific detector before influencing another's quantum state. We have further investigated the feasibility of utilizing single-particle non-locality in a three-party scenario, demonstrating how it can give rise to two-party entangillation, which in turn leads to the phenomenon of quantum teleportation being executed with perfect fidelity without the necessity for an initial entangled channel. In this process, our study has been accompanied by numerical simulations that have been compared to experimental results obtained using both mature and next-generation quantum systems. We have also explored the limitations of these systems, highlighting the distinction between coherent and incoherent entanglement as well as the decay of coherent entanglement due to various decoherence effects. A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Numerical results demonstrate the benefits of this novel method, notably in situations with insufficient pilot transmission, where the GMM alone serves as feedback, yielding the largest performance gain. Furthermore, the design is integrated into a joint power loading and precoder codebook optimization problem, solved using an iterative algorithm, with simulated results showing the potential for additional performance enhancement. Numerical examples are provided using real-world data, including the Vodafone 4G network parameters, highlighting the algorithm's flexibility with varying system conditions and allowing for different GMM-based codebook configurations. The proposed technique's advantages are shown to extend beyond beamforming feedback, with the potential to enhance other applications involving GMMs, channel selection, and frequency hopping. The codebook design method is made available online, enabling users to generate precoder codebooks tailored to their specific network environments. The algorithm's iterative nature takes approximately one to two minutes to solution, with the option to adjust parameters such as GMM size, codebook size, and optimization accuracy. The approach is initially tested using 500 GMM components and a codebook consisting of 81 entries, with the option to exchange the GMM with different sizes and codebooks of varying sizes. The algorithm's performance is assessed using various metrics, including the GMM responsibility, codebook entry similarity, and output power, with the recommended parameter settings producing the best results across these criteria. The algorithm's robustness is evaluated using different GMM and codebook configurations, with the results showing the stability of the proposed method, able to converge to the optimal solution even with varying initial conditions, indicating the effectiveness of the iterative approach. The algorithm's potential is also demonstrated in scenarios with multiple terminals, demonstrating the flexibility of the GMM-based codebook design approach, with the potential for further exploration in other areas, such as channel selection and frequency hopping

A type of genuine two-dimensional crosscurrent that flows counter to the heat flux direction has been lacking in scientific knowledge since its one-dimensional counterpart was discovered. A setup for realizing these currents on a three-dimensional cubic lattice has been devised by coupling a Hofstadter model to two separate heat baths of varying temperatures. Research demonstrates that the robustness of these currents can withstand various imperfections and tilting within certain nonequilibrium conditions. Additionally, boundary currents with robust stability were found, and the condition of being three-dimensionally robust indicates they require tunneling capabilities across all three spatial dimensions. The model exhibits robust surface currents applicable to both bosons and fermions, and the mechanisms of discrete symmetries were found to significantly contribute to the surface currents' stability. The minimal three-dimensional cubic lattice model exhibits robust surface currents with three-dimensional tunnelling and withfulness that is not seen in lower dimensional models, and the lack of any sign of the Friedel oscillations indicates that the model is completely "clean" of any kind of scattering. The model's robust surface currents can withstand any kind of impurity, whether it be point-like, gradient-like, time-like, lattice-like, chemical potential-like, or any combination of these, as long as there is sufficient nonequilibrium conditions, and the robust surface currents were found to be non-chiral, three-dimensionally robust, and can be exacted from the bulk by changing the chemical potential rather than the hopping amplitude. The model's surface current robustness can withstand any tilting of the lattice potential, any kind of boundary conditions, and any combination of the above-mentioned impurities, as long as there is sufficient nonequilibrium conditions, and the robust surface currents were found numerically using the iDMTG algorithm with several hundred thousand sampling points for each parameter set. The research indicates that the surface currents' stability is the result of discrete symmetries rather than any kind of topological protection, and the model's surface current robustness can be realized on any kind of lattice as long as it is three-dimensionally robust. For asymptotically flat spacetimes, where light is emitted at a distance from the gravitational source, research indicates that the Bondi mass aspect must satisfy specific requirements to reach the point of infinity without obstruction. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. We also introduce a straightforward method to compile individual game scenarios quickly, mapping them to a vector of integers with minimal loss of information, resulting in a significant further boost in simulation speed of about ten times, while retaining solution similarity at approximately eighty percent. Our data and software are available for download, awaiting use by the virtual agent research community. Our benchmark is easy to run on a variety of platforms, including a pixel-based desktop environment, and consists of both visual representations of text-based game scenarios and the express version of the games itself. We strongly believe that faster, more complex text-based games will continue to play a crucial role in evaluating virtual agent capabilities across various domains. Our mission is to contribute to the advancement of this essential research tool, hoping it will benefit the community for many years to come. Our code and data are accessible on GitHub at https://github.com/tuebingen-aia/textworldexpress, along with the express versions of the existing challenging text-based games - 'MiniGolf', 'Adventure', and 'Zork'. We urge researchers to leverage our work, the ease with which it was created, and the possibilities it offers, to contribute their own fast text-based games for the community's benefit. Our goal is to continually improve and expand the portfolio of fast text-based games available to the virtual agent research community, until such time that the need for them ceases to be essential. Our initial contribution lays the groundwork for this vision, and we look forward to building upon it in the future. Our research is an extension of our earlier work presented at the Conference on Artificial Intelligence, 2020. Deep learning models such as Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) have been highly effective in various sequence analysis tasks but suffer from limitations in their practical application due to their size. This problem is particularly pronounced in video recognition, which involves high-dimensional data. In an attempt to overcome these constraints and unlock the full potential of LSTMs, this research proposes an integrated architecture that combines internal state and input data at multiple levels to enhance performance and reduce model size. The suggested design, termed Multi-Level Gated LSTM (MLGL), successfully uses a coarse code from a pre-trained compact LSTM as its baseline, and significantly improves accuracy by operating on multiple levels of abstraction. The proposed MLGL architecture achieves superior performance on two video recognition datasets, Cifar-10 and Kinetics-400, surpassing the state-of-the-art results at the time of submission with the added benefit of utilizing 60 times less data than traditional methods. The code for this research has been made publicly available on GitHub. The proposed MLGL architecture has the potential to be applied to other sequence analysis tasks beyond video recognition. The proposed architecture has inherent noise reduction properties that enable efficient learning on feature extracts from pre-trained compact LSTMs. The research on the proposed architecture provides a solution to the data dimensionality problem typical of video recognition and extends the applicability to other high-dimensional data scenarios. The proposed architecture has the capability to exploit coarse codes from various pre-trained compact LSTMs, enabling the evaluation of different backbones and encoders, which can be easily extended to other applications. The integrated design also enables the architecture to be viewed as a form of deep compressed sensing, where the multiple level structure provides the geometric and algebraic conditions required for accurate recovery, thereby enabling the recovery of complex patterns from highly compressed codes. The research proposes a new form of blind deconvolution, multi-level deconvolution, which is a natural extension of the proposed architecture and provides the mathematical framework required for its evaluation. The concept of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is often expressed through its effect on the mass-to-charge ratio of a particle. Another approach posits its fundamental expression is tied to the convexity of a particle's charge spectrum. We advance this idea by examining a conformal field theory with a semi-simple global symmetry group and propose the Charge Convexity Conjecture, stating the spectrum of charges within the conformal window is driven by a single convex function. We investigate the impact of changing the number of fundamental monopoles in a certain type of Emden transform on the charge spectrum and find it follows a specific power-law pattern consistent with the proposed conjecture. Furthermore, we find that the radius of the conformal window scales with the number of fundamental monopoles in accordance with 't Hooft's prediction. We also consider extensions to our framework incorporating multiple conformal window regimes and non-trivial hybridization between fundamental monopoles. Our research findings are underpinned by thorough analytical and numerical field theory calculations, with additional insights gained from a simple harmonic oscillator model. Our proposed Charge Convexity Conjecture offers a novel explanation for the observed scaling of the conformal window with the number of fundamental monopoles. Our work provides a potential new framework for understanding the physics driving the weak gravity conjecture, alongside other observed phenomena in theories with a U(1) global symmetry. Our results are consistent with the established behavior of the Standard Model in the context of its embedding in the Standard Model Landscape. Our research also sheds light on the Charge Convexity Conjecture's extension to theories with multiple conformal window regimes and non-trivial hybridization between fundamental monopoles. Given a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic and its primary ideal in terms of an $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, we establish criteria for $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function of that ideal. These criteria make use of a specific polynomial and its coefficient. Additionally, we provide a lower bound for the tight Hilbert function that extends a previous result from Goto and Nakamura, which specifically holds true in equidimensional excellent local rings. If the ring has a specific dimension, we demonstrate the connection between the tight Hilbert function and its lower bound, achieving this condition implies that the ring is $F$-rational. Based on a suggestion by Ha and Nguyen, we further investigate the relationship between $F$-rationality and the tight Hilbert function in a particular type of local ring with a specific prime characteristic. We conclude by presenting an example that demonstrates the impossibility of characterizing $F$-rationality based on the tight Hilbert function alone, even in a type of local ring with a specific prime characteristic and specific dimension. Additionally, we offer a counterexample to the speculation provided by Ha and Nguyen concerning the relationship between $F$-rationality and the coefficient of a particular polynomial in the tight Hilbert function. We also furnish a more general approach to finding the tight Hilbert function in a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic, based on a particular $\mathfrak{m}$-primary parameter, which may be either non-zero or one. We utilize this approach to determine the tight Hilbert function in certain types of local rings with a specific prime characteristic, which include local rings considered $F$-rational by Ha and Nguyen as well as local rings that are not $F$-rational. We conclude this research paper by proposing several problems for future study concerning the tight Hilbert function in a Noetherian local ring with a specific prime characteristic. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. Additionally, when all-or-none design is used, there is an elevated risk of failure to fulfill orders during peak periods, and this may result in involuntary electricity curtailment for end-users unless sufficient reserve power is available. Nonetheless, when participants are allowed to cancel parts of their orders, this risk is mitigated. Schemes that penalize participants for failed redispatch also demonstrate undesirable effects in this scenario. The model code and example results are available on GitHub at the Ancillary Services Acquisition Model webpage.
The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model consists of the following components: MESA GBIC framework (v1.1.0), PyPSA-IOPSEA toolset (v0.4.0), Pypsa solver interface (v1.3.1), CPLEX solver (v12.10.0.0), GCBIO interface (v1.1.0), Matplotlib library (v3.4.3), Seaborn library (v0.9.0), Scipy library (v1.4.1), NumPy library (v1.19.2), Pandas library (v1.3.5), and Cy

Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact temperatures as high as 300 km above the clouds. The reduction in the strength of this wave during the summer leads to a decrease in the formation of new vortices in the south and an increase in the size of the existing one. The increased temperature in the vortex in the north reached as high as 160 degrees Kelvin above the equilibrium temperature, which is likely the result of the reflection of sunlight from large ice particles rather than an increase in the temperature of the surrounding atmosphere. The decrease in the number of vortices in the south and the increase in the size of the one in the north resulted in the formation of a persistent chemical haze on the north pole, which in the past had formed in the south. This led to a decrease in the amount of ozone in the south and an increase in the amount of methane. The research on the South Polar Stratospheric Vortex demonstrates the long-lasting impact of the formation of these polar vortices on the atmospheric chemistry of Saturn and highlights the influence of the solar insulation on the formation of ice particles deep in the planet's atmosphere. The study also reveals the intricate connections between the atmospheric systems at different heights and latitudes in the Saturn system. The comprehensive analysis of the data collected from the 16-month-long exploration of the Saturn system enables the creation of detailed movies of the temperature and chemical composition of the upper atmosphere of the planet. We create a linearisation functor for full linearisation that transforms a graded bundle of degree k into a k-fold vector bundle. Our analysis defines the image of the full linearisation functor, resulting in a subcategory of k-fold vector bundles. These vector bundles are equipped with symmetric morphisms associated with the symmetric group Sn. A significant observation arises in the degree 2 scenario, k=2, where this added structure leads to the concept of self-dual vector bundles, though it's worth noting that the term "self-dual" may cause confusion. It is advisable to use the term "symmetric" instead. Another finding reveals that the process of full linearisation can be viewed as an change of context from graded bundles to these newly defined symmetric bundles, though this process is not reversible. Ultimately, our investigation provides examples of symmetric bundles arising from full linearisation. These examples include segments of curves, surfaces identified by their self-isomorphisms, and Kummer configurations. Moreover, we discover that the process of full linearisation can also be applied to vector bundles over curves, though this leads to a loss of important information, such as the bundle's rank. Nonetheless, this approach can still be used to fully linearise line bundles, or more broadly, invertible bundles. Perhaps the most notable outcome of this approach comes from applying the process to the Picard group of the curve, though this leads to a new category of weighted bundles. These weighted bundles are linked to the full linearisation of the original curve, thereby ensuring the process is meaningful. Ultimately, this approach paves the way for a deeper analysis of the Picard group of the curve in question. Moreover, this investigation highlights the potential applications of full linearisation to various other mathematical constructs, including coherent sheaves and their properties. Perhaps the most notable finding arises in the degree 2 scenario, where the process of full linearisation can be viewed as the result of a group action associated with the braid group B2, though this is not a universally applicable conclusion. It is also noteworthy that the process of full linearisation can be seen as linking the duals of Serre duality and the Hom sheaf. Ultimately, this investigation provides a foundation for further research aimed at connecting full linearisation to other mathematical constructs, such as the Grothendieck ring of the curve in question. Moreover, this research paves the way for extending the process of full linearisation to higher degrees of graded bundles, though this extension requires a different approach. We introduce a novel mixed finite element approach for single-phase Darcy flow within a fractured porous media, incorporating two types of fractures. These fractures can be viewed as interfaces within a $d$-dimensional space, where $d$ equals either $2$ or $3$. A significant distinction is drawn between fractures with notably high and low permeability compared to their surrounding medium, categorized as conductive and blocking fractures respectively. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. We plan to enhance and refine this research in the future, with the aim of providing a valuable toolkit for the cognitive science community. We also invite fellow researchers to collaborate with us and contribute their own data sets for further analysis. We intend to maintain an updated version of the software, incorporating valuable feedback from the scientific community, with the ultimate goal of establishing standardized methods for Bayes factor analysis that can be applied across various disciplines. In the process, we hope to promote greater transparency in the analysis of scientific hypotheses by providing accessible code and expertise to the cognitive science community, with the potential for these methods to be adapted for use in other fields of research. Discourse indicators such as "by contrast" and "happily" facilitate the identification of connections between sentences. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. Experimental evaluations on existing datasets demonstrate the versatility of this approach and the derived characteristics of DiscSense are distinct from existing, often manual, annotations of discourse indicators. Furthermore, a comparison is made between characteristics automatically predicted by the model and existing manual annotations, revealing both similarities and divergences. Ultimately, this research lays the groundwork for a deeper understanding of the intricate connection between discourse indicators, semantic relations, and the English language structure. A thorough examination of the resultant dataset and predicted characteristics is also conducted on multiple existing semantically annotated datasets, spanning three categories of discourse indicators based on their supposed meanings. A discernible correlation is observed between the complexity of these categories and the model's prediction accuracy. A utility of this research is highlighted through the enhancement of BERT-based models on classification tasks involving semantic relations, utilizing the predicted discourse indicators as additional classification features. A notable improvement in accuracy is achieved on certain datasets, demonstrating the practical implications of this research. A summary of the findings, potential limitations, and future research possibilities is presented. A novel approach is proposed for assigning discourse indicator categories based on part-of-speech tags, a more unified and a universally accepted classification system, which is applicable to the derived characteristics of DiscSense. A potential future direction is also explored through the generation of artificial sentences and corresponding discourse indicators for the purpose of training natural language inference models. We investigate a general matrix optimization problem subject to a fixed-rank positive semidefinite constraint and perform the Burer-Monteiro factorization to analyze its landscape under a particular Riemannian quotient geometry. Assuming standard strong convexity and smoothness properties for the objective function f, we find that its factorized version exhibits distinct behaviors in three regions: (1) near the target parameter of interest, it is geodesically strongly convex and smooth; (2) it has neighborhoods of strict saddle points; and (3) it has large gradients in remaining areas. We contribute a global landscape analysis under the Riemannian quotient geometry for the first time and provide a geometric explanation for the effectiveness of vanilla gradient descent in this setting. When f satisfies a weaker convexity property, we discover a geodesically convex neighborhood around local minimizers. To achieve these results, we analyze a matrix factorization problem with a least squares objective, providing a critical connection, and also establish an independent result regarding the convexity of geodesic balls under the Riemannian quotient geometry. We demonstrate the applicability and usefulness of these findings with theoretical and empirical studies on various applications, including tensor completion, community detection, and multiview embedding. Our open-source implementation is available at https://github.com/Qianqing Clair/ RMLandS4Nij. We also provide a geographic baseline extractor as a supplement to this work. When applied to facial expression images, it shows promising results, as illustrated in the supplementary materials. A graph's edge coloring can be described as assigning different colors to edges based on a specific distance constraint between any two colored edges, effectively mirroring a particular arrangement of the original graph's colors on its reverse. This interpretation leads to a new problem formulation that involves finding the minimum number of colors required for a given condition to be satisfied on the graph's reverse, which we have termed the minimum $k$-colorable distance of a graph ($\chi_d^k$). This concept is particularly interesting for its connection to strong edge coloring, and we have a non-negative result for $\chi_d^2$, alongside specific examples and the observation that it is possible to achieve the maximum $\chi_d^2$ value for certain types of graphs. Additionally, we have an algorithm solving $\chi_d^2$ for tree graphs with the time complexity of O(|E|), and a declaration that determining $\chi_d^k$ for an arbitrary k is solvable in polynomial time on cographs. Furthermore, we have an inequality relating the minimum number of colors required for a given distance condition on a graph and its components, as well as the maximum $\chi_d^2$ value for certain graph configurations that arise from combining two specific types of graphs. This research originated from an problem related to the improvement of an earlier result regarding the maximum number of colors that can be used in a strong edge coloring. Introducing "social-learning" variations of two algorithms led to successful attainment of Nash Equilibrium, unlike "individual learning" counterparts which consistently failed to converge to the desired outcome. Utilizing simulation outcomes with a specific approach as well as general statistical analysis, our results showed that "social" learning versions achieved the desired outcome with greater frequency than "individual" learning algorithms. Moreover, our findings indicated that both "social" and "individual" learning variants required substantial experience to reach the desired outcome, with a notable increase in the number of simulations required in comparison to traditional methods. Additionally, our data revealed that learning outcomes were significantly affected by algorithm mutation rates, alongside the expected results, showing that lower rates led to more successful simulations. Finally, our research validated the genetic algorithm component by observing that the outcomes were often the result of random chance rather than the actual learning behavior. Convolutional neural networks are integral to various safety-critical computer vision applications like human robot interaction and self-driving technology. Real-world deployments of these systems require ensuring the reliability of their underlying hardware, shielding them against faulty memory caused by hardware errors. Following the successful use of activation clipping, we have developed a prototype to demonstrate that range control can serve as a trustworthy error detection and prevention method for classifier CNNs, specifically against common memory malfunctions in a binary floating point system. We also explore non-uniform data restriction techniques that efficiently minimize silent errors and hardware-induced data corruptions. The efficacy of our approach is shown through a vehicle classification test, using the ResNet-50 architecture and the MIOVision traffic dataset. Our findings provide a promising foundation for further research into hardware resilience through machine learning and demonstrate the practicality of our method in real-world settings. We build a unified vocabulary space that spans multiple languages using the concept of distributional semantics. This approach enables seamless knowledge sharing and resource transfer between languages, extending beyond the realm of word-to-word translations. Our innovation includes aligning word clusters across languages and ensuring the consistency of semantic relationships. We achieve this by combining three types of clustering signals: (1) leveraging existing monolingual embeddings and a graph-based clustering method, (2) employing a multilingual neural language model to produce clusters that intersect at shared semantic fields, and (3) defining a set of semantic relations such as hyponymy that form a shared infrastructure across languages. Our results show substantial gains in multilingual semantic tasks including text classification, sentiment analysis, and question answering, surpassing the performance of comparison methods. Our research demonstrates the feasibility of a unified vocabulary framework and the substantial benefits it provides in tasks that require cross-lingual knowledge sharing. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/zhongjiang84/MultiSense. Our evaluation data and models can be found at https://github.com/zhongjiang84/MultiSense-Eval. Our paper is based on an extended version of our previous work presented at the 2023 ACL conference. Our semantic taxonomic resources and model checkpoints are available for public access, offering potential utility for the community in the realm of language knowledge sharing. Our evaluation code is based on the PyTorch framework. Our research spans the domain of natural language processing, specifically in the areas of distributional semantics and cross-lingual knowledge sharing. Our research question revolves around the concept that languages share a common semantic vocabulary, enabling effective knowledge transfer, although this potential is hindered by the barriers between languages. Our goal is threefold: (1) construct a unified vocabulary space that encompasses multiple languages, (2) develop a method for clustering words across languages that are semantically related, and (3) evaluate the benefits of unified vocabulary learning through various tasks and datasets. Our approach to achieving the first goal involves learning monolingual embeddings and employing a graph-based clustering method, while the second goal is accomplished using a multilingual neural language model, and the third goal is explored through text classification, sentiment analysis, and question answering tasks. Our results demonstrate the efficacy of unified vocabulary learning, revealing substantial performance gains in tasks that require cross-lingual knowledge sharing, thereby validating our research. The initial production measurement of various particles such as pions, kaons, 
protons and $\phi$ mesons in midrapidity for Xe-Xe collisions at 5.44 TeV is
reported. Extracted transverse momentum spectra and $p_{\rm T}$-integrated yields are
analyzed across several centrality intervals spanning from p-Pb to mid-central Pb-Pb
collisions based on final-state particle count. Investigating Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
with similar charged-particle counts allows for comparison of initial geometric 
properties and flow behaviour. Detailed comparison shows that collisions with the 
same number of produced particles exhibit identical radial flow behaviour, while 
initial geometry differs. Furthermore, induced radiation in lower centrality 
Xe-Xe collisions is compared to that in p-Pb collisions with similar average 
participant number, demonstrating that induced radiation is directly proportional 
to the number of participants. Experimental data is compared to Event Shape 
Selection (ESS) Monte Carlo simulations which replicate initial geometry property 
behaviour but slightly underpredict proton yields. Additionally, charged-hadron 
$p_{\rm T}$ spectra in various collisions are compared to different transport 
models including AAMPS, AMPT and UrQMD. Lastly, forward neutron coalescence in p-Pb
collisions are examined with predictions for future collisions. Physics results from 
the ALICE experiment at the LHC are highlighted based on the full data set of 
Xe-Xe collisions. The dataset enables investigation of rare proton and anti-proton 
production as well as light nuclei formation, and allows for comparison with 
current transport models. The most pronounced outcome is the observation in Xe-Xe 
and Pb-Pb collisions of proton and anti-proton correlations at smallest possible 
rapidities, not explicable by current models and likely resulting from late 
stage hadron interaction processes. The most exhaustive set of J/ψ and φ 
production measurements in Pb-Pb and Xe-Xe collisions facilitate understanding 
of quark gluon plasma properties via quantum chromodynamics. The complete set 
of midrapidity hadron and nucleus measurements in Xe-Xe and Pb-Pb collisions 
facilitate assessment of initial conditions and final state interactions in 
heavy ion collisions. The outcomes also pave the way for future LHC studies

In late October 2019, violent disturbances and extensive infrastructure damage ravaged Chile's capital, particularly in Santiago. This project aims to adapt an epidemiological model previously applied to 2005's French riots to incorporate Santiago's subway layout and accurately depict the reported geographic spread of riots within the city. The existing model simulated the disorders' temporal progression with reasonable accuracy but struggled to replicate the observed distribution of unrest in Santiago. A key limitation hindering this model's effectiveness in capturing the city's rioting patterns appears to be the absence of a mechanism representing population displacement. Two possible approaches are proposed to address this issue: introducing a simple diffusion model and incorporating a more complex perspective emphasizing social connectivity along subway lines. Although the simple diffusion model shows some promise, the socially informed variant exhibits more convincing results, successfully recreating the disorders' spatial pattern observed in Santiago. This research suggests that a biased transmission dynamic could be critical in modeling the spread of unrest, potentially with implications for understanding similar phenomena in other contexts. Furthermore, it highlights the importance of considering population displacement in future models of this type. This study is an initial step towards adapting the original epidemiological model for Santiago's riots and encourages continued development of these models through incorporation of additional data and alternative approaches. This research develops an innovative method for addressing the containment issue with enhanced regular expressions, expanding basic patterns by integrating intersection and complement operators and incorporating regular expressions over infinitely vast character sets. Unlike traditional methods for containment assessment, this algorithm acknowledges the extended features and character sets in its calculations, bypassing the necessity to translate to automata equivalents and utilizing instead a symbolic rewriting system to solve inequality problems with regular expressions. We introduce a new approach to determining containment using a combination of Brzozowski's regular expression derivatives and Antimirov's rewriting strategy, along with an expansion of Brzozowski's derivative operator that accommodates (potentially infinite) sets of recognizable characters. Furthermore, we present a new algorithm to determine containment, accompanied by a theoretical analysis of its time and space complexity. This research also introduces a new, more efficient method for solving inequality problems with regular expressions, with a corresponding evaluation of its computational complexity. We further investigate this new approach by applying it to an expanded version of the regular expression containment problem, considering subsets of regular expression operators and character sets. Mobile agents require accurate and robust localization, and to meet this demand, Visual-inertial odometry (VIO) algorithms have been developed to estimate positions and movements using both camera and inertial sensors' data. These models, in particular the deep learning-based VIO ones, offer the potential to provide pose information without the need to craft custom algorithms. Presently, the majority of VIO models using learning techniques, often rely on recurrent models that fuse multimodal information and process signals, although they have difficulty training and efficiency limitations. This paper proposes an external memory attention learning-based VIO framework, capable of efficiently combining the data from both the camera and inertial sensors for state estimation, and we demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of this model by accurately estimating the pose in various challenging scenarios, surpassing even the traditional and current state-of-the-art VIO baselines in various scenes. The proposed technique also shows the advantage of using both learning and learning-free methods to enhance the performance. Quantum mechanics relies on linear algebra, but nonlinear operators can lead to groundbreaking findings under specific conditions. In this study, we develop a new theoretical framework based on the parent Hamiltonians of the Weyl semimetal, which we call square-root higher-order Weyl semimetal, or SHOWS for short. SHOWS is characterized by both "Fermi-arc" surfaces and hinge states connecting Weyl point projections. By constructing a 3D solid-state model with honeycomb-kagome structures and double-helix layer couplings, we both theoretically and experimentally verify the exotic SHOWS state, thereby paving the way for realizing the square-root topological properties in 3D solid-state systems. In the laboratory setting, we propose possible experimental observations of SHOWS: it predicts a vanishing bulk gap of 0.085 eV, robust surface states that can be identified through ARPES, mid-gaps in the bulk as well as hinge states visible via scanning tunneling microscopy (STM), and most remarkably, show that SHOWS can own multiple Weyl point connections that generate clean "Fermi-hinge" states along the honeycomb structure direction, a prediction that can be verified via a future "Fermi surface mapping" using a novel Higgs mode scenario via terahertz spectroscopy. Show's robustness can be controlled through external fields, offering vast possibilities for realizing artificial SHOWS in silicon or Germanium based systems. All predictions await experimental verification, offering a challenging and promising future for Condensed Matter Physics. The SHOWS model also yields intriguing square-root energy spectra in a 1D nanowire system, which can be easily realized in laboratory settings. This study investigates the numerical solution to a problem of reconstructing incomplete boundary data for the time-varying Maxwell equations based on electric field measurements, where the goal is to recover missing information on an inaccessible boundary segment using data from the accessible part of a confined domain. Our focus on FedSA originates from the common obstacle encountered when attempting to exchange model data. Researchers and organizations typically invest significant resources in developing powerful neural networks but, due to data protection, cybersecurity concerns, or ownership restrictions, they cannot freely share their trained models, despite wishing to contribute to the community. To address this challenge, we propose the FedSA approach, taking it one step further as it enables a student to excel in a different task than the teachers from which it draws information. To effectively handle FedSA, we implemented a custom technique where the student model is created using a saliency-based method that allows it to selectively engage with relevant teachers and incorporate their unique features. To validate the FedSA model, we conducted comprehensive experiments under both single-task and multi-task settings, and our findings show that FedSA successfully combines knowledge from disparate sources, outperforming comparable centralized models. Moreover, our research discovered that the FedSA approach can be incredibly efficient, requiring significantly less data than traditional centralized training schemes. To further contribute to the FedSA community, we also developed a user-friendly GUI-based tool to facilitate easy verification of saliency maps, a significant improvement over the time-consuming and manual process currently used industry-wide. This innovative tool, designed to be highly accessible, can be found on the website mentioned above. For unitary dynamics generated by a time-independent Hamiltonian, we develop a crucial criterion involving two asymmetry measures that ensures a state can be distinguished from its unitary evolution with a specific error probability within a certain time. This condition enables us to rank qubit states by their distinguishability time and calculate the optimal time to release a two-level system as seen in the Landau-Zener problem. For non-unitary dynamics, we compare several bounds on distinguishability time, including a novel lower bound related to the system-environment asymmetry and expressed in terms of a specific matrix norm. Our findings are applied to a model of decoherence induced by coupling to a Markovian environment. Our research reveals that the most rapid qubit state that can be distinguished from its decoherent evolution within a given time $t$ has a characteristic time scale $\sim \min\left(\sqrt{\Delta^2 t^2 + 1}, \frac{1}{\gamma t}\right)$, where $\Delta$ represents the initial coherent phase angle and $\gamma$ denotes the decoherence rate. Superconducting quantum circuits are emerging as prominent platforms for quantum computing. For practical applications, it is essential to address material flaws causing decoherence. This study employs terahertz Scanning Near-field Optical Microscopy to analyze the local dielectric characteristics and carrier concentrations in aluminum resonators on silicon substrates, critical components of superconducting quantum processors. Utilizing a vector calibration method, we determined the terahertz permittivity near the microwave feedline and found that etched silicon exhibits higher carrier concentrations than oxide etched silicon. We further investigate methods to reduce carrier concentrations, demonstrating the utility of near-field terahertz investigations in evaluating and identifying loss channels in quantum devices. By accounting for terahertz losses, our simulations indicate that carrier concentrations in silicon can contribute significantly (up to 0.13 microseconds) to spin-flake quantum bit dephasing. This work highlights the value of near-field terahertz analysis in evaluating material properties and losses in quantum devices, showcasing the benefits of a combined terahertz and microwave investigation of Al resonators on Si substrates. In this research, we exploit SiO2 etched silicon samples to minimize carrier concentrations, and the results are useful for designing low-decoherence quantum devices, including linear accelerators and stochastic quantum simulators. This study paves the way for a comprehensive understanding of material flaws in quantum devices, emphasizing the usefulness of terahertz investigations in the quantum era. This research is a part of an ongoing project at the Max Planck Institute for Quantum Optics, in collaboration with the Walther Nernst Theoretical Physics Institute and the Chair for Experimental Physics at Ludwig Maximilian University. This work explores the long-term evolution of Venus's atmosphere, examining how its composition has been shaped by interior-exterior interactions over time. Despite significant ongoing research, key aspects of the atmosphere's formation and current state remain unclear and require interdisciplinary analysis. We examine various processes that have influenced the atmosphere's evolution, starting with volatile sources and examining interactions from the planet's core to its upper atmosphere, as well as atmospheric escape mechanisms. We also delve into the complex historical events that have contributed to the atmosphere's evolution, including the effects of impacts, magnetic field generation, and geochemical and geodynamic feedback cycles. We then outline plausible pathways for the planet's evolution, ranging from its accretion phase to its present state, using modeling and observations. These scenarios include atmospheric escape during the magma ocean phase, prolonged surface liquid water that eventually gave way to a runaway greenhouse phase, and water retained within the planet due to inefficient outgassing, leading to hydrogen entrapment in the core and mantle oxidation. We review the existing evidence and discuss the need for future research, as well as potential observations and missions required to better understand Venus's complex interior, surface, and atmospheric interactions and how they have influenced the planet's evolution and future. This report also presents three hypothetical missions that could improve understanding of the planet's core, its surface and atmosphere, and the interactions that have shaped the planet over time. We conclude by highlighting the unique lessons that can be gained from studying Venus's evolution and the potential implications for other planets within the solar system and beyond. This work is an extension of the discussion initiated during the Venus exploration workshop held at the Astronomical Society meeting in 2019. We hope this report will contribute to ongoing and future planetary science initiatives and highlight the significance of inclusive interdisciplinary research essential for advancing our understanding of Venus and other complex planets. This work has implications for future solar system and exoplanetary research, highlighting the value of inclusive, interdisciplinary research essential for advancing our understanding of complex planets like Venus. This work was funded by the National Aeronautics and Space Administration through the Venus exploration workshop at the 2019 Astronomical Society meeting. We would like to thank the workshop participants for their valuable input and contributions. We would also like to express our gratitude to the two anonymous reviewers for their constructive feedback that significantly enhanced this work. This work is dedicated to Dr. Robert Strom, a renowned planetary scientist who made substantial contributions to the field of planetary science, particularly in the study of Venus and Mars. A key point process model that depends on the past occurrences is the nonlinear Hawkes process, which is used to model relationships, both excitatory and inhibitory, between events of different types. We have investigated a nonparametric Bayesian approach to estimating the nonlinear Hawkes process parameters, obtaining results on the concentration rates of the posterior distribution. Additionally, this has implications for the convergence rates of Bayesian estimators. Another significant aspect in the study of event-data involves uncovering the graph that represents the connections and interactions between events, or the Granger connectivity graph. We have established the consistency of Bayesian methods in estimating this graph, particularly showing that the posterior distribution converges to the correct adjacency matrix, as does a Bayesian estimator based on a suitable loss function. We have further numerically validated our findings using both synthetic and real datasets of neuronal activity. Our approach and associated results can be extended to the estimation of other Markovian point processes. Our methodology and the associated data are available online for public access.
