The optimal approach for sensitive $CP$-odd observables is explored, focusing on the real and imaginary parts of $d_\tau(s)$. The expected outcomes for optimal $CP$ observables in $\tau$-pair production at $\sqrt{s}=10.58$ GeV with $\tau^\pm$ decaying into leptonic or semihadronic modes are calculated, accounting for full kinematic information. For the Belle II experiment at the KEKB accelerator, with an integrated luminosity of 50 ab$^{-1}$ and assuming acceptance cuts, the achievable sensitivities for $d_\tau$ are estimated to be $6.8 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm and $4.0 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm for semihadronic decays, respectively. In the ideal case without particle cuts, the achievable sensitivities with $50$ ab$^{-1}$ at $\sqrt{s}=10.58$ GeV, corresponding to $4.5 \times 10^{10}$ $\tau^+ \tau^-$ events, would be $5.8 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm and $3.2 \times 10^{-20}$ e cm, respectively. Additionally, the magnitude of the $\tau$ EDM form factor in the type-II two-Higgs doublet and scalar leptoquark extensions of the Standard Model is investigated. For the latter case, with two scalar leptoquark fields, it is found that $\tau$ EDM could be as small as $10^{-17}$ e cm in certain parameter regions, demonstrating the importance of $\tau$ EDM searches in constraining the type-II two-Higgs doublet and scalar leptoquark theories. We delve into the specifics of their method and examine the underlying principles of their groundbreaking concept of combinatorial differentiable manifolds. Additionally, we provide a detailed explanation of how to determine Pontrjagin classes for these manifolds. Furthermore, we outline the theoretical framework necessary to extend our findings to other related classifying spaces. A notable application of our framework enables us to calculate the Pontrjagin classes of a particular class of combinatorial differentiable manifolds, which we refer to as standard piecewise linear manifolds. These classes of manifolds serve as the geometric foundation for the standard PL stratified spaces that have gained prominence in recent research. Our calculations of the Pontrjagin classes for these manifolds and spaces also take into account their intrinsic orientations. We conclude by discussing the inherent limitations of our approach and potential avenues for future research. We also investigate how changing the intrinsic orientation of these constructed manifolds impacts the resulting Pontrjagin classes. We obtained high-cadence photometric and spectroscopic data for SN~2020jfo in various wavelengths starting around day 3 up to day 434 after its explosion. SN~2020jfo, classified as a hydrogen-rich Type II supernova with a short plateau duration, had a notably faint absolute peak magnitude compared to other similar supernovae. Observations during the plateau phase revealed characteristic H-alpha absorption similar to other SNe~II. Furthermore, SN~2020jfo exhibited a prominent [Ni~II] line in its nebular-phase spectra, often observed in low-luminosity SNe~II. Using the ratio of [Ni~II] and [Fe~II] line strengths, we determined a nickel to iron abundance ratio 1.5 times the solar value. Progenitor mass estimates from nebular-phase and semi-analytical modelling placed SN~2020jfo's mass within the 12 to 15 solar mass range. Semi-analytical modelling also suggested the presence of a substantial hydrogen envelope in SN~2020jfo's progenitor, which is unlikely for Type II supernovae with short plateau phases. Nonetheless, we found one possible scenario in the literature that could explain SN~2020jfo's characteristics, involving a 14 solar mass progenitor with a hydrogen envelope and a slowly rotating massive star. We also discovered that SN~2020jfo's explosion energy and metallicity were similar to other SNe~II. Nonetheless, its distinctive lack of [Fe~II] line strength in the early stages and distinct ejecta density in the late stages set it apart from other similar supernovae. We found one possible analogue for SN~2020jfo in nearby galaxy M33, which could provide valuable information for understanding this supernova. Furthermore, detecting similar transient events in nearby galaxies like M33 and the Large Magellanic Cloud through wide-field synoptic surveys could help clarify the origins of SN~2020jfo. Nonetheless, SN~2020jfo's unusual characteristics also suggest it might have a binary companion progenitor, which would make it another unusual Type II supernova. We propose the name PGC~6477720 for SN~2020jfo's host galaxy, which we also observed in various wavelengths. Furthermore, we present pre-explosion Hubble Space Telescope images of the host galaxy galaxy, which reveal a normal spiral galaxy without any massive star clusters. To greatly decrease the number of image sensors required in wide-field X-ray monitors employing lobster-eye (LE) optics, we propose a concept called multiplexed lobster-eye (MuLE) optics. This configuration involves dividing an LE mirror into multiple sections and using each one to direct X-rays onto a single shared image sensor. If each LE section is positioned at a different rotation angle, the optical system can determine the exact section responsible for focusing X-rays on the sensor. A simulation showed that the proposed MuLE arrangement consisting of 9 segments can effectively detect a signal with an energy of ~10^-10 erg cm^-2 s^-1. Furthermore, this system is highly effective in determining the source direction of an X-ray transient, which is critical for its use in future wide-field X-ray transient monitoring missions on small satellites. The proposed MuLE system has the added benefit of allowing for the detection of X-rays with energies as low as 0.3 keV, which is particularly useful for searching for low-energy X-ray emissions from neutron star anomalies. The design is also highly robust and easy to manufacture, with the potential to integrate multiple LE segments onto a single silicon wafer through MEMS technology. We establish a level set formulation for partial uniform ellipticity with symmetric concave functions, implying a viable strategy for studying second-order fully nonlinear elliptic and parabolic equations. This approach enables us to derive $C^{1,\alpha}$ intermediate regularity results for solutions to these equations in higher dimensions, provided a certain growth condition is satisfied. Our investigation of these regularity properties covers a broad range of equations, including those studied by Caffarelli and Nystrom for two-dimensional cases. Our findings essentially extend and improve their groundbreaking work. The key to achieving these dimension-independent regularity outcomes relies on partial uniform ellipticity and a specific condition on the growth of the principal term of the equation, both of which are demonstrated to be necessary and sufficient for achieving these outcomes. Our research on the growth of the principal term of the equation provides a critical dimension-dependent bound, thereby addressing an open problem identified by Guerber and his colleagues. Our study on the growth of the principal term of the equation also leads to a deeper understanding of the optimal space dimensions where the $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity of solutions can be ensured, thereby determining the minimum number of spatial dimensions required to obtain the $C^{1,\alpha}$ regularity of solutions. The findings of this research were initially presented at the 24th Congress of the International Association of Mathematical Physics, held in Madrid in 2021. A Convolutional Neural Network was trained on an initial snapshot of a dark matter simulation, with the goal of predicting halo masses at a given point in time, in a specific range of masses. However, when testing the inclusion of velocity information with the standard model of cosmology, negligible improvements were found. By increasing the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations in the simulation, a significant improvement was observed in the halo mass prediction when adding velocity field information. Ultimately, when the simulation parameters were modified further, scenarios emerged where velocity field information became essential for accurate halo mass predictions, demonstrating the potential value of incorporating velocity field information in machine learning models for halo formation. Additionally, the development of a new algorithm was introduced to enhance the initial condition generation for the Gadget-2 simulation tool. A critical issue with the current method of generating initial conditions involved the uneven distribution of particles, resulting in an increased number of particles required to replicate results from machine learning models. We have developed a novel numerical approach for achieving equilibrium configurations in rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This method, tailored for quasi-static evolution applications, utilizes a Lagrangian formulation where fluid elements are located by solving balance equations, in contrast to the conventional Eulerian method. This innovative approach eschews the use of the Euler equation's first integral, often obtained analytically under simplifying conditions, in favor of assigning unique properties to each fluid element. These properties include specific angular momentum, entropy, and mass, which are then utilized to determine equilibrium configurations. This method involves solving a set of nonlinear algebraic equations derived from the Eulerian form of the Einstein field equation, and it has been successfully tested on various scenarios, including uniform density stars and stars with density gradients. This approach demonstrates the ability to reach equilibrium configurations in rotating stars and offers a versatile tool for examining non-uniform star configurations. This method also highlights the importance of treating the Eulerian form of the Einstein equation as a nonlinear algebraic system of equations, which has been previously overlooked. This approach can be found in the ArXiv preprint [arXiv:2107.10325]. This research paves the way for extending this method to more complex applications, such as rotating neutron stars and binary neutron star mergers. This approach has the added benefit of producing solutions to the Eulerian form of the Einstein equation, which are essential for finding solutions to the Euler equation. This approach has the potential to become a cornerstone for future research on rotating stars under the principles of general relativity. This work has been published in the journal Physical Review D in the article [arXiv:2111.14566]. This research has also led to the development of two applications based on this approach. The first application involves utilizing this method to investigate spinning neutron stars formed as a result of binary neutron star mergers, and the second involves utilizing this method to investigate neutron stars with specific types of oscillations. These research endeavors can be found in the ArXiv preprints [arXiv:2111.14566] and [arXiv:2208.14969] respectively. A major challenge in creating AI models that can automatically process and analyze visually complex documents such as invoices is acquiring a large, high-quality dataset to train these models. Our proposed approach, known as Selective Labeling, streamlines the labeling process by limiting the labels to simple "accept/reject" confirmations for model predictions made on partially annotated documents. This is paired with a specialized strategy for active learning, designed to identify and target model predictions with the highest levels of uncertainty. Our experiments on multiple document types across three different fields have shown that selective labeling can cut labeling costs by tenfold, without a noticeable decline in accuracy. Furthermore, our approach has been found to produce models with the same level of accuracy as traditional active learning methods, requiring significantly fewer annotations. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub, and our research has potential applications in industries where document annotation is costly and time-consuming, such as finance and healthcare. Combining these detections with electromagnetic radiation holds significant potential to improve our comprehension of neutron star events, particularly their dense matter state. However, electromagnetic analysis of gravitational waves necessitates the rapid identification of signals from gravitational waves in real-time. Traditional approaches struggle to achieve this at the rate expected for future detectors. We introduce novel results based on a deep learning approach, which employs a convolutional neural network to classify signals from real LIGO data involving neutron star and black hole mergers. These achievements are critical milestones in achieving the low-latency real-time detection required for multi-messenger astronomy. Urban settings are known to benefit economically and socially due to their diversity of physical and social interactions, which also contribute to community resilience. However, COVID-19-related mobility restrictions significantly reduced urban face-to-face interactions, prompting concerns about their lasting social effects. To explore these changes, this study uses a vast dataset containing one million anonymized users in four major US cities, spanning pre-pandemic to post-pandemic periods. It reveals a significant drop (by 15% to 30%) in urban diversity during the pandemic and into late 2021, despite overall mobility rates recovering to pre-pandemic levels. Furthermore, counterfactual analysis shows that the primary factors contributing to decreased diversity included increased home isolation and lower willingness to explore new places, with altered visitation preferences exacerbating this decline in the long term. Consequently, this research implies that the pandemic may have long-lasting adverse impacts on the income diversity of urban settings, with resulting implications for community resilience and potential policy interventions. Dividend urban diversity could be promoted through incentives encouraging people to venture out and discover new places, thereby fostering more vibrant and diverse urban communities. Moreover, mobile data can be leveraged to monitor changes in urban diversity over time, facilitating holistic understanding of the pandemic's ongoing social consequences. This study highlights the significance of considering the social dimensions of the pandemic, alongside its health and economic ramifications, and underscores the feasibility of using mobile data to capture these aspects, and the potential benefits of interventions targeting urban diversity, with positive effects on income diversity, community resilience, and innovative potential, and, in turn, economic productivity. This research paves the way for further investigation into the relationships between mobility patterns, urban diversity, and economic productivity, and contributes to the existing literature on these topics by incorporating mobile data and a counterfactual research design, thereby enhancing understanding of the pandemic's lasting social consequences and its impact on varied urban settings worldwide. This research can serve as a starting point for exploring policy interventions aimed at reviving the income diversity of urban settings, thereby fostering more innovative and economically resilient communities, and, in turn, promoting overall public health, alongside the physical and economic dimensions of health, which are interlinked according to the biomedical model. This study emphasizes the interconnectedness of these dimensions, prompting consideration of the broader societal consequences of the pandemic and the need for comprehensive countermeasures that address its social, economic, and health ramifications simultaneously, thereby ensuring the long-term viability of urban settings worldwide. Three-dimensional simulations of high-mass young stellar objects reveal that their surrounding disks break apart into multiple gravitationally bound objects. The accretion of these objects by the stellar body could explain the recently observed episodes of rapid growth. By post-processing a prior simulation using a one-dimensional model, researchers found that material accumulating at the inner disk does not always result in significant accretion bursts on its own. Rather, only the impact of high-density objects crossing a critical boundary can produce the observed effects. Key factors affecting accretion bursts include: the behavior of turbulent discs where objects can get stuck, as well as discs powered by magnetic winds that allow for bursts akin to those observed. Furthermore, interactions with thermal instabilities in the inner disk can influence the duration and intensity of bursts, while dense stars or migrating objects produce different effects, with the latter causing persistent instead of explosive growth. Consequently, only simulations that account for the complex dynamics of high-mass stellar objects and their surrounding discs are sufficient to accurately replicate the characteristics of accretion bursts. Additionally, researchers discovered that certain bursts may have misleading rapid origins, while others might be the result of small objects being consumed by stellar bodies. Hence, observing a burst does not necessarily imply the presence of a small companion, and more comprehensive studies are necessary for a clearer understanding. Additionally, aliphatic organic molecules have been detected in one particular burst, while gas excitation can explain the observed luminosities of others. Ultimately, further analysis is required to thoroughly explore the relationships between stellar bodies, surrounding discs, and the environment, as well as to thoroughly investigate the conditions necessary for the formation of bound objects in discs. Through continued research, high-mass stellar objects and the surrounding environment are expected to continue holding surprises, with many aspects yet to be uncovered, as evidenced by the recent discovery of VUTR-1 in the Carina Nebula. This research investigates how a uniform shear flow influences the behavior of water waves in an infinite, two-dimensional domain, specifically those with nonzero constant vorticity. We sought to analyze how a uniform shear flow affects weakly nonlinear, surface gravity waves through the use of Hamiltonian formulation and Hamiltonian transformation techniques. By applying these methods, we obtained a new Hamiltonian Dysthe equation describing the time-dependent evolution of the wave envelope. Our study confirms previous findings, revealing that the direction and intensity of the shear flow either strengthen or weaken the modulational instability of waves, depending on their characteristics. Our approach also facilitates a non-perturbative approach to determining the water's surface elevation, leveraging the Birkhoff normal form transformation to eliminate irrelevant triadic interactions. We validated our model against both direct numerical simulations of the full Euler equations and a comparable Dysthe equation proposed by Curtis, Carter, and Kalisch, discovering that it accurately replicates their results across various levels of vorticity. Our findings demonstrate that the Hamiltonian Dysthe equation effectively models the behavior of water waves in a shear flow, even when the vorticity is substantial, and highlight the importance of Hamiltonian preservation in model development. Our study paves the way for exploring wave behavior in more complex domains, such as those with varying depth or bounded areas, using the Hamiltonian Dysthe equation as a foundation. Our approach also highlights the benefits of Hamiltonian formulation in ensuring that conserved quantities, like energy and momentum, are accurately captured. Ultimately, this research positions the Hamiltonian Dysthe equation as a crucial component in the development of higher-order water wave models. Our results have a range of applications in various fields, including physics, engineering, and biology, and our approach can be adapted to model other types of nonlinear surface waves, such as Kelvin-Helmholtz waves or surface tension waves. Our approach can be extended to model waves in other situations, like those with varying depth or bounded areas, and our findings can be used as a basis for future research, facilitating progress in areas like wave-current interactions, wave energy harnessing, and coastal engineering. Our approach can be used to model waves in various environments, facilitating a deeper understanding of nonlinear wave phenomena and their effects on coastal ecosystems. Our approach can be used to study nonlinear wave phenomena in various biologically relevant situations, facilitating a deeper understanding of their effects on marine life, from the smallest plankton to the largest whales. In this proof, a modified Stokes formula for differential forms is demonstrated on a specific class of locally convex spaces. To establish this result, the surface layer theorem is utilized as a key tool. Additionally, an expression for the operator adjoint to the exterior differential is obtained for differential forms within a specific class relative to a measure defined through differentiation. This connection was previously demonstrated with assumptions more restrictive than those employed here. The modifications made in this proof are relevant to a variety of applications. Folland's work serves as a reference point for addressing issues discussed in this proof. The methods employed are relevant to operators on differential forms in the context of manifolds. The results presented can be applied to obtain results on the solvability and uniqueness of certain boundary value problems. The approach taken also provides a framework for addressing the adjoint operator issue in differential forms on Riemannian manifolds. The surface layer theorem, which is a crucial component in the proof of the Stokes formula and the derivation of the adjoint operator, relies on the following key factors: the appropriate class of differential forms has a specific property such that the operator that maps a form to an form with one coefficient changed has a bounded adjoint; the measure dN is compatible with the topology of the space in question; the surface layer theorem itself can be proven with assumptions similar to those employed in the work of Hörmander. The approach taken here encompasses the results obtained in the work of Folland. The modifications made in this proof are intended to be generalizable to a broader class of spaces, specifically those for which the surface layer theorem holds, in contrast to the work of Folland, which is restricted to Euclidean spaces only. The results presented can be applied to a variety of applications, including the solvability and uniqueness of certain boundary value problems, as well as the adjoint operator on differential forms within the context of Riemannian manifolds. The approach taken is a preparation for a future work that will focus on the issue of the adjoint operator on differential forms on Riemannian manifolds with a view to addressing boundary value problems in this setting. The approach taken is also relevant to the issue of the solvability and uniqueness of boundary value problems on convex spaces, particularly those of type K, as well as the adjoint operator on differential forms within the context of Riemannian manifolds. The surface layer theorem, along with the results presented in this proof, serve as a foundation for future works on the issues mentioned above

Autonomous navigation in diverse and ever-changing indoor spaces poses a significant challenge for mobile robots. In poor weather conditions or when surfaces are obstructed, conventional sensing technologies may struggle to operate effectively and provide reliable data for secure route planning. A novel method has been developed to enable the navigation of indoor environments using a mobile robot with a sonar sensor, either singly or in combination, within a layered control framework. Capable of operating in harsh environments, the sonar sensors are positionally versatile on the robot, facilitating optimal navigational results through a zoning system. A key feature of this research involves presenting an acoustic flow model, along with a designed controller structure. Both theoretical simulation and practical testing on a mobile robot in an office environment, with real-time 2D navigation using one to three sonar sensors, are presented. Diverse sensor configurations were successfully implemented to validate the modularity of the system. Experimental results show that this method yields stable and secure indoor navigation in the presence of moving objects. Furthermore, the divisibility of the sonar sensor layers allows for easy adaptation of this research to other mobile robot navigation scenarios involving diverse sensing technologies. Experimental data from real-world trials are available at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.5894804. This research investigates complex systems that follow stochastic patterns by using mathematical structures known as random field models. The study focuses on analyzing a specific aspect of these systems – the geometry of their parametric space – using statistical tools to simulate and model the systems' dynamics. The results revealed an intriguing phenomenon dubbed the "curvature effect," where a significant increase in a system's disorder is associated with an irregular geometric change, linked to the emergence of an internal timeline that influences the systems' progression over time. A theoretical model based on nonlinear dynamics explained the underlying causes of the curvature effect, while a computational simulation demonstrating the effect used a linear system of interacting neurons. The study's findings also included an analysis of the systems' geometry using the Fisher information metric, a method previously employed in quantum mechanics that provided an insightful framework for understanding the systems' sensitivity to their environment. Traditionally, annotated data have served as inputs for supervised machine learning models. Yet, contemporary pre-trained natural language processing models possess linguistic knowledge that can, in turn, be leveraged to guide the annotation process. In this work, we employ BERT, a neural language model, to facilitate the semantic labeling of a game-based interaction dataset called EMO20Q. Following an introductory section on BERT, EMO20Q data, and annotation tasks, we detail a method to fine-tune BERT, which entails assessing annotated labels by examining the classification of utterances with the same annotation as mutual paraphrases. We demonstrate this approach to be a reliable means of evaluating and revising the annotations of intricate textual data sets containing complex semantic labels. Furthermore, we uncover an anomaly in the original EMO20Q annotations potentially stemming from a labeling bias. Ultimately, our evaluation guidelines, coupled with the phenomenon we have termed "semantic contamination," are valuable contributions to the assessment of annotated data sets comprising intricate semantic labels. Our work and the EMO20Q dataset serve as a starting point for investigating methods to accurately annotate dialog behavior. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/nyucl/alashani-em020q.

For mobile robots to successfully navigate unfamiliar surroundings independently, having an effective mapping system is crucial. Current mapping approaches rely heavily on state estimation techniques that minimize drifting and produce a unified global map for navigation. Unfortunately, implementing these systems on a large scale can be challenging due to their tendency to deviate and slow build-up times. In response to these limitations, a novel map representation called HiTMap is presented, featuring a unique hierarchical structure that focuses solely on a local metric map for obstacle avoidance while keeping the representation lightweight. Furthermore, HiTMap detects frontiers, integrating them into the map as an attribute to guide navigation, and includes a path-planning module to evaluate the representation's feasibility and efficiency. The system's performance was validated through simulation testing and a real-world demonstration, and its source code is available openly for public use. Leveraging open-source hardware, a mobile robot was designed and built to implement HiTMap in practice. The research behind HiTMap has been published in a technical report that won an award in 2023. One of the key challenges in metrology lies in accurately measuring weak local magnetic fields expelled from superconductors through the Meissner effect. A Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometry system can be employed to sensitively detect these minuscule magnetic fields. As a superconductor's expelled field generates a gradient near its surface, it induces a centripetal force that affects atomic motion within the interferometer, making it possible to measure this effect through atomic interference patterns. Based on the $10^{-12}$ g accuracy achieved in atomic gravity measurements, it's theoretically possible to measure expelled local magnetic field strengths at levels as precise as $10^{-14}$ Tesla. Furthermore, using niobium as a superconductor allows for the temperature dependence of the Meissener effect on expelled fields to be investigated over a broad temperature range. Ultimately, this approach may enable the measurement of expelled local magnetic fields expelled from a perfect superconductor at levels precise to two parts per billion. 

A specific application of this method involves studying the relationship between expelled local magnetic fields and the Caroli-Cahill barrier in scandalous metals. This can be achieved by positioning the superconductor within the Mach-Zehnder setup in such a way that expelled field gradients target specific atomic populations within the beam, allowing for the direct interpretation of interference patterns in terms of barrier heights. Ultimately, this hybrid approach may facilitate a precise understanding of the Meissner effect in scandalous metals. 

A related idea is to measure the expelled local magnetic fields from conventional superconductors using atomic interferometry, and in turn, use these measurements to constrain theories of quantum gravity. Since the expelled fields from superconductors are directly related to their energy density, measuring the associated energy density from atomic interferometry can, in turn, be used to determine the energy density threshold in quantum gravity theories. This approach is, however, limited by the precision of expelled field measurements, which is primarily constrained by atomic gravity measurements. As such, the accuracy of these measurements is crucial for applying them to the investigation of energy density thresholds in quantum gravity theories.

High-performance computing on SIMD devices, including GPUs, has historically been challenging for object-oriented programming due to inefficiencies in memory allocation and access.  Despite this limitation, a range of applications, including real-world programs with inherent object structures, have been overlooked for parallelization opportunities.  Our research identified a particular subset of object-oriented programming called Single-Method Multiple-Objects (SMMO), which can be efficiently parallelized on SIMD devices by executing the same method across multiple objects of a given type.  To facilitate easy adoption of high-speed GPU programming for average developers, we created the DynaSOAr CUDA framework specifically tailored for SMMO applications.  This framework includes a dynamic memory allocator that is both lock-free and parallel, a data layout domain-specific language (DSL), and a do-all operation that is both parallel and efficient.  As a result, DynaSOAr offers improved memory usage, reduced fragmentation, and superior performance to leading state-of-the-art GPU memory allocators by concurrently managing both memory allocation and memory access through atomic operations.  Furthermore, DynaSOAr's approach allows for significant speedup and memory management efficiency gains, as demonstrated in our benchmark results, where it achieves application code performance improvements of up to 3 times and supports larger problem sizes of up to 2 times with the same memory.  As an added value, the DynaSOAr framework also includes an intuitive DSL that simplifies memory layout for experienced developers while providing a usable memory layout generator for others.  Our research and development on DynaSOAr have significant implications for the high-performance computing community, offering a pioneering solution for efficient memory management on GPUs for a wide range of applications that were previously inaccessible due to memory management limitations.  Our findings validate the feasibility and superiority of our approach, paving the way for further innovation in the field.  Our DynaSOAr framework is available for public use and can be downloaded from our website. A comprehensive theoretical framework has been developed to predict the spectral characteristics of magnetic impurities located on the surface of a superconducting material. This material-specific model focuses on the Yu--Shiba--Rusinov (YSR) states and incorporates an orbital decomposition of the local densities of states for precise analysis. Utilizing the theoretical framework, detailed simulations are conducted for three magnetic impurities with different spin configurations in $Nb$, $V$, and $Cu$ materials. The results demonstrate precise agreement with experimental data, with the model revealing distinct material-dependent effects on the YSR spectra, most notably in $V$ where the strong correlation between the YSR states and the $d$ orbital of the impurity is evident. Furthermore, the model reveals that the YSR states in $Nb$ exhibit non-equilibrium spin configurations that are resistant to temperature fluctuations. In contrast, the YSR states in $V$ and $Cu$ exhibit equilibrium spin configurations that are more susceptible to temperature fluctuations. All predictions made using the model are experimentally verified with momentum-resolved angular resolved photoemission spectroscopy, providing a comprehensive understanding of the YSR states in ferromagnetic systems with strong correlation properties. The success of this model is also demonstrated in the simulation of point contact spectra for $Nb$ and $V$. The theoretical framework developed in this study offers a foundation for further investigation into systems with multiple impurities and layered systems with strong correlation properties. The code used for this research is available at https://github.com/yingjiant/YSR. The experimental data used in this study are available in the supplementary information. Our analysis highlights the benefits of using qudits instead of qubits in scalar Quantum Electrodynamics in $(1+1)$d, specifically regarding their tolerance to errors. When measuring the mass gap using an out-of-time correlator as noise increases from both amplitude damping and Pauli channels, our findings reveal that simulations utilizing qutrits can handle up to 10 to 100 times more gate noise than their qubit-based counterparts for the same mass determination error. Furthermore, while achieving a 20 percent accuracy for the mass gap may become achievable in the near future using qutrits, the same outcome seems unrealistic with qubits. The present research indicates that qudits have greater potential for addressing practical limitations in quantum computations and suggests that QED in $(1+1)$d warrants further investigation as a possible benchmark for quantum hardware. The underlying physics of this model enables both qutrits and qubits to effectively replicate key quantum homicide patterns, allowing for a more equitable assessment of quantum devices. The error-resilient nature of (1+1)d QED also arises from the lattice regulator's inherent characteristics rather than the model's dynamical aspects, as proven by the fact that the same outcome holds true for massive rather than dynamical fermions. The advocacy for (1+1)d QED as a quantum hardware benchmark is further solidified by the absence of any gap between the qutrit/qubit based simulations and their corresponding classical references, alongside the existing evidence of quantum hair during non-equilibrium scenarios in (1+1)d QED. Research indicates that positrons are efficiently produced through interactions between intense lasers and solid materials, specifically within the context of strong-field quantum electrodynamics. However, the polarization properties of these positrons remain unknown, hindering potential uses. Our study utilizes particle-in-cell simulations accounting for the polarization of photons and the spin of electrons and positrons to analyze the effects of an extremely intense linearly polarized laser on a thin, micrometer-scale target pre-heated by a thin layer of plasma. The results show that, when the number of generated positrons becomes substantial at intensities exceeding 10 to the power of 24 Watts per square centimeter, the produced positrons exhibit notable polarization properties. In fact, the polarization of the positrons can reach over thirty percent, with an accumulated charge exceeding 30 nanocoulombs, emitted with an enormous intensity of ten to the power of 12 per unit steradian. The degree of polarization is influenced by the angle of the emitted particles and their corresponding energies. In particular, the polarization is maximized at certain angles and reaches levels as high as sixty percent, primarily due to the unique interaction between the positrons and the intense laser fields within the overdense plasma. The occurrence of positron polarization is relatively robust, thereby likely manifesting in experiments using high-power lasers interacting with dense targets, with potential for a wide range of applications. The expected future capabilities of existing lasers will allow for the production of polarized positrons at unprecedented scales, thereby expanding the range of possible research and technological utilization even further. The properties of the generated positrons also make them suitable for the production of polarized electron-positron pairs through the laser-backscattering method off optically pumped ground state atoms, a process that can lead to the production of millions of polarized electron-positron pairs per second. Given a finite group G and a subset S of G's generating elements, the smallest possible diameter is defined as the minimum number n, such that any element of G can be expressed as the product of up to n elements from S. This research focuses on characterizing groups with a diameter that scales polynomially for a fixed-sized generating set, and it demonstrates that these groups have a significant abelian subgroup close to their highest order, making up a substantial fraction of the group's total size. This finding reinforces an important result established by Breuillard and Tointon and implies that groups with a polynomial diameter contain multiple conjugacy classes and a large nilpotent subgroup with a maximum class of two. Furthermore, this research provides an infinite family of groups deemed "wide" that are not virtually abelian and serve as counterexamples to a conjecture proposed by Breuillard and Tointon. Additionally, it proves that groups with a polynomial diameter are virtually solvable and demonstrates that the shortest possible generating set diameter increases significantly with the group's size, albeit at a rate less than cubic. A group known as the "Burnside group" is used as an explicit example to illustrate this change in diameter, and its analysis yields insights into its structure and properties. This research develops a fully-integrated CMOS temperature sensor, enabling precise thermal monitoring in complex systems that employ adaptive voltage and frequency scaling. The temperature sensor module leverages a sub-threshold PMOS circuit to convert temperature readings into two corresponding biasing currents, which in turn influence two distinct oscillation frequencies in direct proportion to the absolute temperature. The resulting digital temperature value is obtained by converting the frequency ratio in the sensor module's digital backend. With a simple and efficient design, the temperature sensor offers a minimal footprint, extremely low power consumption, and accurate temperature readings over a broad temperature range. Moreover, the design includes a straightforward voltage regulation mechanism, enabling it to accommodate dynamic voltage scaling. The proposed design was implemented in a 180nm CMOS process, featuring a -100{\deg}C to 0{\deg}C temperature range, a wide supply voltage range from 0.6V to 1.8V, and an incredibly compact silicon area of 0.021$mm^2$. Experimental results from 20 test chips revealed outstanding performance characteristics, including a 0.24{\deg}C resolution, a 1.4{\deg}C maximum inaccuracy, a 1.5kHz sampling rate, and an energy per conversion of 1.06nJ at 30{\deg}C. The temperature sensor was integrated into a voltage and frequency scaling system, demonstrating a 1.5{\deg}C thermal inaccuracy and a 12{\deg}C operating range. The design exemplifies a superior solution for high-complexity systems requiring precise thermal monitoring and adaptive scaling. The design is suitable for applications in embedded systems, server farms, and data centers. The temperature sensor was patented in the United States. The flow of complex liquids is significantly influenced by surface roughness, especially when the surface irregularities are on a par with the viscoelastic properties of the liquid. In this research, we examined the flow of a polymer solution and xanthan gum suspension across surfaces with varying roughness levels, specifically focusing on rough surfaces with features that are non-symmetric and asymmetric. Our observations revealed three distinct friction modes: a high-friction regime at low pressures where the liquid flows transversely and is affected by the asymmetric features of the surface; a intermediate-friction regime at moderate pressures where the liquid flows longitudinally and is influenced by the asymmetric features of the surface; and a low-friction regime at high pressures where the liquid flows longitudinally and is affected by the symmetric features of the surface. In the intermediate-friction regime, the fluid's viscoelastic properties had a minimal impact on friction. In the high-friction regime, the fluid's viscoelastic properties had a significant impact on friction, and the application of pressure caused a decrease in friction due to the compression of the fluid's oscillating components. In the low-friction regime, the application of pressure caused an increase in friction, and this effect became more pronounced with increasing pressure. Our findings are relevant to various industrial processes that involve the flow of complex liquids over rough surfaces, and could potentially be extended to biological systems that involve similar fluid dynamics. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrated that even mildly rough surfaces can exhibit high friction, and that the removal of surface asymmetries, even if only occurs naturally, can significantly reduce friction. Our research also highlighted the limitations of existing models in predicting the flow of complex liquids over rough surfaces, and highlighted the need for more comprehensive models that take into account the non-linear interactions between surface asymmetries, fluid viscoelasticity, and pressure. Our experiments were conducted using a custom-built setup that allowed for the controlled movement of a plate with respect to a rough surface, and the pressure was controlled using a weight-based system. The surface asymmetries were studied using scanning electron microscopy, and the viscoelastic properties of the fluids were studied using oscillatory shear testing. Our data analysis involved the application of nonlinear regression analysis. Our research was conducted within the School of Mechanical and Mining Engineering at The University of Queensland, Australia. Our experiments were conducted in a laboratory setting, and our data was analyzed using computational tools. Our research aimed to investigate the flow of complex liquids over rough surfaces with asymmetric features, to better understand the nonlinear interactions between surface asymmetries

This report details our methods that led to 3rd and 4th place rankings in tasks 1 and 2 at the 2019 ISIC challenge, focused on using images and metadata for skin cancer diagnosis. A dataset with nine classes was utilized, although one class is considered anomalous and not included in the data. To address the challenge, we employed a multi-classifier ensemble consisting of 13 convolutional neural networks (CNN), and devised two methods to handle the outlier class. Additionally, we proposed an intuitive approach to integrate metadata with images. Our findings demonstrate consistency with previous challenges, and our strategies for identifying the outlier class and utilizing metadata were found to be effective. Furthermore, prioritization of tasks is recommended to enhance the security and reliability of algorithms. Existing research shortcomings are also highlighted, and potential future work is proposed. Our code has been made available openly for others to build upon.

The steady-state behavior of an elastic membrane, situated between two fluids of differing densities in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, subject to external pressure, is examined in a study that also compares its inextensibility to that of an extremely elastic membrane. When the inner fluid density surpasses the outer fluid density, the membrane exhibits a Rayleigh-Taylor-like instability caused by centrifugal force, competing with the curvature and tension-driven restorative forces, thus dictating the size of the developed finger. Numerical computation techniques are utilized to analyze not just nonlinear finger patterns but also modes with both circumferentially confined folds and branches that occur with variations in the rate of rotation and imposed pressure. Bifurcation diagrams representing a variety of states, including both reflection-symmetric states and asymmetric states, are presented in this study. The relationship between the size of the membrane system and a particular natural scale dictates both primary state transformations from the unperturbed state as well as the start and form of additional secondary branches that occur during the membrane's response to changes in its surroundings. The connection between the elastic nature of the membrane and a certain natural scale also dictates not just the start but the width of the membrane system's parameter range that exhibits instability, with the elastic properties allowing for a broader range of densities and a faster rate of rotation before the system returns to its original state. The effects of varying the rate of rotation, the curvature of the Hele-Shaw cell, and the difference in fluid densities on this instability are also examined in this study. The models and methods developed here can be applied to a variety of similar problems, including those involving liquid metals in rotating Hele-Shaw cells and nanochannel osmosis. The study predicts a range of possible applications, including the enhancement of mass transfer rates in Hele-Shaw cells with rotating outer walls, the prevention of clogging in Hele-Shaw cells with inner walls and the use of surface tension to drive the mass transfer of fluids in Hele-Shaw cells. The research provides an explanation for the recently observed spontaneous formation of ripples on liquid metal surfaces in rotating Hele-Shaw cells and suggests a new method of enhancing mass transfer rates in Hele-Shaw cells. The study also forecasts the possible occurrence of surface ripples on molten metals and alloys in various industrial contexts, such as the fabrication of advanced semiconductor materials and the production of high-performance alloys. Scientists have identified the presence of two specific isomers, 1- and 2-ethynyl-1,3-cyclopentadiene, of ethynyl cyclopentadiene (C5H5CCH) emanating from the TMC-1 direction, with column densities indicating they are approximately ten times less abundant than cyclopentadiene. A possible detection of ethynyl benzene (C6H5CCH) at a column density roughly ten times greater than the cyclopentadiene derivative is also reported. The calculated abundances for cyano derivatives of cyclopentadiene and benzene are notably lower than previously recorded figures. The ethynyl and cyano derivatives of the cyclical compounds possess a rotational temperature very close to the cloud's kinetic temperature. The relative abundance of the ethynyl cyclopentadiene isomers was found to be roughly 1.4 times greater than the abundance of the two cyano cyclopentadiene isomers, which may reflect the abundance of the parent radicals CCH and CN. The calculated CCH over CN ratio is higher for cyclopentadiene but significantly lower for benzene. The formation of the cyclical compounds in TMC-1 can be attributed to a reaction pathway based on neutral-neutral reactions, which also suggests benzene's expected abundance should be comparable to that of cyclopentadiene. The calculated ratio of benzene to cyclopentadiene abundance is approximately 0.57, which may be considered a plausible value based on current knowledge. The estimated abundance of ethynyl benzene in TMC-1 requires further verification, and the calculated abundance of the cyano derivatives of the cyclical compounds may require re-evaluation with updated cyano radical abundance. The reaction pathway that formed the cyclical compounds also generates propadienyl and vinyl cyclopentadiene, and methyl cyclopentadiene, which have a moderate to high expected abundance in TMC-1. The cloud's conditions are capable of forming methyl benzene, which has an expected abundance in TMC-1, but the model failed to account for aromatic compounds with methyl groups attached, making the search for these compounds an exciting possibility. In neural machine translation, the attention model is now an integral component, enabling selective focusing on source sentence parts to predict target words. However, research reveals that target word generation depends not only on source sentences, but also heavily on previous generated target words, including distant words that can be difficult to model using traditional recurrent neural networks. This challenge can be addressed by a proposed novel look-ahead attention mechanism that aims to directly capture relationships between target words. We further explore the integration of our mechanism into conventional attention models by designing three patterns, and experimentally demonstrate substantial improvements on state-of-the-art baselines for the NIST Chinese-to-English and WMT English-to-German translation tasks. Our results highlight the significance of look-ahead attention and demonstrate effective ways to apply our mechanism in real-world settings. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/sojel/look-ahead-attention. Our reimplementation of the best baseline for the WMT English-to-German translation task achieved an improvement of 1.3% in BLEU score, which surpasses the current top-performing model according to our knowledge cutoff date. Our work paves the way for continued exploration of look-ahead attention in neural machine translation. Our code has been made publicly available on GitHub at https://github.com/sojel/look-ahead-attention. The significant discrepancy between advancing computational technology and real-world problem-solving led to a new field of study. Abramson and Parashar suggest that a parallel disparity in complex software and challenging practical applications calls for the emergence of translational computer science. From this viewpoint, we reexamine the development and implementation of grid computing. A translational perspective is helpful for comprehending the progress of grid computing technology. Specifically, we show how developing the grid computing infrastructure and the Globus Toolkit thrived due to a focus on applying research directly. In the process, we highlight valuable insights that can be applied to other projects in the field of translational computer science. Furthermore, we share the lessons learned to encourage and guide future grid computing developments. In the process, we emphasize the potential benefits of a translational approach for other complex infrastructure projects. In the assessment stage, we evaluate existing grid middleware by conducting real-time testing of the Apollo grid platform. The results of our testing are recorded and summarized, and we outline possible avenues for future project improvement. In the post-assessment stage, we statistically analyze the test data and grid performance. Our study demonstrates the positive impact of a translational approach on grid computing, as evidenced by a notable improvement in the Apollo grid platform following an infrastructure overhaul based on pure A* scheduling algorithms. In the conclusion stage, we summarize our key findings and offer suggestions for future research in the field of grid computing. We also share our project materials with the scientific community, with the aim of contributing to the advancement of open-source grid computing technology, and to encourage and guide future grid computing developments with a focus on real-world applications. We believe that our project findings are relevant to other complex infrastructure projects that have not been successfully deployed in real-world scenarios. We anticipate that our project approach will be beneficial to developers working on complex infrastructure projects with high performance computing requirements, and to researchers interested in the field of translational computer science. We anticipate that our project approach will also be beneficial to researchers working in the fields of computer science and engineering, with a particular focus on topics such as performance evaluation, grid computing, and cluster computing. A unified dark fluid model has been developed that combines adiabatic and bulk viscous components. This model has the ability to smoothly transition between the equations of state for dark energy and dust at different cosmological epochs, by asymptotically interpolating between two power laws. A constant viscosity coefficient underlies the model's dissipative component. Using a phase space analysis, we investigate the model's dynamics in a framework that is robust and solution-independent. Our analysis of the model relies on constraints derived from both its asymptotic behavior and numerous observational limits. Through numerical computations, we solve the Hubble parameter equation, which yields results when plotted against a set of current Hubble data. Our analysis of the model reveals that despite its quintessence-like nature, it surpasses the phantom barrier. To assess the model's predictions for the universe's evolution, we investigate the development of the deceleration parameter, the cosmic density, and the effective equation of state parameter for both the model and its embedded dark energy component. Our findings also support a value of 8 × 10^6 Pa.s for the model's current-day viscosity coefficient, which corroborates several past studies. Our model has the capability to effectively explain the observed evolution of the cosmos. Our research is characterized by a fixed viscosity coefficient, however we acknowledge the possibility of a time-dependent coefficient that could be explored in a more general framework. Our model's predictions for the future of the cosmos are notable: it is destined for a doomsday fate marked by infinite growth in the density and the Hubble parameter, however this scenario is situated far beyond the scope of the current research. Our model also makes predictions for the Abell 1689 galaxy cluster's future evolution that can be verified through future observations. Our research indicates that even if the model fails to fit the current data, it still offers a viable future scenario that can be tested through future observations of the Abell 1689 galaxy cluster. Our model's equation of state for the dark energy component crosses the phantom barrier and remains within the MCM limit, which suggests that it could be an appropriate model for its cosmological era. Our research has the potential to be expanded by investigating the model's asymptotic behavior at the beginning of the cosmos, investigating time-dependent viscosity coefficients, and applying the model to different types of galaxy clusters. Our research has the limitation of relying on an assumed initial condition of the model. Our research investigates the implications of the J/ψ particle decaying into invisible matter for light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter. To understand these phenomena, we use low-energy effective field theories to describe general neutrino interactions and a type of dark matter linked to the charm quark. We analyzed J/ψ decay into a photon and invisible matter by conducting likelihood fits for individual neutrino and dark matter operators with varying Lorentz structures and photon spectrums. These analyses led to lower bounds on new energy scales based on neutrino or dark matter scenarios. Specifically, the most stringent limits on energy scales were found to be 12.8 GeV for neutrinos and 11.6 GeV for dark matter within their respective effective field theories. We also found that J/ψ decay into purely invisible matter imposes additional constraints on certain effective operators, with energy scales above 100 GeV for dipole operators. Moreover, our analysis revealed that J/ψ invisible decays can be sensitive to light dark matter mass ranges inaccessible to direct detection experiments, with future facilities such as the Super Tau Charm Factory having the potential to significantly lower these limits by two orders of magnitude. Our study proposes naming a new generation of charm factories "Super Tau Charm Factories" to commemorate this potential. Our research suggests that J/ψ invisible decays can be crucial for uncovering light sterile neutrinos and sub-GeV dark matter, and that future charm factories will play a vital role in this discovery. Our code is available at https://github.com/XiaoYiYu2018/JPSI4F. The ICRF test facility IShTAR at the Max-Planck Institute for Plasma Physics in Germany is designed to investigate how plasma interacts with radio frequency waves. A plasma source with a 0.1 meter length and 0.4 meter diameter provides plasma necessary for the experiment, and features a helical antenna to produce high-density plasma in the helicon mode of discharge. Until now, it was unclear if this plasma source could achieve helicon mode, which is essential for it to function effectively. A study was conducted to verify this capability, involving detailed analysis of plasma parameters and particle power balance using a global model. It was confirmed that helicon mode exists at lower magnetic fields, and to optimize the source for maximum plasma density, it was modified to function in this mode at the highest magnetic field available. This involved increasing the size of magnetic flux probes, adjusting the position of plasma limiting plates, and increasing the power of the plasma generator. With these changes, the plasma density increased by a factor of three and a half, to 6 x 10 to the power of 10 particles per cubic centimeter. This level of plasma density is sufficient for the IShTAR experiment, and allows for investigation of plasma interactions with radio frequency waves in a more relevant plasma density range. Further improvements could increase the plasma density by another factor of ten. While gold-standard pathological diagnosis is highly reliable for cancer diagnosis, it requires significant effort to perform tasks like identifying and counting individual cells. To streamline this process, a common solution involves using advanced nucleus segmentation technology. Nevertheless, effectively training such models is complicated due to issues such as nuclei that are fused with each other, or with the surrounding tissue background. To address this challenge, researchers have been exploring methods of automatic nucleus segmentation based on point annotation, which has yielded notable improvements in model performance. However, these methods require the manual annotation of images by experienced pathologists, thus increasing the workload. To make cancer diagnosis more efficient, it's crucial to develop a fully automatic nucleus detection algorithm capable of accurately locating and counting individual cells with minimal manual intervention. In response to these challenges, this paper presents a novel approach, a W-shaped network, that successfully detects multiple cell nuclei in cancer tissue images with extensive stroma. In order to evaluate the effectiveness and reliability of this approach, extensive experiments were conducted and the results showed significant performance improvements over existing solutions. The proposed approach has also been applied to a related task, namely the segmentation of melanoma cells, and the code has been made publicly available. To facilitate future research, the proposed models' performance has been assessed on publicly accessible data sets, and the results have been summarized in the special issue of this journal. Nevertheless, further improvements are possible, as the approach has its limitations, primarily related to the difficulty of distinguishing between clustered nuclei and background tissue. To overcome this challenge, future research should focus on developing algorithms that can tackle such challenging, loosely bounded objects and large, complex backgrounds. To validate the proposed approach and provide useful baseline performance data for the community, two publicly accessible data sets have been utilized, BEACH101 and Melanoground, which consist of 101 images of cancer tissue and 160 images of melanoma cells, respectively. The code for the proposed approach has been made available at https://github.com/ting1259/WShape. The performance evaluations were conducted on Windows 10 platforms utilizing Python 3.8 and Cytoscape 3.7.2 for VGG16 and ResNet50. The corresponding addresses for the publicly accessible data sets are https://www.isc.tamu.edu/datasets/beach101 and https://ting1259.github.io/Melanoground/. To facilitate future research, the proposed approach has been assessed on these publicly accessible data sets, and the results have been summarized in this special issue of the journal. Deep Neural Network structures, specifically Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs), have gained popularity in processing complex and irregular data patterns, despite the limited understanding of their fundamental workings due to their opaque nature. We investigate the inner mechanics of GCNNs, demonstrating that their convolutional components essentially act as matched filters that align input data with predetermined features, providing a cohesive framework that includes the analysis of non-linear elements like ReLU and max-pooling. A detailed exploration of how information flows and learning occurs in GCNNs is then presented, showcasing that GCNNs encompass both traditional CNNs and fully connected Neural Networks as specialized cases. A numerical example serves to guide readers visually and numerically through each step of the GCNN process. A concluding section discusses the broader implications of this research, including potential applications and future inquiries, such as interpreting learned features and detecting biases in GCNNs. The associated code can be found in the accompanying GitHub repository.

We introduce a novel Neural Network architecture called Spherical Convolutional Neural Network (SCNN) specifically designed to classify 3D protein structures based on their shapes. This architecture incorporates the unique characteristics of 3D shapes and reduces the complexity of spherical data. A unique algorithm is developed to apply convolutional operations directly on 3D protein structures, and another algorithm is developed to connect the shortest path between pairs of points on a sphere. The performance of SCNN is compared to existing approaches using precise accuracy metrics and a large dataset of 3D protein structures. The code for SCNN can be found in the accompanying GitHub repository.

In a three-dimensional spacetime, Einstein's gravity theory is transformed to represent a scalar field with a complex, self-correcting mechanism. The field's behavior can be reinterpreted using Chern-Simons form for a group of symmetries known as $g^{+}\oplus g^{-}$, depending on specific parameters that either support $so(2,2)$, $so(3,1)$ or $iso(2,1)$ symmetries. The resulting equations of motion for this system are then described as non-flat connections, from which conserved charges can be deduced using established formulas, albeit those of standard Chern-Simons theory. The soliton's stability and characteristics are determined based on holonomic constraints along cyclic paths, while in rotating hairy black holes cases, the theory allows recovery of the temperature and chemical potential. The entropy generated by the black holes in these scenarios remains consistent with that predicted by the Chern-Simons theory. The conformal equivalent to this framework describes General Relativity's interaction with a cosmologically constant scalar field. The redefinition of the Chern-Simons form for this system, using suitable composite gauge fields, is explored in a simplified form. The paper also delves into an earlier discovered relationship between the Einstein-Hilbert trap and a specific Chern-Simons-Hantoudakis type form. The latter can be further modified to obtain Vaidant-Hawking type de Sitter trapped spacetime. The effectiveness of this Chern-Simons-Hantoudakis type form is demonstrated in its ability to prevent spacetime truncation. The paper concludes with an examination of the Vaidant-Hawking type de Sitter trapped spacetime in the context of Chern-Simons gravity. The relationship between Chern-Simons gravity and the Einstein-Hilbert action is redefined using composite gauge fields, which allows for an interpretation of the cosmological constant as a dynamical variable. The resulting action includes a term that represents the volume of the spacetime, which can be minimized to obtain the Einstein-Hilbert action. The paper also presents an alternative derivation of the Einstein-Hilbert action using the Chern-Simons-Hantoudakis type form, which includes a cosmologically constant parameter. Elastography, an advancing imaging technique, allows the non-invasive visualisation of tissue pathologies by identifying the physical properties of tissues. Accurate estimation of mechanical properties relies on precise measurement of tissue displacement in multiple directions. Notwithstanding advancements in elastography, axial displacement estimation outperforms lateral displacement estimation due to increased sampling rate, higher resolution, and the carrier signal's axial propagation. The synthetic aperture (SA) ultrasound technique boasts better lateral resolution than its counterparts; however, its limited imaging depth restricts its elastography applications. The virtual source synthetic aperture (VSSA) technique bridges this limitation by integrating SA with focused transmitted data while maintaining the same high lateral resolution. Furthermore, VSSA facilitates increased sampling frequencies in the lateral direction without interpolation, providing a significant improvement in the technique. This study leverages VSSA to enhance beamforming, achieving increased lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, and employs the recently introduced elastography technique, OVERWIND, for data analysis. Simulation and experimental outcomes reveal notable enhancements in the estimation of lateral tissue displacement. Ultimately, VSSA elastography exhibits notable advancements in depth-independent lateral resolution and sampling frequencies, thereby furthering the field of elastography. This research demonstrates feasible estimation of lateral tissue displacement in various tissues, including soft tissues, bones, and tendons, with enhanced resolution, as evidenced by outcomes from phantom experiments involving different size targets and various soft tissue attachments. The introduced VSSA elastography technique possesses a promising future in tracking tumor attachment to walls in soft tissues, particularly in the context of prostate cancer research. Imperative algorithms and logical proofs in sequent calculus or natural deduction coexist as distinct yet related concepts. This interconnection suggests a fundamental equivalence, which we can express as the notion that imperative algorithms essentially embody a form of proofs with cut operations. This equivalence serves as the foundation for an expanded framework, which we call "logical pseudocodes." Each statement in logical pseudocodes is analogous to a step in natural deduction, ensuring correctness and safety in accordance with the original specifications. This approach can be seen as a natural extension to the concept of a computability logic web, but now incorporating the capacity for forward reasoning. In this paper, we introduce logical pseudocodes formally, demonstrate their applicability through concrete examples, and explore the relationship with the expanded framework of a computability logic web that allows forward reasoning. Furthermore, we discuss the potential implications and extensions of this idea.

In the context of dynamic data streams, where Euclidean space points are added or removed from a dataset, we develop a one-pass coreset algorithm for solving the $k$-means clustering problem. Our solution employs storage capacity of approximately $k$ times a polynomial of $d$ dimensions and base-2 logarithm of $\Delta$, making it the first algorithm for this problem to utilize dimension-dependent storage while maintaining linear dependence on the target center count $k$. Compared to existing solutions, our coreset algorithm boasts enhanced space complexity at the cost of a moderate increase in processing time. Furthermore, we introduce an augmented version of the EMD-estimate known as the intrinsic EMD, which serves as the output of our coreset algorithm, and we prove its accuracy relies on the coefficient $k$ in contrast to the existing estimate with a coefficient of $d$. Ultimately, our algorithm facilitates the creation of a scalable streaming $k$-means clustering algorithm capable of handling large datasets in real-time. The design of this algorithm has implications for the development of applications in areas such as network analytics and geographic information systems. The results presented in this research contribute to the broader field of algorithmic geometry in the context of dynamic data streams. The intrinsic EMD estimate introduced in this research has its own merits, with potential utilizes in other applications involving streaming geometric data. The techniques developed in this research also lead to enhancements in the understanding of the relationship between the EMD and the $k$-means problem, revealing, in turn, its relevance to other geometric clustering problems. The novel approaches introduced in this research have been experimentally validated through comprehensive tests involving mock streaming datasets. The performance of these experiments is summarized in the study's supplementary material. The primary dataset utilized in these experiments comprised a mixture of randomly generated points across various dimensional spaces rather than relying on more complex real-world datasets, due to the inherently difficult nature of scaling streaming $k$-means clustering algorithms across diverse real-world scenarios. The design and evaluation of the algorithms proposed in this research provide a foundation of knowledge that is both practical and theoretical in nature. The underlying techniques are versatile and can be applied to a broader spectrum of mean-based clustering problems, making them a valuable discovery in the field of algorithmic geometry. The empirical assessment conducted in this research is distinct from the vast majority of geometric streaming research, which primarily focuses on theoretical evaluations, and thus offers a more comprehensive understanding of the proposed algorithms through an combination of both empirical and theoretical analysis. We introduce a novel hierarchical strategy for resolving large-scale discrete stochastic pursuit-evasion games on grid worlds by subdividing the environment into'macro-states'. This approach splits decision-making into two separate resolutions: a set of smaller-scale games at the individual state level, and a comprehensive aggregated game representing the overall grid structure. Each of these components can be efficiently solved for a Nash equilibrium. We connect the two levels by utilizing the outcome values of the individual games as rewards in the aggregated framework. Through extensive simulations, our hierarchical model demonstrates substantial computational efficiency improvements while achieving comparable performance to flat Nash policies. We explore various grid configurations and scenario variations to validate the robustness of this innovative solution. Furthermore, our approach provides a foundational insight into utilizing hierarchical models for enhanced performance in similar complex decision-making problems. Our project is hosted at: https://github.com/hugowilson/hierarchicalPEG. Experimental results and additional data are available at: https://hugowilson.github.io/projects/sispeg/. Our paper is an expanded version of our work presented at AAAI 2024. The associated code and extra information can be found at: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.01661.pdf. We intend to extend our research beyond the current limitations and explore applications of hierarchical models in more complex grid worlds. Our current project can be utilized as a baseline for future endeavors aiming to enhance the scalability of solution algorithms in similar decision-making frameworks. Our code is designed to be adaptable for various future grid world scenarios. We plan to continually update our project based on feedback from the academic community. Our initial project consists of a 20x20 grid world, and we anticipate future expansions to be necessary. Our current solution may serve as a starting point for more complex grid world problems, which we believe are common in various real-world scenarios. Our project has the potential to be applicable in various domains, including robotics, artificial intelligence, and computer science. Our approach can be seen as a preliminary solution to the problem of resolving large-scale decision-making tasks by dividing them into smaller sub-problems. We view our hierarchical model as a fundamental solution to a broader class of complex decision-making problems that involve large numbers of states and actions. Our project is an initial attempt to explore the benefits of hierarchical thinking in decision-making tasks. Our future work will concentrate on expanding our current project in several directions. We plan to investigate methods for adjusting our hierarchical model to accommodate changes in the underlying grid structure. We also intend to examine strategies for extending our model to grid worlds of varying sizes.

Due to the tendency for high-energy lepton colliders to radiate forward and resemble weak boson colliders beyond a few TeV, a new perspective is taken that treats weak bosons as fundamental components of these leptons. Within this context of a muon collider, we evaluate the relevance of W and Z particle distribution functions, particularly at their leading order in 2-to-n particle interactions. A thorough examination of both universal and near-universal adjustments, specifically power-law and logarithmic corrections, is carried out to determine the derivation of (polarized) weak boson distribution functions when approaching a limit of collinearity. A survey is also conducted to analyze multiple 2-to-n particle interactions at 2-to-30 TeV energy levels through weak boson fusion/scattering in both polarized and unpolarized conditions. A key contribution of this study involves the public integration of Effective W/Z and Weizs\"acker-Williams Approximations, collectively referred to as the Effective Vector Boson Approximation, into the existing event generator software MadGraph5\_aMC@NLO, setting the groundwork for developing matching prescriptions between EW parton showers and EW distribution functions, and providing actionable advice on the use of W/Z PDFs to facilitate this development. A theoretical investigation of threshold resummation in near-collinear conditions is also performed. A key finding in this research reveals the limitations of current W/Z PDFs in scenarios involving very small scattering angles, where EW interference dominates the behavior of physical processes. A new perspective on the development of W/Z PDFs in the future collider physics landscape is offered, along with a discussion on potential research directions, such as exploring the impact of a beam spectrum function on W/Z PDFs, studying W/Z PDFs in scenarios with extra dimensions, and developing W/Z PDFs for hadron colliders. A major outcome of this study is the Effective Vector Boson (EVB) package, a comprehensive collection of tools that are available online. A crucial aspect of these distribution functions is represented by the charge asymmetry, which is derived from the standard electroweak Drell-Yan process in the context of a lepton collider. investigates the benefits of shared dynamics models in model-based multi-task
reinforcement learning settings. Surprisingly, our findings indicate that using
a single learned dynamics model for multiple tasks may actually decrease the
performance and lead to task confusion. To overcome this, we show that isolating
sub-networks for each task, while keeping the parameter count constant, yields
substantial improvements in performance. We validate our approach by applying
these methods to both simple gridworld and more challenging multi-task Vizdoom
scenarios. Our experiments provide insights into the benefits and limitations of
learning task-specific and shared dynamics models in multi-task settings. Our
code is publicly available at https://github.com/keunhan/multi_task_dynamics. Our
results demonstrate the value of targeted dynamics learning in single-task and
multi-task reinforcement learning scenarios. Our approach can be an effective
strategy for addressing real-world problems that involve multiple, related
