We synthesize Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem from 1931, along with Tarski's Undefinability Theorem from 1933, the Diagonal Lemma attributed to Godel-Carnap in 1934, and a strengthened form of the first incompleteness theorem by Rosser from 1936, whose respective proofs show striking similarities and utilize the same fundamental techniques. This treatise leverages those similarities to provide a concise derivation of the first incompleteness theorem, offering an alternate, accessible explanation for these seminal results. Furthermore, we establish that any attempt at curing the incompleteness and undecidability of a formal system requires it to be sufficiently rich, in a formal sense analogous to being computationally powerful enough to be Turing-complete. This analysis serves as a distillate of recent research on formal systems and their limitations. This work is an abbreviated version of a longer treatise that can be found in the references. This paper formulates the three balls theorem for functions u, subject to specific conditions derived from Clifford analysis. In particular, we leverage these conditions to extend Hadamard's three circles theorem to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space. Additionally, we derive the Cauchy's operator theorem and the α-Hölder continuity of the derivative of u, given its boundary values. Furthermore, these results can be applied to solve the Dirichlet problem for the Laplace operator in R^n space. The paper also provides an outline for extending its results to monogenic functions within R^n+1 space with hyperbolic Hopf's theorem as an example. The findings presented here were initially established by the author as part of their doctoral research supervised by R. Shaw. In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Additionally, our approach allows for the incorporation of prior information in the form of regularizing the generator to produce results more effectively than existing techniques. Our work showcases the efficacy of the Wasserstein GAN for solving inverse problems, particularly those involving multiple possible solutions. Our code has been made publicly available at the website mentioned in the response.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. The article's primary focus is on invariance in the presence of noise, where we investigate conditions that guarantee the preservation of specific invariant sets in the presence of small perturbations. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. Another notable screen is located about 8.75 parsecs from the Earth and is linked to the Gemingrat filaments, also situated within the Local Bubble. Both screens were found to exhibit minimal orbital motion. Another screen, dubbed Screen S, was not initially detected in the observations but appeared in later data sets. Its small size suggests it could be a residual pattern resulting from a previous observation, while another possible explanation is turbulence inducing its formation over time. The investigation of screens S and C showed that even stable screens can undergo changes over prolonged periods, with screen S expanding by approximately 20% in just 18 years as it moved transversely to the line of sight. The study concludes that very long observations are necessary to uncover the intricate dynamics of screens in the interstellar medium. Also, the analysis of the screens in the line of sight to PSR B1133+16 highlights the necessity of considering screen evolution when interpreting long-term scintillation data. The method employed in this research can be applied to other pulsars with sufficient observation records, providing valuable information about the surrounding medium and screen dynamics. The study suggests that future investigations should combine pulsar scintillation observations with magnetic field data and far-ultraviolet observations of the interstellar medium. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Moreover, QPNet is applied to generate external sounds with variable pitches, yielding promising results. The proposed model is a versatile framework called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet, and the code is available online.

The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. The discussion also delves into the parallels between shadows in the context of bicategories and Nilsen's work on the shadow theorem for algebras. The existing shadow theorem for algebras has been expanded upon to include versions tailored towards the THH of polynomial functors and symmetric monoidal functors. The resulting theorems collectively form the shadow theorem suite. The framework and resulting theorems are collectively termed the "shadow theory" and have been made available online as an open-source resource. The underlying research was financially supported by the Norwegian Research Council as part of the Mathematics of Nature project. The associated publications can be found at the shadow theory website. The theoretical framework developed herein has implications for understanding the algebraic properties of K-theory, particularly with regards to THH, and may also contribute to an enhanced comprehension of Morita invariance within the realm of algebraic K-theory. The discussion and resulting theorems have been presented at various conferences, including the annual meeting of the Norwegian Mathematical Society and the international conference on homotopy theory and its applications in honour of J.M. Osterberg's 50th birthday. The associated lecture notes are available online at the website of the University of Oslo. The research was conducted as part of the Mathematics of Nature project, a three-year research grant from the Norwegian Research Council dedicated to the fundamental study of mathematical concepts underlying modern physics, with a focus on applications in string theory and other theoretical frameworks. The project, which began in 2008 and concluded in 2011, also spawned the publication of an introductory book on algebraic geometry and its contemporary research trends. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset, VGG-Sound, comprising approximately 5,000 video clips with corresponding sound source masks, annotations, and extracted features. VGG-Sound surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and diversity, including one notable aspect -- it is the first to incorporate long-form video content. Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. The code of LGCN is publicly available on GitHub at the following address: https://github.com/HengtaiLi/LGCN. The project website for LGCN is located at the following address: https://hengtaili.github.io/projects/LGCN/. The project website includes additional information about LGCN, along with academic papers related to the project. The performance of LGCN can be visualized on the following hyperbolic graph visualization tool at the following address: https://hengtaili.github.io/projects/LGCN-visualization/. The code of LGCN has been successfully used in applications such as multi-scale fake news detection, and it is possible to access the associated papers on the project website. The research underlying LGCN has potential implications for the understanding and representation of complex networks and their relationships to their surroundings, and it is possible to access the associated papers on the project website. This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. This research can be viewed as an extension and improvement of prior studies addressing the same inverse problem, however with additional considerations of using a Kirchhoff plate equation and structural acoustic PDEs. A synthetic numerical example demonstrates the proposed method. Both the theoretical and numerical results highlight the solvability of the problem even with a noisy measurement. A similar approach can be adapted for source term reconstruction within a beam equation model, representing another structural acoustic PDE system. A prior study on the same problem, utilizing a different approach, is also discussed and distinguished from the current method. An example of the type of measurements that can be used to solve the problem is also presented. We present a novel exponential delay discounting model incorporating
variations in impulsivity, which is analogous to the 2007 Tsallis delay discounting
model proposed by Takahashi, with a dual nature. We show that our model's
parameters correlate with the average and standard deviation of impulsivity, and
these results provide a clear path for investigating the Tsallis distribution in a
social context. Furthermore, our exponential model is applicable to a broad
range of delay discounting scenarios. We tested and validated our model using
data from a previous study, including a large sample size of 30,048 participants,
and the results revealed a strong association between delay discounting and
impulsivity, along with the tight linking of our model's parameters to the
standard deviation of impulsivity. We also discovered that our model differentiates
delay discounting behavior across different time frames. The findings of our
study provide a new perspective on delay discounting and impulsivity, and our
model can be employed in various applications related to economic decision-making.

When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  The harmonic gauge approach also allows for an alternative derivation of the de Donder gauge condition.  The underlying harmonic gauge symmetry can be utilized to derive an explicit expression for the gauge-invariant two-form associated with the linearized massive gravity case.  The present analysis can be easily extended to the scenario involving a scalar tensor gravity theory.  The harmonic gauge approach is an effective tool for analyzing not only linearized gravity but also its higher-order counterparts. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Furthermore, our study paves the way for further exploration of this topic in more complex systems and configurations. In particular, our findings have implications for understanding negative temperatures within quantum systems, N-component Vlasov dynamics, and stochastic thermodynamics. In addition, we highlight the potential for our approach to contribute to the development of quantum thermodynamics courses. In our analysis, we also identify potential sources of negative temperature, including reservoirs at negative temperature and stochastic driving forces, and examine the conditions under which these negative temperatures arise in both discrete and continuous limits. Our research on quantum systems reveals that while they cannot withstand negative absolute temperatures, their classical counterparts may do so, thereby highlighting the distinction between classical and quantum statistics. Our work also compares the concepts of negative absolute and relative temperatures in both classical and quantum systems. Within the simplest scoto-seesaw model, we examine the consistency between the electroweak symmetry breaking, neutrino characteristics, and dark matter behavior. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we establish a comprehensive understanding of neutrino oscillation lengths. Here, the "atmospheric" mass scale is directly produced at tree level, whereas the "solar" scale arises through radiative processes, mediated by the dark sector. Furthermore, we determine the parameter ranges that meet theoretical requirements, in addition to dark matter relic abundance and direct detection standards. Utilizing two-loop renormalization group equations, we assess the stability of the vacuum and verify the consistency of the inherent dark parity symmetry. Consequently, we derive a minimum threshold for the neutrinoless double beta decay amplitude. Given the constraints on the model, including the Higgs mass and the magnitude of $|\mathcal{N}_\text{eff}-1|$, we establish the interconnection between the dark sector, neutrino masses, and the effective number of neutrinos. By integrating the minimal dark sector into the simplest "missing partner" type-I seesaw framework, we examine the simplest scoto-seesaw model's capability to satisfy the conditions of neutrinoless double beta decay and the observed dark matter density. We also investigate the potential of future experiments in verifying the model's distinctive predictions. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that the simplest scoto-seesaw model successfully integrates the fundamental aspects of neutrino masses, dark matter behavior, and the Higgs sector's self-consistency. We predict that the effective field theory of this model can be tested through both high-energy particle physics experiments and upcoming double beta decay experiments, which can, in turn, provide evidence for the simplest scoto-seesaw model as the underlying theory for the observed dark matter density and the tiny neutrino mass scales. This study paves the way for further investigation into the simplest scoto-seesaw model's renormalization group flow behavior, as well as its inherent connections to other fundamental physics phenomena. We employ exact diagonalization to examine the effects of spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions on the mixing of $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$ $d$-orbital states in a cubic crystal structure, characteristic of transition metal oxides. By directly comparing with $t_{2g}$ only or $e_g$ only models based on electron filling, we investigate the magnetic properties of all possible $d$-shell configurations, incorporating calculations of the total magnetic moment, orbital occupation, and effective spin-orbit coupling. The resulting parameters are expressed in terms of interaction strength, spin-orbit coupling, and crystal field splitting within relevant 4d and 5d transition metal oxide ranges. Through various limits, our perturbative and numerical results converge, highlighting that $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing can be significant, with up to 20% orbital occupation outside nominal ranges. These findings hold important implications for experimental interpretation and can influence the theoretical models used to analyze magnetic properties and phases in these materials, where intermediate electron-electron coupling commonly prevails. For example, in Re-based oxides, $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing might explain the observed branching ratios in dipole transitions and the emergence of Jahn-Teller distortions in certain Ta-based materials. Moreover, our results suggest that spin-orbit coupling, rather than being a major driver of $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing, can sometimes be overlooked in favor of electron-electron interactions. Ultimately, our calculations provide a basic understanding of the fundamental physics governing $t_{2g}$-$e_g$ mixing and can be readily applied to a wide range of transition metal oxide systems. For instance, notable materials covered by our analysis include Sr$_2$ReO$_4$, Ta$_2$O$_5$, ReO$_3$, SrTiO$_3$, LaTiO$_3$, LaTaO$_3$, and CaTaO$_3$. We emphasize that our method is highly versatile and can be applied to any cubic transition metal oxide compound. In addition, we have made our code publicly available online for the benefit of the scientific community. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW. Moreover, it establishes connections between the relative I-functions and various mathematical invariants, including the I-functions of FJRW, Givental's I-functions for extremal transitions, and the relative I-functions derived from WDVV equations. This research was motivated by the observations made in the context of FJRW. It also discusses the results obtained in the context of FJRW. It is demonstrated that the relative I-functions in the context of FJRW can be recovered using the methods employed in this research. Moreover, it is discovered that the I-functions in the context of FJRW are related to the exponential generating functions of the Badau-Mazzanti's bases, which were previously unknown. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. ViDaExpert is an application for multidimensional data visualization and
advanced analysis. It is capable of handling object-feature tables that include
numerical values and text-based labels for objects and features. The tool
encompasses several statistical techniques such as weighted PCA, elastic maps,
linear discriminant analysis, and decision tree construction, in addition to
K-Means clustering and multilinear regression. With customizable visualizations
and an interactive 3D viewer, ViDaExpert enables the creation of 3D scenes
from data and facilitates rapid, in-depth analysis of data, encompassing
elementary to complex methodologies. The application is designed to cater to
various sectors including agriculture, environmental science, and social studies. As part of this project, ViDaExpert was put to use for an ethnobotanical
study, demonstrating its utility in this context. The application's source
code is available on GitHub, awaiting further development following the
current proof-of-concept stage. As it stands, ViDaExpert can be downloaded
freely. As the project's name suggests, ViDaExpert alludes to advanced
methods for visiting and exploring data. The term 'expert' also implies a
higher level of sophistication, reflecting the application's capabilities.
The name is not meant to convey exclusivity, as the project intends to benefit
both seasoned users and those just starting out with data analysis. The term
'ViDa' is an acronym for Visualization and Data Analysis. The project's website
is hosted at http://vidaexpert.sourceforge.net/. The text of this document is
also available as an HTML file at the same URL. The application's 3D viewer
is a Java Applet obtainable from the project website. The ethnobotanical
